questions.loText: Calculate the value of a firm’s debt and equity, the volatility of firm value, and the volatility of firm equity using the Merton model.
questions.source: Workbook A5.2 • S5, S7 • Map #2 • options in ascending order (workbook key C)
questions.question:
A fixed-income portfolio manager at a European insurer is valuing a block of a company’s zero-coupon debt using Merton’s model. The CRO also wants to know how leverage transmits asset shocks to the shareholders. Inputs:

- Value of assets: EUR 50 million; asset volatility: 30%
- Face value of debt due in 3 years: EUR 40 million
- Risk-free rate: 2% per annum, continuously compounded

Which of the following is closest to the market value of the company’s debt today, and to the approximate instantaneous return on the company’s equity if the value of its assets falls by 6%?

options.text: Debt EUR 33.6 million; return on equity −14.4%
Debt EUR 33.6 million; return on equity −18.3%
Debt EUR 35.0 million; return on equity −15.8%
Debt EUR 37.7 million; return on equity −14.4%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 –** $d_{1}$ **and** $d_{2}$

$d_{1} = \frac{\text{ln}(50/40) + (0.02 + 0.30^{2}/2)(3)}{0.30\sqrt{3}} = \frac{0.2231 + 0.1950}{0.5196} = 0.8047, d_{2} = 0.2851$

$$N(d_{1}) = 0.7895, N (d_{2}) = 0.6122$$

**Step 2 – Equity value**

$$E_{0} = 50(0.7895) - 40\text{e}^{-0.06}(0.6122) = 39.475 - 37.671(0.6122) = 16.41$$

⇒ The shareholders’ call on the assets is worth EUR 16.41 million.

**Step 3 – Debt value**

$$D_{0} = V_{0} - E_{0} = 50 - 16.41 = 33.59$$

⇒ Versus a risk-free value of $40\text{e}^{-0.06} = 37.67$: an expected loss of (37.67 − 33.59)/37.67 = 10.8%.

**Step 4 – Leverage ratio and multiplier**

$$\frac{V_{0}}{E_{0}} = \frac{50}{16.41} = 3.046, N (d_{1})\frac{V_{0}}{E_{0}} = 0.7895 \times3.046 = 2.405$$

⇒ Each 1% move in asset value moves equity by about 2.4%. The same multiplier gives $\sigma_{E} =$ 2.405 × 30% = 72.2% (eq. 9.5).

**Step 5 – Return on equity**

$$\frac{\Delta E}{E_{0}} \approx N (d_{1})\frac{V_{0}}{E_{0}} \frac{\Delta V}{V_{0}} = 2.405 \times(-6\%) = -14.4\%$$

**Interpretation**

Debt is worth EUR 33.6 million; creditors are effectively short a put on the assets. The leverage ratio of about 3 is damped by the delta $N (d_{1})$ because part of any asset loss is absorbed by the creditors’ put; a 6% asset loss becomes roughly a 14.4% equity loss. The three-year horizon is no obstacle: the model is defined for any $T$ .

**LO:** CR-9 l: Calculate the value of a firm’s debt and equity, the volatility of firm value, and the volatility of firm equity using the Merton model. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.8, eqs. 9.4 and 9.5, Example 9.4

CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A5.2 • S5, S7 • Map #2 • options in ascending order (workbook key C) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 l.10)

b.reason: Used the raw leverage ratio without the delta: 3.046×(−6%) = −18.3%, treating equity as if it absorbed every asset loss.

c.reason: Did not discount the strike: $E_{0} = 50(0.7895) - 40(0.6122) = 14.99$, so debt = 35.01 and the multiplier becomes 0.7895 × 50/14.99, giving −15.8%.

d.reason: Reported the risk-free PV of the promised payment, $40\text{e}^{-0.06} = 37.67$, as the debt value, ignoring default risk.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate distance to default and default probability using the Merton model.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.8 and 9.8.3 • shapes A5·S1, S6
questions.question:
A credit analyst at a Korean bank converts each corporate borrower’s Merton distance to default into an internal band. The bank’s policy specifies the full-form distance to default, $d_{2}$, computed with the risk-free rate over the life of the borrower’s debt:

- Bands: DD of 3.0 or more: A; 2.0 to below 3.0: BBB; 1.0 to below 2.0: BB; below 1.0: B
- Borrower (KRW billion): value of assets 500; zero-coupon debt of 300 due in 2 years; asset volatility 22%; equity volatility 50%; risk-free rate 4% (continuously compounded)

Which of the following gives the borrower’s distance to default and band?

options.text: DD 0.48; band B
DD 1.74; band BB
DD 2.05; band BBB
DD 2.32; band BBB

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Numerator over the two-year life**

ln$(500/300)+(0.04-0.22^{2}/2)\times2 = 0.5108+(0.04-0.0242)\times2 = 0.5108+0.0316 = 0.5424$

**Step 2 – Two-year standard deviation**

$$\sigma_{V} \sqrt{T} = 0.22\sqrt{2} = 0.3111$$

**Step 3 – Distance to default and band**

$d_{2} = \frac{0.5424}{0.3111} = 1.74 \Rightarrow$ band BB

⇒ The risk-neutral two-year PD is $N(-1.74) = 4.1\%$.

**Interpretation**

The two-year horizon matters: the one-year short form would put the borrower a full band higher. The 50% equity volatility is a red herring; it only calibrates $\sigma_{V}$ .

**LO:** CR-9 m: Calculate distance to default and default probability using the Merton model. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.8 and 9.8.3; Workbook A5 (Map #2: “finding distance to default and assign a rating based on the score”)

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.8 and 9.8.3 • shapes A5·S1, S6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 m.3)

a.reason: Used the equity volatility in place of asset volatility: (0.5108 + (0.04 − 0.125) × $2)/(0.50\sqrt{2}) = 0.48$, band B.

c.reason: Reported $d_{1} = d_{2} + \sigma_{V} \sqrt{T} = 1.74 + 0.31 = 2.05$, band BBB.

d.reason: Used the one-year short form ln(500/300)/0.22 = 2.32, ignoring the drift and the two-year horizon: band BBB.

questions.loText: Calculate distance to default and default probability using the Merton model.
questions.source: Workbook A5.1 • S3, S4, S7 • Aug-2026 • Map #2
questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Singapore bank is estimating the risk-neutral default probability of a corporate borrower using Merton’s model. The bank’s CVA desk stores each counterparty’s default risk as a constant average hazard rate, so the analyst must also convert the Merton output. The asset value and asset volatility have already been solved from the equity data:

- Value of assets $V_{0}$: SGD 150 million; asset volatility $\sigma_{V}$ : 25%
- Zero-coupon debt due in 2 years: SGD 120 million
- Risk-free rate: 3% per annum, continuously compounded

Which of the following is closest to the two-year risk-neutral probability of default and the corresponding average hazard rate per year?

options.text: PD 16.4%; average hazard rate 9.0%
PD 26.6%; average hazard rate 15.5%
PD 26.6%; average hazard rate 13.3%
PD 33.0%; average hazard rate 20.0%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 –** $d_{1}$

$$d_{1} = \frac{\text{ln}(150/120) + (0.03 + 0.25^{2}/2)(2)}{0.25\sqrt{2}} = \frac{0.2231 + 0.1225}{0.3536} = 0.9776$$

**Step 2 –** $d_{2}$ **(distance to default)**

$$d_{2} = d_{1} - \sigma_{V} \sqrt{T} = 0.9776 - 0.3536 = 0.6241$$

⇒ Assets need to fall about 0.62 two-year standard deviations for default to be triggered.

**Step 3 – Risk-neutral PD**

$$Q(2) = N (-d_{2}) = N (-0.6241) = 0.2663$$

⇒ A 26.6% risk-neutral probability that $V_{T} < D$ at year 2, so the equity call option is not exercised.

**Step 4 – Average hazard rate**

$$\bar{\lambda} = -\frac{1}{T} \text{ln}(1 - Q(T )) = -\frac{1}{2} \text{ln}(1 - 0.2663) = \frac{0.3096}{2} = 0.1548$$

⇒ A constant default intensity of 15.5% per year reproduces a 26.6% two-year cumulative default probability.

**Interpretation**

Because the PD comes from an option pricing model with assets growing at $r$, both numbers are risk-neutral, which is the right type for a CVA desk (valuation). The two-year horizon is no obstacle: the drift is multiplied by $T$ and the volatility by $\sqrt{T}$.

**LO:** CR-9 m: Calculate distance to default and default probability using the Merton model. CR-9 e: Define the hazard rate and use it to define probability functions for default time as well as to calculate conditional and unconditional default probabilities. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.8 and 9.8.3; 9.2.1 eq. 9.2

CR-10 • Credit Value at Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A5.1 • S3, S4, S7 • Aug-2026 • Map #2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 m.9)

a.reason: Used $N (-d_{1}) = N (-0.9776) = 0.164$ instead of $N(-d_{2})$; the hazard rate $- \text{ln}(1 - 0.164)/2 = 0.090$ inherits the error.

c.reason: Correct PD, but divided the cumulative PD by $T$ : 0.2663/2 = 0.133. This ignores survival compounding in $Q = 1 - \text{e}^{-\bar{\lambda} T}$ and understates the hazard rate.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratingsbased (IRB) approach.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.10, 10.2 and 10.4 (footnote 7); Workbook A31 and D20 notes • shape
questions.question:
D20·S3

The head of model validation at a bank is reviewing an internal memo on how Basel II IRB capital uses Vasicek’s model. Which of the following statements in the memo is correct?

options.text: In the IRB implementation, the maturity adjustment is the channel through which downgrade risk enters, because Vasicek’s model itself counts defaults only.
Vasicek’s model captures losses from both downgrades and defaults, which is why regulators chose it for IRB capital.
Because it uses a Gaussian copula, Vasicek’s model generates strong tail dependence between defaults in a crisis.
Under Advanced IRB each bank sets the correlation $\rho$ from the equity-return correlations of its own obligors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Vasicek’s model counts**

GARP 10.4: “Vasicek’s model and Credit Risk Plus estimate the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults. The impact of downgrades is not considered.” Footnote 7 adds that the maturity adjustment does allow for downgrades in the regulatory implementation.

⇒ A is correct, and B is the sibling swap with CreditMetrics.

**Step 2 – Tail dependence and who sets** $\rho$

GARP 10.2: the model “incorporates very little tail correlation”. Under IRB the correlation comes from the Basel formula for each asset class, not from the bank.

⇒ C and D are false.

**Interpretation**

This is the D20 audit format: three statements each borrow a true fact from the wrong place (CreditMetrics’ downgrades, a fat-tailed copula, an economic capital calibration), and one states the regulatory link correctly.

**LO:** CR-10 d: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratings-based (IRB) approach. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19 (GARP CR Ch.10), 10.2 and 10.4 with footnote 7; Carey, Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis (ORR-21), The IRB Approach

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10, 10.2 and 10.4 (footnote 7); Workbook A31 and D20 notes • shape (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 d.6)

b.reason: Sibling swap: downgrades plus defaults is CreditMetrics. Vasicek counts defaults only.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the Gaussian copula has little tail correlation; another copula is needed to add it.

d.reason: Scope error: equity correlations calibrate a bank’s own economic capital model. Under Foundation and Advanced IRB alike, $\rho$ is set by the Basel formula.

questions.loText: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratingsbased (IRB) approach.
questions.source: Workbook A31.2 • S2 • Aug-2026 • numerical, kept outside the TYPE rule
questions.question:
A model validation analyst at a UK building society is checking the IRB risk-weighted assets reported for its residential mortgage book. The data are:

- EAD: GBP 400 million
- Average one-year PD: 1.50%; average LGD: 25%
- Average remaining contractual maturity: 18 years
- Confidence level 99.9%; Basel II retail treatment applies

Which of the following is closest to the risk-weighted assets for this book?

options.text: GBP 163.2 million
GBP 182.0 million
GBP 191.9 million
GBP 575.5 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Correlation**

Residential mortgages use the fixed retail correlation $\rho= 0.15$.

**Step 2 – WCDR**

$$z = \frac{N^{-1}(0.015) + \sqrt{0.15} \times3.0902}{\sqrt{0.85}} = \frac{-2.1701 + 1.1968}{0.9220} = -1.0556$$

WCDR $= N (-1.0556) = 0.1456$

⇒ In the 99.9th percentile year, 14.56% of the mortgage pool defaults.

**Step 3 – Capital (no maturity adjustment for retail)**

$K = 400 \times0.25 \times(0.1456 - 0.0150) = \text{GBP} 13.06$ million

**Step 4 – RWA**

RWA $= 12.5 \times13.06 = \text{GBP} 163.2$ million

**Interpretation**

A risk weight of 163.2/400 = 40.8%. The 18-year maturity is a red herring: retail exposures carry no maturity adjustment.

**LO:** ORR-21 f: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach. CR-10 d: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratings-based (IRB) approach. • **Reference:** Carey, Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis, Retail Exposures Under IRB; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19, 10.2

**Source:** Workbook A31.2 • S2 • Aug-2026 • numerical, kept outside the TYPE rule (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 d.8)

c.reason: Applied the corporate correlation formula ($\rho= 0.1767$): WCDR = 0.1685, RWA = 12.5 × 100 × (0.1685 − 0.015) = 191.9.

d.reason: Applied a maturity adjustment with $M = 18$ ($b = 0.1215$, MA = 3.526), which retail does not have: 163.2 × 3.526 = 575.5.

questions.loText: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratingsbased (IRB) approach.
questions.source: Workbook A31.1 • S1 • Aug-2026 • numerical, kept outside the TYPE rule
questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at a German universal bank using the Advanced IRB approach is computing the Basel II capital for a single corporate term loan. The data are:

- EAD: EUR 250 million
- One-year PD: 0.80%; LGD: 40%
- Remaining maturity: 4 years
- Correlation from the Basel corporate formula; confidence level 99.9%

Which of the following is closest to the required capital for this loan?

options.text: EUR 11.8 million
EUR 14.4 million
EUR 15.1 million
EUR 18.4 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Correlation weight and corporate correlation**

$$w = \frac{1 - \text{e}^{-50\times0.008}}{1 - \text{e}^{-50}} = 0.3297, \rho= 0.12(0.3297) + 0.24(0.6703) = 0.2004$$

⇒ About 20% of each obligor’s asset variance comes from the single systematic factor.

**Step 2 – Argument of** $N (\cdot)$

$$z = \frac{N^{-1}(0.008) + \sqrt{0.2004} \times3.0902}{\sqrt{1 - 0.2004}} = \frac{-2.4089 + 1.3835}{0.8942} = -1.1468$$

**Step 3 – WCDR**

WCDR $= N (-1.1468) = 0.1257$

⇒ In the 1-in-1,000-year bad year, 12.57% of loans like this default, against 0.80% on average.

**Step 4 – Maturity adjustment**

$$b = [0.11852 - 0.05478 \text{ln}(0.008)]^{2} = 0.38302^{2} = 0.1467$$

MA $= \frac{1 + (4 - 2.5)(0.1467)}{1 - 1.5(0.1467)} = \frac{1.2201}{0.7799} = 1.5643$

⇒ A 4-year loan can be downgraded without defaulting, so capital is scaled up by about 56%.

**Step 5 – Capital**

$K = 250 \times0.40 \times(0.1257 - 0.0080) \times1.5643 = \text{EUR} 18.4$ million

**Interpretation**

RWA $= 12.5\times18.4 = \text{EUR} 230.2$ million. Expected loss, $250\times0.40\times0.008 = \text{EUR} 0.8$ million, is covered by reserves and pricing, not capital.

**LO:** CR-10 d: Describe the application of the Vasicek’s model to estimate capital requirements under the Basel II internal-ratings-based (IRB) approach. ORR-21 f: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19, 10.2 eq. 10.1; Carey, Capital Regulation Before the Global Financial Crisis, Bank, Corporate, and Sovereign Exposures Under IRB

CR-16 • Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A31.1 • S1 • Aug-2026 • numerical, kept outside the TYPE rule (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 d.9)

a.reason: Omitted the maturity adjustment: 250 × 0.40 × 0.1177 = 11.8.

b.reason: Swapped the correlation weights so that $\rho$ rises with PD: $\rho= 0.24(0.3297) +$ 0.12(0.6703) = 0.1596, WCDR = 0.1001, capital = 100 × 0.0921 × 1.5643 = 14.4.

c.reason: Used the Foundation default $M = 2.5$ (MA = 1.2821) although the Advanced IRB stem gives 4 years: 100 × 0.1177 × 1.2821 = 15.1.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics of termination provisions and trade compressions and explain their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
questions.source: Workbook A21.6 • S5, S6, S7 • Map #27
questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank is reviewing the unit that manages collateral and other counterparty risk mitigants, and is drafting findings for the audit committee. Which of the following statements is correct to include?

options.text: A rating-based break clause offers the same benefits as a mandatory break: counterparty risk reduction, CVA reduction, capital relief and LCR relief.
Liquidity risk from holding non-cash margin falls on the margin giver, which bears the bid-offer costs and price falls when the securities are sold after a default.
Because a compression cycle lowers the total notional of all participants, it guarantees that each participant ends with a lower notional to every counterparty.
Daily portfolio reconciliation reduces margin disputes, and a history of disputes is one reason Basel III requires a longer MPoR, raising capital and rewarding lower operational risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Disputes, reconciliation and operational risk**

Reconciliations “aim to minimise the chance of a dispute by agreeing on valuations and margin requirements across portfolios”; most large portfolios are reconciled daily. Basel III recognises the operational risk of collateralisation by requiring a larger MPoR where a netting set exceeds 5,000 trades or holds illiquid margin or exotics, and “a history of margin call disputes also requires a larger MPoR”. Larger MPoRs mean higher capital and so an incentive to reduce operational risk.

⇒ D is correct.

**Interpretation**

The auditor should test reconciliation frequency and dispute logs alongside capital: an operational weakness in margining shows up directly as a longer MPoR and a higher capital charge.

**LO:** CR-17 f: Explain the process for the reconciliation of collateral disputes. CR-17 j: Explain how market risk, operational risk, and liquidity risk (including funding liquidity risk) can arise through collateralization. CR-16 d: Describe the mechanics of termination provisions and trade compressions and explain their advantages and disadvantages. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.6, 16.2.4; Ch.7, 17.1.1 Table 17.1, 17.2.7, 17.5.3 and 17.5.4

CR-17 • Margin (Collateral) and Settlement • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A21.6 • S5, S6, S7 • Map #27 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-16 d.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap: Table 17.1 gives all four benefits only to mandatory breaks; a rating-based break gives at most some counterparty risk reduction, Basel explicitly rules out capital relief from rating triggers, and the LCR forces banks to pre-fund them.

b.reason: Role misassignment: liquidation risk sits with the non-defaulting party that holds the margin and must sell it for cash to rehedge; haircuts are set to cover it. The giver’s risk is funding liquidity risk when it must post.

c.reason: Absolute claim: compression aims to reduce the total notional of all parties, and “it does not necessarily follow that an individual party will experience a lower notional”; positions between pairs can even rise or change sign, which is why participants set constraints.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the credit support amount (margin) under various scenarios.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3.6 eq. 17.3 and Table 17.8
questions.question:
A collateral manager at a dealer receives margin from a hedge fund under a CSA with a zero threshold, no minimum transfer amount and no rounding. The hedge fund also posts initial margin (an independent amount) that the CSA recalculates daily from the risk of the portfolio. The positions are (USD million):

|  | Yesterday | Today |
|---|---|---|
| Portfolio value to the dealer | 420 | 455 |
| Variation margin held by the dealer | 420 |  |
| Initial margin requirement | 60 | 52 |
| Initial margin held (segregated) | 60 |  |

Which of the following correctly describes today’s margin transfers?

options.text: The hedge fund delivers a single net amount of USD 27 million.
The hedge fund delivers USD 35 million of variation margin, and the dealer separately returns USD 8 million of initial margin.
The hedge fund delivers USD 35 million of variation margin; the initial margin stays at USD 60 million because it is fixed at inception.
The hedge fund delivers USD 87 million: USD 35 million of variation margin plus a new USD 52 million of initial margin.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Variation margin (eq. 17.3, threshold zero)**

max(455 − 0, 0) − 420 = 35

⇒ The hedge fund delivers USD 35 million of variation margin.

**Step 2 – Initial margin**

The requirement fell from 60 to 52 while 60 is held: USD 8 million is returned.

**Step 3 – Keep them apart**

Initial margin is computed separately (the independent amount), is not netted against variation margin, and may be segregated.

⇒ Two transfers in opposite directions: 35 in, 8 out.

**Interpretation**

After the transfers the dealer holds 455 of variation margin plus 52 of initial margin against an exposure of 455. Variation margin tracks the value; initial margin tracks the riskiness of the value, which fell. GARP Table 17.8 shows the same pattern (value 350 to 375, initial margin 50 to 45).

**LO:** CR-17 c: Calculate the credit support amount (margin) under various scenarios. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.3.4; 17.3.6 eqs. 17.2 and 17.3, Table 17.8

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3.6 eq. 17.3 and Table 17.8 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-17 c.2)

a.reason: Netted the two: 35 − 8 = 27. Initial margin is not netted with variation margin.

c.reason: Treated initial margin as static. GARP: the term “may suggest a static quantity”, but it is now recalculated over time.

d.reason: Added the new requirement in full, ignoring the 60 already held: 35 + 52 = 87.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the credit support amount (margin) under various scenarios.
questions.source: Workbook A21.2 • S1, S2, S8 • Aug-2026 • Map #27
questions.question:
A treasury operations analyst at a UK bank is processing today’s margin under a two-way CSA with another bank. The data are:

- Portfolio value to the UK bank: −GBP 24.3 million
- Threshold for each party: GBP 5.0 million
- Margin already posted by the UK bank (credit support balance from its view): −GBP 18.9 million
- Minimum transfer amount: GBP 0.5 million; no rounding; independent amount: none

Which of the following is the correct action for the UK bank today?

options.text: No transfer
Post GBP 0.4 million
Post GBP 5.4 million
Request the return of GBP 4.6 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Counterparty term**

max$(\text{value} - K_{C} , 0) = \text{max}(-24.3 - 5, 0) = 0$

⇒ The portfolio is negative to the UK bank, so it cannot call margin.

**Step 2 – Own term**

max$(-\text{value} - K_{P} , 0) = \text{max}(24.3 - 5, 0) = 19.3$

⇒ The UK bank’s own GBP 5.0 million threshold is the uncollateralised amount it is allowed to owe.

**Step 3 – Credit support amount**

$0 - 19.3 - (-18.9) = -\text{GBP} 0.4$ million

⇒ A negative amount would mean the UK bank posts.

**Step 4 – MTA test**

\| − 0.4\| = 0.4 \< 0.5: the amount is below the minimum transfer amount, so no margin moves today.

**Interpretation**

The counterparty holds GBP 18.9 million against a liability of GBP 24.3 million: GBP 5.4 million uncollateralised, of which 5.0 is the agreed threshold and 0.4 the MTA gap. Full data are supplied, yet the threshold-plus-MTA test fails, which is the red-herring pattern the map flags. The 0.4 will be called once the shortfall reaches the MTA, which is why MTAs make collateralised exposure path dependent.

**LO:** CR-17 c: Calculate the credit support amount (margin) under various scenarios. CR-17 g: Explain the features of a collateralization agreement. CR-17 h: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.3.4; 17.3.6 eq. 17.3 and Table 17.7

CR-17 • Margin (Collateral) and Settlement • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A21.2 • S1, S2, S8 • Aug-2026 • Map #27 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-17 c.8)

b.reason: Ignored the MTA test and posted the raw credit support amount of 0.4.

c.reason: Ignored the UK bank’s own threshold: 24.3 − 18.9 = 5.4.

d.reason: Deducted both parties’ thresholds: required 24.3 − 5 − 5 = 14.3 against 18.9 posted, so it wrongly asks for 4.6 back. Only the out-of-the-money party’s own threshold applies.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process for the reconciliation of collateral disputes.
questions.source: Workbook A21.4 • S4, S5, S8 • Aug-2026 • Map #27
questions.question: A collateral manager at a Canadian bank is recommending CSA terms for three new relationships: a triple-A supranational development bank, an unrated hedge fund, and a dealer bank. Which of the following recommendations is consistent with the reading?

options.text: Accept the supranational’s one-way CSA in its favour, since a one-way CSA adds risk only for the party that receives the margin.
Sign a two-way CSA with zero thresholds with the dealer bank, the interbank standard, which aims to benefit both parties on counterparty risk.
Link the hedge fund’s threshold to its net asset value so that the threshold rises as the net asset value falls, easing its workload under stress.
Let both parties act as valuation agent on every CSA, since two valuation agents remove the potential for disputes over margin calls.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The dealer relationship**

Gregory: “Two-way CSAs with zero thresholds are standard in the interbank market and aim to be beneficial (from a counterparty risk point of view, at least) to both parties.” Both parties post against a negative value, so both exposures are mitigated.

⇒ The plain two-way CSA from the August recall: each party’s own threshold (here zero) governs when it posts.

**Step 2 – The other two relationships**

The supranational will want to receive but not post (an infinite threshold for itself): a one-way CSA that is extra risk for the bank as margin giver, worse than no CSA, and costly in funding and capital. For the hedge fund, an unrated party, terms can be linked to other metrics such as net asset value, but they must tighten as quality falls (lower threshold, then initial margin).

**Interpretation**

The bank should price the supranational’s one-way CSA through xVA rather than treat it as riskfree, and keep the hedge fund’s trigger mechanics aware of cliff-edge and liquidity effects.

**LO:** CR-17 f: Explain the process for the reconciliation of collateral disputes. CR-17 d: Describe the role of a valuation agent. CR-17 g: Explain the features of a collateralization agreement. CR-17 h: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.2.7, 17.3.2 and 17.3.4 Table 17.4

CR-17 • Margin (Collateral) and Settlement • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A21.4 • S4, S5, S8 • Aug-2026 • Map #27 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-17 f.7)

a.reason: Role misassignment: a one-way CSA “represents additional risk for the margin giver”, putting it in a worse situation than no CSA. The receiver (the supranational) is the party that benefits.

c.reason: Polarity flip: credit-quality links minimise workload when quality is high and tighten terms (lower threshold, initial margin) as it deteriorates; a threshold that rises as net asset value falls loosens collateralisation exactly when risk is highest.

d.reason: Absolute claim: where both counterparties are valuation agents, each calling for margin when it has an exposure, “the potential for margin disputes is significant”. Reconciliation reduces disputes; nothing removes them.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3.4 Table 17.4 and “The dangers of credit rating triggers”
questions.question: The treasurer of an A+ rated bank is reviewing the bank’s own CSAs, many of which use GARP’s rating-linked schedule: at A+ the bank’s threshold is zero with no initial margin; at A and A− it must also post initial margin of 1% of notional; at BBB+, 2%. Which of the following statements about these rating-linked terms is correct?

options.text: Basel capital rules give the bank’s counterparties capital relief for the triggers, since a downgrade would bring in margin before any default.
The liquidity coverage ratio requires the bank to pre-fund the contingent outflow, for example 2% initial margin for a three-notch downgrade to BBB+.
The triggers are effective because rating agencies typically downgrade well before a firm’s financial diﬀiculties become acute.
Because each counterparty’s trigger operates separately, a single-notch downgrade can have only a small and gradual effect on the bank’s liquidity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Regulation recognises the asymmetry**

Basel capital rules give no capital benefit for rating triggers and assume a counterparty defaults without first being downgraded. The liquidity coverage ratio, by contrast, requires a bank to pre-fund outflows such as ratings-contingent initial margin.

⇒ B: an A+ bank funds 2% initial margin for a three-notch downgrade (A+ to A, A−, BBB+).

**Step 2 – The two problems with triggers**

Ratings react too slowly to be a reliable mitigant, and many similar triggers firing on one downgrade create liquidity problems and cliff-edge effects.

**Interpretation**

The bank pays twice for rating triggers: it gets no capital relief when it receives them, and it must hold liquidity against them when it gives them.

**LO:** CR-17 h: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.3.4 Table 17.4 and box “The dangers of credit rating triggers”; 17.1.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3.4 Table 17.4 and “The dangers of credit rating triggers” (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-17 h.6)

a.reason: Basel explicitly rules out capital relief from rating triggers (BCBS 2011b).

c.reason: Ratings are “somewhat unreactive”; by the time of the downgrade the diﬀiculties may be too acute (the monolines).

d.reason: Cliff-edge effects: a single-notch downgrade can trigger many counterparties at once, as with AIG.

questions.loText: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality.
questions.source: Workbook A21.1 • S1, S8 • Aug-2026 • Map #27 • numerical, kept as a workbook question
questions.question:
A collateral manager at a US bank is computing today’s margin call under a two-way CSA with a European insurer. Thresholds are rating-linked (AA: USD 50 million; AA−: USD 25 million; A+: zero). The data are:

- Portfolio value to the bank: +USD 58.6 million
- Insurer’s rating: downgraded overnight from AA to AA−
- Credit support balance already held by the bank: USD 8.0 million (cash)
- Minimum transfer amount: USD 0.5 million; rounding: amounts rounded up to the nearest USD 0.25 million

Which of the following is closest to the margin the bank can call?

options.text: USD 0.75 million
USD 25.25 million
USD 25.50 million
USD 25.75 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Applicable threshold**

After the downgrade to AA−, $K_{C} =$ USD 25 million (the AA threshold of USD 50 million no longer applies).

⇒ The rating link tightens collateral terms as the insurer’s credit quality falls.

**Step 2 – Required margin**

max$(\text{value} - K_{C} , 0) = \text{max}(58.6 - 25, 0) = \text{USD} 33.6$ million

**Step 3 – Credit support amount before MTA and rounding**

$33.6 - \text{max}(-58.6 - K_{P} , 0) - 8.0 = 33.6 - 0 - 8.0 = \text{USD} 25.6$ million

⇒ The bank’s own threshold term is zero because the portfolio has positive value to the bank.

**Step 4 – MTA test and rounding**

25.6 > 0.5, so a call is valid and the full amount is called. Rounded up to the nearest 0.25: USD 25.75 million.

**Interpretation**

The downgrade alone triggers a USD 25.75 million call on the insurer: the cliff-edge liquidity effect Gregory warns about with rating triggers (the AIG pattern).

**LO:** CR-17 h: Differentiate between a two-way and one-way CSA agreement and describe how collateral parameters can be linked to credit quality. CR-17 b: Describe the terms of a collateral agreement and features of a credit support annex (CSA) within the ISDA Master Agreement including threshold, initial margin, minimum transfer amount and rounding, haircuts, credit quality, and credit support amount. CR-17 c: Calculate the credit support amount (margin) under various scenarios. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.3.4 Table 17.4; 17.3.6 eq. 17.3

CR-17 • Margin (Collateral) and Settlement • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A21.1 • S1, S8 • Aug-2026 • Map #27 • numerical, kept as a workbook question (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-17 h.7)

a.reason: Used the pre-downgrade AA threshold: 58.6 − 50 − 8.0 = 0.6, which passes the MTA and rounds up to 0.75.

b.reason: Deducted the MTA from the amount: 25.6 − 0.5 = 25.1, rounded up to 25.25. The MTA only gates the transfer.

c.reason: Rounded down instead of up as the CSA specifies: 25.50.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how market risk, operational risk, and liquidity risk (including funding liquidity risk) can arise through collateralization.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.5.2, 17.5.3 and 17.6.2 • shape A21·S6 (role misassignment)
questions.question: A collateral risk oﬀicer at a dealer bank is training new staff on a two-way CSA with a corporate client. The corporate is out of the money on a large swap and meets the bank’s daily margin calls by posting government bonds. Which of the following assigns a risk to the correct party?

options.text: Liquidation risk falls on the corporate as margin giver, which bears the bid-offer cost and price falls if the bonds are sold after a default.
Funding liquidity risk falls mainly on the corporate, which must source eligible collateral within short timescales whenever the swap moves further against it.
Market risk over the margin period of risk falls on the corporate, since the bank as margin receiver is fully protected until close-out.
Operational risk falls only on the bank as valuation agent, so the corporate, which does not calculate the calls, carries none.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The giver’s risk**

The corporate must post eligible collateral within short timescales whenever the swap moves against it. GARP: end users face funding liquidity risk when posting margin, and may default while solvent if they cannot meet a call in eligible securities.

⇒ B.

**Step 2 – The receiver’s risks**

The bank, holding the bonds, would have to sell them after a default (liquidation risk) and carries the market risk over the MPoR, since its exposure can rise before close-out.

**Interpretation**

Each risk has a home: liquidation and MPoR market risk with the receiver, funding liquidity risk with the giver, operational risk with both.

**LO:** CR-17 j: Explain how market risk, operational risk, and liquidity risk (including funding liquidity risk) can arise through collateralization. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.5.2, 17.5.3, 17.5.4 and 17.6.2

CR-19 • Future Value and Exposure • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.5.2, 17.5.3 and 17.6.2 • shape A21·S6 (role misassignment) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-17 j.9)

a.reason: Role misassignment: liquidation risk sits with the holder of the margin, the bank, which must sell it to rehedge.

c.reason: Role misassignment: the MPoR is the receiver’s uncollateralised period; the bank is not protected during it.

d.reason: Absolute claim: missed calls and failed deliveries hit the giver as well; operational risk falls on both parties.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of collateralization on exposure and assess the risk associated with the remargining period, threshold, and minimum transfer amount.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.3.3, eq. 19.5, Table 19.3 and Figure 19.23
questions.question: A counterparty risk analyst at a Dutch bank is explaining to the credit committee how a new two-way CSA with zero thresholds, daily variation margin and no initial margin will change the bank’s exposure to a hedge fund. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Because margin received is subtracted from the portfolio value, the CSA can only reduce the bank’s positive exposure; margin the bank posts can never create exposure to the hedge fund.

Exposure will remain, because margin arrives with a delay over the margin period of risk, and margin the bank has posted but not had returned when the hedge fund defaults is itself a positive exposure.
A threshold acts like initial margin, so agreeing a threshold of EUR 10 million instead of zero would move the profile from strongly collateralised towards overcollateralised.
With zero thresholds and daily calls the exposure profile is close to zero at every horizon, so adding initial margin would bring no further reduction.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Margin enters exposure with its sign**

Positive exposure $= \text{max}(\text{value} - \text{margin}, 0)$ (eq. 19.5). Received margin is positive and reduces it; posted margin is negative, so posted margin that exceeds what the bank owes adds to it. In GARP’s Table 19.3, scenario 5, the bank has posted 16 against a value of −15 and has a positive exposure of 1.

⇒ Two-way margin can create exposure as well as reduce it.

**Step 2 – What is left with zero thresholds**

GARP’s three imperfections remain: granularity (MTA, rounding), the delay over the MPoR, and variation in the value of non-cash margin. A strongly collateralised profile is much lower than an uncollateralised one but still material; only initial margin reduces it further, potentially to zero.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

The committee should expect a residual exposure driven mainly by the MPoR, and should know that its own posted margin is at risk if it is not returned. Both are reasons to model collateralised exposure rather than assume it away.

**LO:** CR-19 h: Explain the impact of collateralization on exposure and assess the risk associated with the remargining period, threshold, and minimum transfer amount. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.3.3, eq. 19.5, Table 19.3, Figures 19.22 and 19.23

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.3.3, eq. 19.5, Table 19.3 and Figure 19.23 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 h.5)

a.reason: Ignores posted margin: margin posted but not returned is an unsecured claim on the defaulter (Table 19.3, scenario 5).

c.reason: Polarity flip: a threshold is a negative initial margin; raising it moves the profile towards partially collateralised, not overcollateralised.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the MPoR leaves a material exposure under strong collateralisation, and initial margin reduces it further (the overcollateralised case).

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of collateralization on exposure and assess the risk associated with the remargining period, threshold, and minimum transfer amount.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.5.2 and Ch.20, 20.5.1 • shape A21·S9
questions.question: The xVA desk of a Japanese bank is moving a five-year interest rate swap portfolio with a corporate counterparty from no CSA to a two-way CSA with a zero threshold, daily variation margin and a 10-business-day margin period of risk, with no initial margin. There are 250 business days per year. Which of the following statements best describes the expected effect?

options.text: CVA falls because the corporate’s default probability is lower once it posts margin; the EPE profile is unchanged.
The best-case fall in exposure is about the ratio of maturity to MPoR, roughly 125 times, because margin covers all but 10 of the 1,250 business days.

The best-case fall in exposure is about the square root of maturity over MPoR, roughly 11 times; in practice it is smaller, and a longer MPoR (for example 20 days for a large or disputed netting set) moves CVA back towards the uncollateralised value.
With a zero threshold and daily calls, collateralised CVA is negligible, so the desk can set it to zero without modelling the MPoR.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where margin enters CVA**

CVA $= -\text{LGD} \sum$ EPE$(t_{i})$ PD$(t_{i-1}, t_{i})$. Margin “only changes EPE”, so the same formula is used with a collateralised EPE; the PD and LGD do not change.

⇒ A is wrong on the mechanism.

**Step 2 – Size of the best-case reduction**

With variation margin only, exposure is limited to the move over the MPoR instead of up to five years, and moves scale with the square root of time:

$$\sqrt{\frac{5 \times250}{10}} = \sqrt{125} = 11.2$$

⇒ About 11 times at best (GARP 17.5.2); “in reality, the result is worse than this estimate”.

**Step 3 – Sensitivity to the MPoR**

A 20-day MPoR gives only $\sqrt{62.5} = 7.9$ times. As the MPoR lengthens, collateral arrives too late to matter and CVA moves back towards the uncollateralised value; only initial margin takes it towards zero.

⇒ C is correct.

**Interpretation**

Ten days has become standard even for accounting CVA, and market participants now model variation margin even with zero thresholds. A collateralised CVA of roughly one tenth (or more) of the uncollateralised figure is the realistic expectation (A21.3, worked as Question CR-20 j.6).

**LO:** CR-19 h: Explain the impact of collateralization on exposure and assess the risk associated with the remargining period, threshold, and minimum transfer amount. CR-20 j: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.5.2; Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.5.1 and 20.5.3

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.5.2 and Ch.20, 20.5.1 • shape A21·S9 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 h.10)

a.reason: Role misassignment: collateral works on exposure, never on the counterparty’s default probability.

b.reason: Linear scaling: 1,250/10 = 125 treats exposure as proportional to time instead of its square root.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the MPoR leaves a material residual even with zero thresholds and daily calls, which is why it is modelled.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization.
questions.question:
An xVA analyst at a US dealer is computing the unilateral CVA on an uncollateralised 5-year interest rate swap with a corporate counterparty, notional USD 200 million. The counterparty’s recovery rate is 40%; the dealer’s own credit spread is 90 bps. The simulated profile is:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discounted EPE (% of notional) | 2.0 | 3.2 | 3.6 | 3.0 | 1.6 |
| Counterparty cumulative PD (%) | 1.5 | 3.2 | 5.0 | 6.9 | 8.9 |

Assuming no wrong-way risk, which of the following is closest to the UCVA (Gregory’s convention: CVA is negative)?

options.text: −USD 0.794 million
−USD 0.476 million
−USD 0.286 million
−USD 0.191 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Marginal PDs from cumulative PDs**

PD$(t_{i-1}, t_{i}) = \text{PD}(0, t_{i}) - \text{PD}(0, t_{i-1})$: 1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 (%).

⇒ The chance of the counterparty defaulting within each year, rising slowly from 1.5% to 2.0%.

**Step 2 – EPE** × **marginal PD per year (%** × **%)**

2.0(1.5) = 3.00, 3.2(1.7) = 5.44, 3.6(1.8) = 6.48, 3.0(1.9) = 5.70, 1.6(2.0) = 3.20; sum = 23.82.

$\Rightarrow\text{Sum} = 23.82 \times10^{-4} = 0.002382$ of notional: the probability-weighted exposure before applying LGD.

**Step 3 – LGD**

LGD $= 1 - R = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60$

⇒ 60% of the exposure is lost if the counterparty defaults.

**Step 4 – UCVA**

UCVA $= -0.60 \times0.002382 \times200 = -\text{USD} 0.286$ million

**Interpretation**

The swap is worth USD 0.286 million less to the dealer than its risk-free value (about 14.3 bps of notional upfront); this is the charge the xVA desk levies on the trader. The dealer’s own spread is a red herring for UCVA (it would enter DVA), and the CVA is negative in Gregory’s convention.

**LO:** CR-20 b: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA). CR-20 c: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.2, eq. 20.3

**Source:** Workbook A6.1 • S1 • Map #6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 c.3)

a.reason: Used cumulative instead of marginal PDs: $\sum\text{EPE} \times\text{PD}_{\text{cum}} = 66.18 \times10^{-4}$, so −0.60 × 0.006618 × 200 = −0.794.

b.reason: Dropped the LGD term, treating the whole exposure as lost: −0.002382 × 200 = −0.476.

d.reason: Used the recovery rate (40%) in place of LGD: −0.40×0.002382×200 = −0.191.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA).
questions.question:
A valuation control oﬀicer at a French bank is computing BCVA for an uncollateralised 5-year swap with a BBB corporate, notional EUR 150 million. Both LGDs are 60%. Survival adjustments are ignored (the bank reports UCVA + UDVA). The profiles are:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discounted EPE (% of notional) | 2.0 | 3.2 | 3.6 | 3.0 | 1.6 |
| Discounted ENE (% of notional) | −1.0 | −1.8 | −2.4 | −2.6 | −2.0 |
| Counterparty marginal PD (%) | 1.5 | 1.7 | 1.8 | 1.9 | 2.0 |
| Bank’s own marginal PD (%) | 0.6 | 0.7 | 0.8 | 0.8 | 0.9 |

Using the convention CVA negative, DVA positive and BCVA $= \text{CVA} +$ DVA, which of the following is closest to the BCVA?

options.text: −EUR 0.145 million
−EUR 0.097 million
−EUR 0.054 million
+EUR 0.069 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – CVA leg (counterparty PD with EPE)**

$\sum\text{EPE} \times\text{PD}_{C} = 3.00 + 5.44 + 6.48 + 5.70 + 3.20 = 23.82 (\times10^{-4})$

CVA $= -0.60 \times0.002382 \times150 = -\text{EUR} 0.2144$ million

⇒ The expected loss from the counterparty defaulting while the bank is owed money.

**Step 2 – DVA leg (own PD with ENE)**

$\sum\text{ENE} \times\text{PD}_{P} = -0.60 - 1.26 - 1.92 - 2.08 - 1.80 = -7.66 (\times10^{-4})$

DVA $= -0.60 \times(-0.000766) \times150 = +\text{EUR} 0.0689$ million

⇒ The “gain” from the bank’s own default while it owes the counterparty money; positive because ENE is negative.

**Step 3 – BCVA**

BCVA $= \text{CVA} + \text{DVA} = -0.2144 + 0.0689 = -\text{EUR} 0.145$ million

**Interpretation**

Recognising DVA cuts the net adjustment by about a third. Basel derecognises the EUR 0.069 million DVA from capital, and many banks pass only part of it into pricing. Subtracting DVA instead of adding it would give −0.283: the sign error the convention is designed to prevent.

**LO:** CR-20 e: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA). CR-20 f: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA. CR-20 g: Calculate DVA, BCVA, and BCVA as a spread. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.3.3, eqs. 20.7a to 20.8b

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A6.2 • S3 • Map #6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 e.6)

c.reason: Used the counterparty’s PD in the DVA leg: $\sum\text{ENE} \times\text{PD}_{C} = -17.82 \times10^{-4}$, DVA = +0.160, BCVA = −0.054.

d.reason: Reported the DVA leg alone (an intermediate result): +0.069.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.3.3 eqs. 20.8a and 20.8b
questions.question: An xVA analyst at a Singapore bank reports both the unilateral DVA (UDVA) and a contingent, survival-adjusted BCVA for an uncollateralised swap with a corporate client, using Gregory’s convention (CVA negative, DVA positive). The client is downgraded and its CDS spread widens sharply; the bank’s own spread and both exposure profiles are unchanged. Which of the following best describes the effect on the bank’s UDVA and on the DVA term inside its BCVA?

options.text: UDVA is unchanged; the DVA term inside BCVA decreases, because each own-default term is weighted by the client’s probability of surviving to the start of the interval.
UDVA is unchanged; the DVA term inside BCVA increases, because the client’s higher default probability makes the bank’s liabilities to it worth less.
UDVA and the DVA term inside BCVA both increase by the same amount, because both are driven by the expected negative exposure.
UDVA decreases, while the DVA term inside BCVA is unchanged, because survival adjustments apply only to the CVA term.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – UDVA**

UDVA $= -\text{LGD}_{P} \sum$ ENE$(t_{i}) \text{PD}_{P} (t_{i-1}, t_{i})$ uses only the bank’s own LGD and PD and its ENE. None of these changed.

⇒ UDVA is unchanged.

**Step 2 – DVA inside BCVA**

Each term also carries the client’s survival to the start of the interval, $1 - \text{PD}_{C} (0, t_{i-1})$. A wider client spread raises the client’s cumulative PD and lowers that survival.

⇒ The DVA term shrinks: the client is now more likely to default first, before the bank’s own default could produce a gain.

**Interpretation**

This is the UDVA versus BCVA distinction in one move. The same downgrade typically makes the CVA leg more negative too, so the bank’s BCVA falls on both counts, while its UDVA does not move.

**LO:** CR-20 f: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.3.3, eqs. 20.8a and 20.8b

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.3.3 eqs. 20.8a and 20.8b (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 f.4)

b.reason: Polarity flip: the client’s credit enters the DVA term only through its survival probability, which falls.

c.reason: UDVA has no counterparty input at all, so it cannot change with the client’s spread.

d.reason: Survival adjustments apply to both legs (eqs. 20.8a and 20.8b), and UDVA does not move.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA.
questions.question: A CVA desk is deciding whether to report contingent (survival-adjusted) or non-contingent CVA and DVA, with CVA negative and DVA positive. Which of the following statements about including survival probabilities is correct?

options.text: Including survival probabilities makes the CVA term sensitive to the institution’s own credit quality, which may be seen as unnatural and which regulation may prohibit.
Including survival probabilities leaves BCVA exactly equal to UCVA plus UDVA, because the reductions in the two legs offset each other.
The survival-adjusted formulas also capture default dependency between the two parties, so no separate correlation assumption is needed.
Market practice has converged on contingent CVA and DVA: surveys show that almost all banks apply survival adjustments.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the survival term does**

It conditions each default on the other party not having defaulted first. Gregory: this “leads to CVA having sensitivity to a party’s own credit quality, which may be seen as unnatural. Regulation may also prohibit doing this.”

⇒ A restates the text.

**Step 2 – Test the others against 20.3.4 and Table 20.3**

Both legs shrink but have opposite signs, so BCVA differs from UCVA + UDVA (−21.5 against −21.8). The formulas assume independent defaults. The 2012 survey split 6 contingent, 7 non-contingent of 19.

**Interpretation**

Survival adjustment, default dependency and close-out are interconnected simplifications; Gregory and German (2013) conclude that the formulas without survival terms are probably the best simple approximation.

**LO:** CR-20 f: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.3.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.3.4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 f.5)

b.reason: Absolute claim: the two reductions do not offset exactly.

c.reason: True fact about the wrong model: survival terms are not a dependency model; the formulas assume independence.

d.reason: Practice is mixed, not converged.

questions.question:
The head of the CVA desk at a Canadian bank is moving the bank’s reported counterparty risk adjustment on an uncollateralised 3-year swap (notional CAD 250 million) from UCVA to a contingent BCVA that includes survival adjustments. The inputs are:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discounted EPE (% of notional) | 3.0 | 4.0 | 3.0 |
| Discounted ENE (% of notional) | −2.0 | −3.5 | −4.5 |
| Counterparty marginal PD (%) | 6.0 | 7.0 | 8.0 |
| Bank’s own marginal PD (%) | 3.0 | 3.5 | 4.0 |

The counterparty’s recovery rate is 40% and the bank’s is 35%. Using Gregory’s convention (CVA negative, DVA positive, BCVA $= \text{CVA} +$ DVA), which of the following is closest to the change in the reported adjustment when the bank moves from UCVA to BCVA?

options.text: −CAD 0.475 million
+CAD 0.539 million
+CAD 0.575 million
+CAD 0.589 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – UCVA (no survival term)**

UCVA $= -0.60 \times[3.0(6.0) + 4.0(7.0) + 3.0(8.0)] \times10^{-4} \times250$

= −0.60 × 0.0070 × 250 = −1.0500

⇒ The currently reported charge: CAD 1.050 million, assuming the bank cannot default.

**Step 2 – Survival probabilities to the start of each year**

Bank: $1 - \text{PD}_{P} (0, t_{i-1}) = 1.000, 0.970, 0.935$. Counterparty: $1 - \text{PD}_{C} (0, t_{i-1}) =$ 1.000, 0.940, 0.870.

⇒ A default only counts if the other party has not defaulted first.

**Step 3 – Contingent CVA leg (eq. 20.8a)**

CVA $= -0.60 \times[18(1.000) + 28(0.970) + 24(0.935)] \times10^{-4} \times250$

= −0.60 × 0.00676 × 250 = −1.0140

**Step 4 – Contingent DVA leg (eq. 20.8b), own LGD** = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65

DVA $= -0.65 \times[-6.0(1.000) - 12.25(0.940) - 18.0(0.870)] \times10^{-4} \times250$

= −0.65 × (−0.0033175) × 250 = +0.5391

⇒ The benefit from the bank’s own default while it owes the counterparty money: positive because ENE is negative.

**Step 5 – BCVA and the change**

BCVA $= \text{CVA} + \text{DVA} = -1.0140 + 0.5391 = -0.4749$

$\Delta= \text{BCVA} - \text{UCVA} = -0.4749 - (-1.0500) = +\text{CAD} 0.575$ million

⇒ The reported adjustment becomes CAD 0.575 million less negative: the DVA of 0.539 plus the survival reduction of the CVA leg, 0.036.

**Interpretation**

Moving to BCVA books a CAD 0.575 million gain, most of it DVA. Basel would derecognise the DVA from the CVA capital charge, and the survival term makes the bank’s CVA depend on its own credit quality, which is why practice is split between contingent and non-contingent BCVA.

**LO:** CR-20 e: Describe debt value adjustment (DVA) and bilateral CVA (BCVA). CR-20 f: Explain the differences between unilateral CVA (UCVA) and BCVA, and between unilateral DVA (UDVA) and BCVA. CR-20 g: Calculate DVA, BCVA, and BCVA as a spread. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.3.3 eqs. 20.8a, 20.8b; 20.3.4

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A6.5 • S3, S4, S6 • Map #6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 f.6)

a.reason: Reported the BCVA itself (−0.475) as the change: the intermediate result planted when the move from UCVA is asked.

b.reason: Reported the DVA leg alone (+0.539), forgetting that the survival term also shrinks the CVA leg from −1.050 to −1.014.

d.reason: Dropped the survival adjustments, so the change equals the UDVA: −0.65 × (−0.003625) × 250 = +0.589; the non-contingent BCVA would be −0.461.

questions.source: Workbook A6.3 • S2, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #6
questions.question:
A risk consultant reviewing pricing at an Indian bank wants quick estimates, as running spreads, of the counterparty risk adjustments on a 5-year swap with a weaker counterparty. The data are:

- Undiscounted EPE profile (% of notional), years 1 to 5: 1.8, 2.6, 3.0, 2.8, 1.8
- Undiscounted ENE profile (% of notional), years 1 to 5: −1.2, −2.0, −2.6, −2.4, −1.8
- Counterparty 5-year credit spread: 180 bps; bank’s own 5-year credit spread: 120 bps
- LGD for both parties: 60%

Using Gregory’s average-exposure approximations (CVA negative, DVA positive), which of the following is closest to the UCVA and the BCVA, each in bps per annum?

options.text: UCVA −4.32 bps; BCVA −1.92 bps
UCVA −4.32 bps; BCVA +2.40 bps
UCVA −2.88 bps; BCVA +0.72 bps
UCVA −2.59 bps; BCVA −1.15 bps

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Average EPE and average ENE**

$$\overline{\text{EPE}} = \frac{1.8+2.6+3.0+2.8+1.8}{5} = 2.4\%, \overline{\text{ENE}} = \frac{-1.2-2.0-2.6-2.4-1.8}{5} = -2.0\%$$

⇒ On average the bank is owed 2.4% of notional and owes 2.0%.

**Step 2 – UCVA as a spread (eq. 20.4)**

UCVA $\approx-\overline{\text{EPE}} \times\text{Spread}_{C} = -0.024 \times180 = -4.32$ bps p.a.

⇒ Ignoring its own default, the bank would charge about 4.3 bps per annum for counterparty risk.

**Step 3 – DVA leg (eq. 20.9)**

$-\overline{\text{ENE}} \times\text{Spread}_{P} = -(-0.020) \times120 = +2.40$ bps p.a.

**Step 4 – BCVA as a spread**

BCVA = −4.32 + 2.40 = −1.92 bps p.a.

**Interpretation**

Because the counterparty is weaker (180 against 120 bps) it pays the bank about 1.9 bps per annum to trade; with equal spreads and symmetric exposure the bilateral charge would be close to zero. The LGD is a red herring: the approximation has no LGD input because the spread already embeds it.

**LO:** CR-20 c: Calculate CVA and CVA as a spread with no wrong-way risk, netting, or collateralization. CR-20 g: Calculate DVA, BCVA, and BCVA as a spread. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.3 eq. 20.4; 20.3.3 eq. 20.9

**Source:** Workbook A6.3 • S2, S5 • Aug-2026 • Map #6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 g.4)

b.reason: Correct UCVA, but reported the DVA leg alone as the BCVA (an intermediate result): +2.40.

c.reason: Swapped the parties’ spreads, applying the bank’s own spread to the EPE and the counterparty’s spread to the ENE: −0.024 × 120 = −2.88; −2.88 + 0.020 × 180 = +0.72.

d.reason: Multiplied by LGD as well, double counting it: 0.60 × (−4.32) = −2.59 and 0.60 × (−1.92) = −1.15.

questions.loText: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread.
questions.question:
A trader at a German bank is pricing a new 5-year EUR swap, notional EUR 150 million, with a counterparty under an existing ISDA netting agreement. The xVA desk reports (Gregory’s convention, CVA negative):

- CVA of the existing netting set: −EUR 1.84 million
- CVA of the netting set including the new swap: −EUR 2.27 million
- Standalone CVA of the new swap: −EUR 0.96 million
- 5-year risky annuity: 4.5; counterparty LGD: 60%

Which of the following is closest to the CVA charge for the new swap, quoted as a running cost in bps per annum on its notional?

options.text: 6.37 bps p.a.
7.85 bps p.a.
14.22 bps p.a.
33.63 bps p.a.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Incremental CVA (upfront)**

CVA$_{\text{incr}} = \text{CVA}_{NS^{'}} - \text{CVA}_{NS} = -2.27 - (-1.84) = -\text{EUR} 0.43$ million

⇒ The new swap partly offsets existing trades, so it adds only EUR 0.43 million of CVA, less than its standalone EUR 0.96 million, as netting guarantees.

**Step 2 – Annuity value of notional**

150 × 4.5 = 675 (EUR million-years)

**Step 3 – Running spread**

$\frac{-0.43}{675} = -0.000637 = -6.37$ bps p.a.

⇒ In Gregory’s convention the CVA is −6.37 bps; the counterparty pays a running cost of 6.37 bps per annum.

**Interpretation**

The trader can quote about 6.4 bps per annum instead of 14.2 bps standalone, which is why an existing netting relationship lets a bank offer better terms (Cooper and Mello). Dividing by the annuity ignores the CVA of the CVA, so the exact recursive charge is slightly larger. The LGD is a red herring: it is already inside the CVA figures, and applying it again would give 3.82 bps.

**LO:** CR-20 h: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation. CR-20 i: Define and calculate incremental CVA and marginal CVA and explain how to convert CVA into a running spread. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.3; 20.4.1 eqs. 20.10 to 20.12

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A6.4 • S2 • Map #6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 i.7)

b.reason: Charged the netting benefit (standalone minus incremental) instead of the incremental CVA: (0.96 − 0.43)/675 = 7.85 bps.

c.reason: Used the standalone CVA, ignoring the netting benefit: 0.96/675 = 14.22 bps.

d.reason: Charged the entire post-trade netting set CVA to the new swap: 2.27/675 = 33.63 bps.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.5.3 (Initial Margin)
questions.question: A collateral manager is explaining to the CVA desk how the terms of a new CSA will affect the CVA on a 10-year receiver swap with a 10-business-day MPoR. CVA is reported as a negative number. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Raising the counterparty’s threshold moves CVA towards zero, because fewer margin calls means less operational exposure.
Initial margin acts as a negative threshold: as initial margin received grows, CVA tends to zero, and as the threshold grows, CVA tends to the uncollateralised value.
Initial margin that the bank posts to the counterparty and that is held segregated reduces the bank’s CVA, because it lowers the counterparty’s exposure to the bank.
A higher minimum transfer amount reduces CVA, because collateral is transferred in larger and therefore more protective amounts.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Threshold and initial margin on one axis**

GARP: “a threshold can be seen to be a negative initial margin and vice versa. For high thresholds, CVA tends to the uncollateralised value, whilst for high initial margin it tends to zero.”

⇒ B restates Figure 20.14.

**Step 2 – Posted initial margin and the MTA**

Segregated initial margin the bank posts “would not show up in any of the above calculations”; it is an MVA cost. A higher MTA leaves exposure uncollateralised until the call is large enough, so it raises CVA.

**Interpretation**

Every term that leaves part of the exposure uncovered (threshold, MTA, longer MPoR) makes CVA more negative; only margin received beyond the portfolio value (initial margin) pushes it towards zero.

**LO:** CR-20 j: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.5.3, Figure 20.14; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 2, Reading 38, LO 38.j

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.5.3 (Initial Margin) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 j.3)

a.reason: Polarity flip: a higher threshold leaves more exposure uncollateralised, so CVA moves towards the uncollateralised value.

c.reason: Posted and received swapped: initial margin the bank posts protects the counterparty and creates MVA for the bank; it does not reduce the bank’s CVA.

d.reason: Polarity flip: a higher MTA delays transfers and increases CVA.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins.
questions.question: An xVA quantitative analyst at a UK bank is documenting the assumptions of the collateralised CVA model for portfolios under two-way, zero-threshold CSAs with daily variation margin calls (CVA reported as a negative number). Which of the following statements should the documentation include?

options.text: Because margin is called daily, the model’s MPoR should be one business day, matching the contractual period between margin calls.
A grace (cure) period after a missed call is a pre-default component of the MPoR, while rehedging and liquidating margin securities are post-default.
Because the MPoR measures the delay in receiving margin, the same MPoR should be used to assess the funding cost of the collateralised portfolio.
Because the MPoR is the primary driver of the need for initial margin, a longer MPoR reduces the initial margin the bank should require.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Components**

Gregory splits the MPoR into pre-default (valuation and margin call; receiving collateral, including any dispute; settlement; grace or cure period) and post-default (macro-hedging; close-out of transactions; rehedging and replacement; liquidation of margin securities).

⇒ The grace period runs before the counterparty is legally in default; liquidation of the margin it posted can only happen after.

**Step 2 – Effect on collateralised exposure and CVA**

Market risk over the MPoR is uncollateralised. With variation margin only, the best-case reduction is about $\sqrt{\text{maturity}/\text{MPoR}}$; reality is worse. Margin changes only EPE in the CVA formula: in Table 20.6 the 10-year pay-fixed swap’s CVA falls from −28.9 to −3.0 bps with a 10-day MPoR. Initial margin (overcollateralisation) pushes CVA towards zero; a threshold acts as a negative initial margin.

**Interpretation**

The model should use a 10-business-day MPoR at least (more for large or disputed netting sets) and size initial margin to the MPoR, since the choice of initial margin is closely tied to the assumed MPoR.

**LO:** CR-17 j: Explain how market risk, operational risk, and liquidity risk (including funding liquidity risk) can arise through collateralization. CR-20 j: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7, 17.3.3 and 17.5.2; Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.5.2 and 20.5.3

**Source:** Workbook A21.5 • S3, S9 • Aug-2026 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 j.4)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the margin call frequency is only one component of the MPoR; “it could, therefore, be that the margin call frequency is daily, but the MPoR is assumed to be 10 days”.

c.reason: Scope error: the MPoR is defined assuming the counterparty’s default and is “not relevant when assessing funding costs”; funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay.

d.reason: Polarity flip: the MPoR is indeed the primary driver of the need for initial margin, but a longer MPoR leaves more uncollateralised market risk and so raises the initial margin needed.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.5.1 and Ch.17, 17.5.2
questions.question: A bank currently models its collateralised CVA with a counterparty using a 10-business-day MPoR, two-way zero-threshold CSA and daily variation margin. Because the netting set now exceeds 5,000 trades, it moves to a 20-business-day MPoR. CVA is reported as a negative number. Which of the following best describes the effect on the collateralised CVA?

options.text: It becomes more negative and moves towards the uncollateralised CVA; the collateralised exposure grows with the square root of the MPoR, so the CVA rises by less than in proportion.
It is unchanged, because margin is still called daily and the MPoR matters only for the funding of the portfolio.
It doubles in magnitude, because the uncollateralised exposure accumulates over twice as many days.
It becomes less negative, because the longer period gives the bank more time to liquidate the collateral at good prices.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Direction**

The MPoR is the window over which the exposure can grow uncollateralised. Lengthening it raises the collateralised EPE at every date, so the CVA becomes more negative and moves towards the uncollateralised CVA (Vardeez, Schweser).

**Step 2 – Size**

Under the square-root-of-time rule, the value change over the MPoR scales with $\sqrt{\text{MPoR}}$: doubling 10 days to 20 makes the collateralised exposure, and so the CVA, about $\sqrt{2} = 1.41$ times larger, not twice as large.

**Interpretation**

This is why Basel III imposes 20 days or more on large or troublesome netting sets: the longer delay to close-out leaves more market risk uncollateralised. The daily call frequency is unchanged and irrelevant to the comparison.

**LO:** CR-20 j: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7, 17.5.2; Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.5.1; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 2, Reading 38, LO 38.j

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.5.1 and Ch.17, 17.5.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 j.5)

b.reason: Sibling swap: the call frequency is not the MPoR, and the MPoR is a counterparty risk concept that is not used for funding.

c.reason: Linear scaling: the exposure grows with the square root of time, so doubling the MPoR multiplies it by about 1.41.

d.reason: Polarity flip: a longer MPoR adds uncollateralised market risk (and liquidation risk on the margin held); it does not reduce CVA.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins.
questions.question:
A CVA desk analyst at a Swiss bank is estimating how far a new two-way, zero-threshold CSA with daily variation margin calls will reduce the CVA on an 8-year portfolio with a hedge fund. The data are:

- Uncollateralised CVA: −EUR 4.2 million
- The netting set contains over 5,000 trades, so the bank applies a 20-business-day MPoR
- 250 business days per year; no initial margin

Using the square-root-of-time approximation in the reading (CVA negative), which of the following is closest to the best-case collateralised CVA?

options.text: −EUR 0.420 million
−EUR 0.348 million
−EUR 0.297 million
−EUR 0.042 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Maturity in business days**

8 × 250 = 2,000 business days

**Step 2 – Reduction factor**

$$\sqrt{\frac{\text{maturity}}{\text{MPoR}}} = \sqrt{\frac{2{,}000}{20}} = \sqrt{100} = 10$$

⇒ With only variation margin, exposure is limited to the market move over the 20-day MPoR instead of up to 8 years, so risk falls by about 10 times at best.

**Step 3 – Collateralised CVA**

CVA$_{\text{coll}} \approx\frac{-4.2}{10} = -\text{EUR} 0.420$ million

**Interpretation**

Even a zero-threshold daily CSA leaves about 10% of the CVA, and Gregory notes reality is worse than this best case; only initial margin can push CVA towards zero. The longer MPoR for large netting sets cuts the benefit compared with the 10-day standard. Margin changes only the EPE in the CVA formula, so the PD and LGD are untouched.

**LO:** CR-20 j: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins. CR-17 j: Explain how market risk, operational risk, and liquidity risk (including funding liquidity risk) can arise through collateralization. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7, 17.5.2 and 17.5.4; Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.5.1 and 20.5.2

**Source:** Workbook A21.3 • S9 • Aug-2026 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 j.6)

b.reason: Used 365 calendar days with a business-day MPoR: $4.2/\sqrt{2{,}920/20} = 0.348$.

c.reason: Used the standard 10-day MPoR instead of the 20 days applied to netting sets over 5,000 trades: $4.2/\sqrt{200} = 0.297$.

d.reason: Scaled linearly instead of by the square root: 4.2 × 20/2,000 = 0.042.
