questions.loText: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.5.2 Table 20.6
questions.question:
A risk manager reviews GARP’s upfront CVA and DVA (bp, Gregory’s convention: CVA negative, DVA positive) for 10-year interest rate swaps, uncollateralised and collateralised with a 10-business-day MPoR. GARP notes that the simple square-root-of-time estimate of the CVA reduction for this maturity is about 8.4 times.

|  | Pay fixed Uncoll. Coll. | Receive fixed Uncoll. Coll. |
|---|---|---|
| CVA | −28.9 −3.0 | −16.6 −3.2 |
| DVA | 7.4 1.5 | 13.2 1.3 |

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Collateral reduced the CVA of both swaps by about the same factor, as the square-root-of-time estimate predicts.

The pay-fixed swap’s CVA fell by more than the estimate because its EPE is positively skewed, the receive-fixed swap’s by less, and the collateralised CVAs are much more symmetric between the two swaps.
Because the collateralised BCVA is small, collateralised interbank counterparties can easily be charged for the remaining CVA.
Collateralised DVA is less controversial than uncollateralised DVA, because daily margin removes any benefit from the party’s own default.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Reduction factors**

Pay fixed: 28.9/3.0 = 9.6 times. Receive fixed: 16.6/3.2 = 5.2 times. The estimate is 8.4.

⇒ The payer’s CVA falls by more than the estimate, the receiver’s by less: GARP attributes this to the positive skew of the payer’s EPE and the negative skew of the receiver’s.

**Step 2 – Symmetry**

Uncollateralised, the two CVAs differ by a factor of almost two (−28.9 against −16.6); collateralised they are close (−3.0 against −3.2), because the MPoR model is symmetric.

**Interpretation**

Margin compresses the exposure to the move over one MPoR, which looks much the same for a payer and a receiver; what remains of the original asymmetry is the skew. BCVA ends up small (−1.5 and −1.9 bp).

**LO:** CR-20 j: Explain the impact of incorporating collateralization into the CVA calculation, including the impact of margin period of risk, thresholds, and initial margins. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.5.1 and 20.5.2, Table 20.6

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.5.2 Table 20.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 j.7)

a.reason: The factors are 9.6 and 5.2, not the same; the estimate ignores the skew of each profile.

c.reason: GARP says the opposite: it is “clearly not possible” to charge interbank counterparties for hedging, and the small BCVA is only some comfort because such costs are hard to charge.

d.reason: GARP calls collateralised DVA “potentially even more controversial”: it relies on the party ceasing to post margin about 10 days before its own default.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk.
questions.source: Workbook A20.1 • S1, S2 • Aug-2026 • Map #26
questions.question:
A counterparty risk oﬀicer at a Singapore bank is classifying four proposed uncollateralised trades before a credit committee. The bank’s rule is to tag a trade wrong-way if its exposure to the counterparty is expected to rise when the counterparty’s credit quality falls, and right-way if the reverse holds.

- Trade 1: the bank receives fixed from a domestic manufacturer on a 7-year interest rate swap, agreed while the economy is strong.
- Trade 2: a copper producer that is hedging its future output pays the floating copper price to the bank and receives a fixed price on a commodity swap.
- Trade 3: in an FX forward with an emerging-market sovereign, the bank pays the sovereign’s local currency and receives US dollars.
- Trade 4: the bank buys CDS protection on its domestic sovereign from a domestic bank.

Which of the following classifications should the oﬀicer record?

options.text: Trade 1 is right-way, because a recession that weakens the manufacturer would also push rates up and move the swap against the bank.
Trade 2 is right-way whatever the producer’s motive, because a producer’s commodity swap always pays the bank when the producer is profitable.
Trade 3 is wrong-way, because a weakening of the local currency would raise the bank’s exposure as the sovereign’s credit quality deteriorates.
Trade 4 is right-way, because buying protection from a seller linked to the reference entity is the right-way side of a CDS.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Apply the test to Trade 3**

What raises the bank’s exposure? The bank pays local currency and receives dollars, so a fall in the local currency makes the forward more valuable to the bank. Does the same event weaken the counterparty? Yes: a currency collapse and a sovereign default go together, either way round (Gregory: “paying its local currency in an FX forward or cross-currency swap”). Unfavourable dependence, so wrong-way.

⇒ Levy and Levin put residual currency values at sovereign default at 17% (AAA) to 62% (CCC): the exposure jumps exactly when the counterparty fails.

**Step 2 – Check the others with the same two questions**

Trade 1: rates fall in a recession, so the receive-fixed swap gains as the manufacturer weakens: wrong-way. Trade 2: the producer owes the bank only when copper is high and it is profitable: right-way, because it is a hedge. Trade 4: the bank’s exposure is the protection’s value, which rises as the sovereign weakens, and the domestic bank weakens with its sovereign: extreme wrong-way.

**Interpretation**

The committee should price or limit Trades 1 and 3 (general WWR) and decline Trade 4, a case of specific WWR that Gregory says should in general be avoided; Trade 2 reduces CVA.

**LO:** CR-20 k: Describe wrong-way risk and contrast it with right-way risk. CR-20 l: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.1 and Table 20.7

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A20.1 • S1, S2 • Aug-2026 • Map #26 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 k.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip: Gregory says rates are likely to be cut in a recession, so the receive-fixed swap moves in the bank’s favour as the manufacturer weakens. That is wrong-way, not right-way.

b.reason: Scope or condition error (absolute claim): Gregory ties the right-way character to hedging (“as opposed to speculation”). Dropping the condition with “whatever the motive” turns a true statement false.

d.reason: Role misassignment: Gregory gives the right-way side to the protection seller. The bank is the buyer: its exposure rises as the reference sovereign weakens, which drags the domestic bank (the seller) down with it, so it is extreme wrong-way.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 (Pykhtin and Sokol)
questions.question: The head of xVA at a European bank argues that, because the bank’s large dealer counterparties all post daily variation margin and initial margin under their CSAs, the bank can largely disregard wrong-way risk on those relationships and should concentrate its WWR analysis on uncollateralised corporate clients. Which response is most consistent with GARP’s discussion of collateral and WWR?

options.text: The argument is flawed: WWR reduces the benefit of collateralisation, that benefit must allow for jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk, and systemic dealers that post margin are the counterparties most exposed to extreme WWR.
The argument is sound: daily variation margin means any rise in exposure before default is collateralised, so WWR can only arise with counterparties that do not post margin.
The argument is flawed, because WWR is lower for systemic counterparties such as dealers, so the bank should concentrate instead on its smaller and weaker counterparties.
The argument is sound, because initial margin is sized to a high confidence level and therefore already covers any jump in exposure at a dealer’s default.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What Pykhtin and Sokol add**

The benefit of margin in a WWR situation must allow for jumps and a period of higher volatility during the MPoR, and WWR should be higher for the default of more systemic parties, such as banks. Overall, WWR has a negative impact on the benefit of collateralisation.

**Step 2 – Apply it to the dealer relationships**

The large dealers post margin, but they are the systemic counterparties whose default comes with jumps and extreme volatility. Their margin does not remove their WWR; it is least effective against it.

⇒ The head of xVA’s argument fails. GARP notes the irony: the counterparties that use margin are the ones subject to extreme WWR, while corporates often do not post margin anyway.

**Interpretation**

Margin should be treated as a partial mitigant whose benefit is reduced by WWR, with stressed MPoR assumptions for systemic names. Uncollateralised corporates still matter, but they are not the only place WWR lives.

**LO:** CR-20 m: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.6 Collateralisation and WWR

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 (Pykhtin and Sokol) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 m.3)

b.reason: Gradual rises are collateralised, but a jump at default inside the MPoR is not; WWR survives daily margin.

c.reason: Polarity flip: WWR is higher for systemic parties, and it increases with credit quality (CR-20 k).

d.reason: Initial margin is set to a high but finite confidence level from market-risk models; it does not automatically cover the jump that a systemic default brings.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.5 and 20.6.6
questions.question: A bank buys five-year CDS protection on its domestic sovereign from a domestic bank. The trade is covered by a CSA with daily variation margin and a zero threshold. The trader argues that the margin makes the trade’s wrong-way risk negligible. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: The trader is right: with a zero threshold and daily margin, the bank is fully collateralised at all times, so the seller’s default cannot cause a loss.
The trader is right, provided the protection seller posts high-quality government bonds of the same sovereign as margin.
The trader is wrong: WWR in credit derivatives is unavoidable and here specific, the credit event and the seller’s distress are likely to arrive together as a jump, so margin may help very little.
The trader is wrong, because the trade is right-way: the bank’s exposure rises as the sovereign weakens, which strengthens the domestic bank selling protection.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Classify the trade**

The bank is owed the protection value, which rises as its sovereign weakens. A domestic bank selling protection on its own sovereign weakens with it. GARP: “a bank selling protection on its own sovereign would be an obvious problem”; for credit derivatives the WWR is unavoidable and may be specific.

**Step 2 – What can margin do?**

The sovereign’s distress and the domestic bank’s distress are likely to come together, as a jump. GARP: “due to the highly contagious and systemic nature of CDS risks, the impact of margin may be hard to assess and indeed may be quite limited.”

⇒ Daily margin and a zero threshold do not make the WWR negligible.

**Interpretation**

This is specific WWR, which GARP says should in general be avoided. If the bank needs the protection, it should buy it from a seller whose credit quality is not tied to the sovereign.

**LO:** CR-20 m: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk. CR-20 l: Identify examples of wrong-way risk and examples of right-way risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.1, 20.6.5 Credit Derivatives and 20.6.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.5 and 20.6.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 m.4)

a.reason: “Fully collateralised at all times” ignores the margin period of risk and the jump at the credit event.

b.reason: Bonds of the same sovereign would be wrong-way collateral: they fall exactly when the protection is needed, making matters worse.

d.reason: Role misassignment: buying protection from a linked seller is the wrong-way side; the seller weakens, not strengthens, as the sovereign weakens.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6; Ch.19, 19.4.3; Ch.17, 17.3.5
questions.question: An Italian bank posts Italian government bonds as variation margin to a US dealer under a CSA that allows the dealer to rehypothecate margin. The dealer’s xVA desk is assessing what this margin achieves. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It provides no counterparty risk benefit at all, because any margin linked to the poster’s credit quality is worthless when the poster defaults.

It is a weaker mitigant than cash or US Treasuries because its value is likely to fall as the bank weakens, but it still reduces exposure to the extent it retains value at default, and being reusable it can still give a funding benefit.
It is as effective as cash, because high-quality sovereign bonds have good liquidity, low default risk and low price volatility.
It mitigates counterparty risk fully but gives no funding benefit, because wrong-way margin cannot be rehypothecated.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Is the margin wrong-way?**

A bank posting bonds of its own sovereign is one of GARP’s “clearly problematic” examples: the bank’s credit quality and its sovereign’s are linked, so the bonds are likely to lose value as the bank weakens. GARP also notes that a CSA may not prevent this, because high-quality sovereign bonds are normally eligible.

**Step 2 – Counterparty risk benefit**

“Wrong-way margin does still provide some benefit as a mitigant as long as it retains some value when the counterparty defaults.” The bonds are a weaker mitigant than cash or US Treasuries, but not worthless.

**Step 3 – Funding benefit**

For margin to help funding it must be reusable. The CSA allows rehypothecation, so the bonds can still give a funding benefit; the wrong-way link affects the credit benefit, not reusability.

**Interpretation**

The desk should apply a larger haircut or prefer other eligible assets, and it should not count the bonds at full value in the CVA. Credit benefit and funding benefit are two separate tests.

**LO:** CR-20 m: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk. CR-20 n: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.

- **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.6; Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.4.3; Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.3.5 Haircuts

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6; Ch.19, 19.4.3; Ch.17, 17.3.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 m.5)

a.reason: Absolute claim: wrong-way margin keeps some value at default, so it still mitigates some exposure.

c.reason: Liquidity and low volatility do not remove the link between the bank’s default and its sovereign’s bonds.

d.reason: Reverses both tests: the credit benefit is reduced, while reusability (and so the funding benefit) depends on rehypothecation rights, not on the wrong-way link.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: Workbook A20.2 • S3, S4, S5 • Map #26
questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing how a European derivatives clearing house and its largest clearing members measure and mitigate wrong-way risk, and is drafting recommendations. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the report?

options.text: Variation and initial margin are effective mitigants of wrong-way risk in all cases, because margin received as the exposure rises offsets the higher exposure before default.
The hazard rate (intensity) approach suits specific wrong-way risk, because correlating credit spreads with exposure drivers produces a strong dependence that matches quanto CDS data.
Setting initial margin and default fund contributions mainly from the market risk of each portfolio may ignore wrong-way risk, which argues for more from higher-quality members.
A payer interest rate swap collateralised by a high-quality government bond is right-way collateral, because a rise in rates raises both the swap value and the bond value.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The CCP statement**

Gregory: CCPs require a minimum credit quality for membership but then charge initial margins and default fund contributions “driven primarily by the market risk of their portfolio”; in doing this “CCPs are in danger of implicitly ignoring WWR”. Because WWR increases with credit quality, this “perversely” suggests greater initial margin and default fund from better-credit-quality, more systemically important members.

⇒ The surviving members’ default fund sits in a senior, systemic second-loss position of a CDO-like waterfall, so under-margined WWR lands on them.

**Interpretation**

The consultant should recommend that the clearing house quantify WWR in initial margin and default fund setting (hard for CDSs), and review eligible margin for adverse selection, since members will post the riskiest assets relative to the haircut.

**LO:** CR-20 m: Discuss the impact of collateral on wrong-way risk. CR-20 n: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral. CR-20 o: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs). CR-20 p: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.3 to 20.6.7

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A20.2 • S3, S4, S5 • Map #26 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 m.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim: margin helps only if exposure rises gradually; a jump at default makes it useless. Jump approaches show collateral as near useless, and Pykhtin and Sokol find WWR reduces the benefit of collateralisation. “In all cases” is false.

b.reason: Sibling swap: the intensity approach generates only weak dependence and may underestimate WWR; Ehlers and Schönbucher show it cannot match quanto CDS data even at ±100% correlation. The jump approach is the one suited to specific WWR and supported by quanto data.

d.reason: Polarity flip: a rate rise raises the payer swap’s value but lowers the bond’s value, so the margin shrinks as the exposure grows: general wrong-way collateral (minor, given low rate volatility). The receiver swap is the right-way case.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 • shape A20·S3
questions.question: A US bank has a five-year cross-currency swap with a Brazilian corporate in which the bank pays Brazilian real (BRL) and receives US dollars. The CSA lets the corporate post cash in BRL or in USD, or short-dated US Treasury bills. Measuring all values in USD, a risk analyst is asked which of these forms of margin is wrong-way collateral for the bank. Which answer is correct?

options.text: USD cash, because a weaker real raises the corporate’s cost of buying the dollars it must post.
BRL cash, because a fall in the real raises the bank’s exposure on the swap and lowers the USD value of the margin at the same time.
US Treasury bills, because rising US rates lower their value just as the swap’s value rises.
None of them, because margin in either currency of the swap offsets the FX risk of the exposure.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What raises the bank’s exposure?**

The bank pays BRL and receives USD. A fall in the real makes the BRL it pays cheaper in dollar terms, so the swap gains value for the bank.

**Step 2 – What does that move do to each form of margin?**

BRL cash loses USD value as the real falls. USD cash has no FX link for a USD-measuring bank. Short-dated Treasury bills have little price sensitivity and no link to the real.

⇒ BRL cash is the currency the bank pays on the swap: GARP’s “margin held in the currency being paid”, where an FX move raises the exposure and cuts the collateral at the same time.

**Interpretation**

GARP calls this a more significant example of general wrong-way margin than the payer swap secured by bonds, because FX moves are larger and, for emerging-market currencies, can jump. The bank should restrict eligibility to USD or apply a heavy FX haircut to BRL.

**LO:** CR-20 n: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.6 Collateralisation and WWR

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 • shape A20·S3 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 n.2)

a.reason: The corporate’s cost of obtaining dollars is a funding issue for the poster; USD cash held by the bank does not lose value when the real falls.

c.reason: Applies the payer-swap example to the wrong trade: short-dated bills barely move with rates, and US rates are not the driver of this swap’s exposure.

d.reason: Margin in the currency being paid moves against the exposure; it does not offset it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3.5, 17.4.4 and 17.5.3
questions.question: A collateral manager is drafting the eligible-margin schedule for a new bilateral CSA with a European bank. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Under the bilateral margin rules, the European bank may post its own bonds as margin, provided a haircut reflecting their price volatility is applied.
Cash margin cannot create wrong-way risk, so euro cash posted by the European bank is free of any adverse linkage.
Even cash can be wrong-way: euro cash from a European bank may be linked to the bank’s own credit quality, and such links are the hardest haircut factor to set prescriptively.
High-quality sovereign bonds are free of wrong-way risk by definition, so accepting them prevents the European bank from posting margin linked to its own credit quality.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Can cash be wrong-way?**

Yes. GARP: “adverse correlations can also be present with cash margin: an example would be receiving euros from European sovereigns or European banks”, and “even a European bank posting cash in euros will give rise to a potentially problematic linkage and wrong-way risk”.

**Step 2 – How haircuts treat it**

The haircut checklist includes any relationship between the margin’s value and the counterparty’s default or the exposure, but this factor is “often the hardest to implement in a prescriptive fashion”.

⇒ C is correct.

**Interpretation**

A severe euro crisis would hit the bank and the euro together. The manager might prefer cash in a currency not linked to the bank’s credit, or accept the linkage knowingly.

**LO:** CR-20 n: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.3.5 Haircuts; 17.4.4 Eligible Assets and Haircuts; 17.5.3 Liquidity, FX, and Wrong-way Risks

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.17, 17.3.5, 17.4.4 and 17.5.3 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 n.5)

a.reason: The bilateral margin rules say margin must not be wrong-way, with a counterparty posting its own bonds or equity as the example; a haircut does not make it eligible.

b.reason: Absolute claim: GARP gives euro cash from European banks or sovereigns as a wrong-way example.

d.reason: High-quality sovereign bonds are normally eligible, which is exactly why a CSA “may not prevent” a bank posting bonds of its own sovereign, a specific wrong-way case.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 • shape A20·S3
questions.question: A model validator is classifying four margin arrangements reviewed this quarter, using GARP’s distinction between general and specific wrong-way risk. Which pairing of arrangement and classification is correct?

options.text: A dealer holding high-quality government bonds as margin against a receiver interest rate swap: general wrong-way margin.
A bank holding, as margin from another bank, bonds issued by that bank’s own sovereign: specific wrong-way margin.
A dealer holding high-quality government bonds as margin against a payer interest rate swap: specific wrong-way margin.
A dealer holding a corporate counterparty’s own senior bonds as margin: general wrong-way margin driven by interest rates.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – General versus specific**

General wrong-way margin comes from a market link between the margin’s value and the exposure (rates, FX). Specific wrong-way margin comes from “a more direct relationship between the type of margin and the counterparty credit quality”.

**Step 2 – Classify each arrangement**

Own-sovereign bonds posted by a bank: the bank’s credit and its sovereign’s are directly linked; GARP lists it with own bonds as specific (“another clearly problematic example”). Payer swap with government bonds: general. Receiver swap with government bonds: right-way. A corporate’s own bonds: specific.

⇒ Only B pairs the arrangement with its correct class.

**Interpretation**

Specific links call for qualitative treatment (eligibility limits, large haircuts); general links can be modelled and priced.

**LO:** CR-20 n: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.1 Table 20.7; 20.6.6

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 • shape A20·S3 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 n.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip: with a receiver swap a rate fall raises both the exposure and the bond’s value, a right-way position.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the payer-swap case is general (market-driven), not specific.

d.reason: Sibling swap: own bonds are linked to the poster’s credit quality, the specific case, not an interest rate effect.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.7 • shape A20·S4
questions.question: A clearing member’s risk committee asks how its default fund contribution to a CCP should be viewed in the light of wrong-way risk. A consultant compares the CCP’s loss waterfall with a collateralised debt obligation (CDO). Which statement best reflects that comparison?

options.text: The member’s default fund contribution is an equity (first-loss) tranche, hit whenever any member defaults, so its risk is mainly idiosyncratic.

The member’s default fund contribution and other loss-allocation exposures form a rather senior second-loss position, behind the defaulter’s resources and CCP equity, so losses reach it mainly in systemic scenarios.
The member’s default fund contribution ranks ahead of the defaulter’s initial margin, so it absorbs the first losses on any member default.
The member’s exposure through the default fund is diversified across many members, so like a senior CDO tranche it carries little systemic risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Map the waterfall to tranches**

The first loss is covered by the defaulter-pays initial margin and default fund, together with CCP equity. Surviving members, through their default fund contributions and other loss-allocation exposures, have a second-loss position.

**Step 2 – How senior is the second loss?**

It should correspond to a relatively unlikely event, otherwise initial margin coverage would be too thin. In CDO terms it is “rather senior”, and senior tranches are heavily concentrated in systemic risk.

⇒ Losses reach the member’s contribution mainly in systemic scenarios, exactly when WWR has made the defaulter’s resources insuﬀicient and other members are under stress.

**Interpretation**

A clearing member should treat its default fund contribution as a systemic, senior-tranche exposure and quantify it (its CVA to the CCP), rather than as a diversified, idiosyncratic one.

**LO:** CR-20 o: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs). • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.7, Figure 20.24

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.7 • shape A20·S4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 o.5)

a.reason: The equity (first-loss) layer is the defaulter’s own resources plus CCP equity, not the surviving members’ default fund.

c.reason: Reverses the waterfall order: the defaulter’s margin and default fund are used first.

d.reason: Seniority does not mean low systemic risk: senior tranches are known to be heavily concentrated in it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.7 • shape A20·S4
questions.question: A regulator’s review of a CCP that clears interest rate swaps and single-name CDSs lists ways in which wrong-way risk could leave the CCP’s resources short after a member default. Each of the following is consistent with GARP’s discussion EXCEPT:

options.text: Initial margins and default fund contributions are driven mainly by the market risk of each portfolio, so the CCP may implicitly ignore wrong-way risk.
Members may choose to post the eligible margin with the greatest risk relative to its haircut, which may also carry the greatest wrong-way risk to the CCP.
Multilateral netting across members breaks the link between a member’s default and the value of its cleared portfolio, so wrong-way risk is confined to bilateral trades.
The default of a large, highly rated, systemically important member is less likely but would be a bigger shock, so the wrong-way risk it brings is greater.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Check each channel against GARP**

A: initial margins and default fund contributions driven by market risk mean CCPs are “in danger of implicitly ignoring WWR”. Consistent. B: members “will naturally choose to post margin that has the greatest risk (relative to its haircut) and may also present the greatest WWR”. Consistent. D: WWR increases with credit quality; a better-quality member is less likely to default but its default is a bigger shock. Consistent.

**Step 2 – The exception**

Multilateral netting reduces the exposure the CCP faces, but a member whose default is linked to the value of its positions still leaves the CCP with that linked loss. GARP says CCPs are particularly prone to WWR, especially for CDSs.

⇒ C is the statement GARP does not support.

**Interpretation**

The three true statements are the CCP’s three WWR channels: market-risk-based margining, adverse selection in the margin it receives, and the size of systemic members’ defaults.

**LO:** CR-20 o: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs). • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.7 Central Clearing and WWR

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.7 • shape A20·S4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 o.6)

a.reason: Consistent with GARP: CCPs disassociate credit quality and exposure.

b.reason: Consistent with GARP: adverse selection in eligible margin, for example a European bank posting European sovereign debt.

d.reason: Consistent with GARP: WWR increases with credit quality, which is why it argues for more margin from systemic members.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.3 • shape A20·S5
questions.question: A bank’s model validation team tests the wrong-way risk produced by its CVA engine for a portfolio of payer interest rate swaps. The engine simulates the counterparty’s credit spread as a stochastic process correlated with interest rates and computes exposure only on paths where a default occurs. Even with the correlation set to +90%, the CVA rises only modestly above the no-WWR figure. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: The result is typical of the intensity (hazard rate) approach, which generates only weak dependence between exposure and default even near its correlation limits, so it may underestimate WWR.
The result shows that the payer swaps carry no material WWR, since the approach captures the full dependence once the correlation approaches 100%.
The engine must in fact be using a structural approach, which is known to give a weaker effect than the intensity approach at the same correlation.
The result is caused by the jump in interest rates the approach assumes at the default time, which offsets the correlation effect.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the method**

A stochastic credit spread correlated with the exposure drivers, with exposure computed only on default paths, is the intensity (hazard rate) approach.

**Step 2 – Explain the result**

GARP: the approach “can be seen to generate only weak dependence between exposure and default, given that the correlations used are close to their maximum and minimum values. Hence ... it may underestimate the true WWR effect.”

⇒ The modest response at +90% is a property of the model, not evidence that the WWR is small.

**Interpretation**

The validator should benchmark against a structural model (much stronger effect at the same correlation) or a jump model for any specific WWR. For payer swaps, positive spread-rate correlation is the WWR direction; history suggests the rate-default relation is generally negative.

**LO:** CR-20 p: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.3 Wrong-Way Risk Models, Figures 20.17 to 20.20

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.3 • shape A20·S5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 p.2)

b.reason: The intensity approach does not capture the full dependence even near ±100%; a weak response is not proof of weak WWR.

c.reason: Reversed: the structural approach gives a much stronger effect than the intensity approach, and it samples pre-computed exposures rather than simulating spreads.

d.reason: The intensity approach has no jump at default; jumps belong to the jump approaches.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.3 • shape A20·S5
questions.question: A counterparty risk manager wants to add general wrong-way risk to the bank’s CVA without re-running its exposure simulation, by linking the counterparty’s default time directly to the pre-computed exposure distribution through a bivariate (for example, Gaussian copula) distribution. Which of the following is the main drawback of this approach?

options.text: It requires exposures to be re-simulated on every path where a default occurs, which makes it computationally expensive.
It produces only a weak dependence between exposure and default, so its CVA barely changes with correlation.
It can only be calibrated by revaluing the portfolio at past dates against the counterparty’s historical credit spread.
Its correlation parameter is opaque and hard to calibrate, and the unconditional exposure distribution may not contain all the information needed to define WWR.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the method**

Mapping the default time and the exposure distribution onto a bivariate distribution, without re-running exposures, is the structural approach.

**Step 2 – Its trade-off**

The advantage is that pre-computed exposure distributions are used and WWR is added on top of the existing methodology. GARP: “this is also a disadvantage since it may not be appropriate to assume that all the relevant information to define WWR is contained within the unconditional exposure distribution”, and “the big drawback ... is that the correlation parameter ... is opaque and, therefore, diﬀicult to calibrate”.

⇒ D states both drawbacks.

**Interpretation**

The structural model gives a much stronger WWR effect than the intensity model at the same correlation, so the hard-to-calibrate correlation matters a great deal for the answer.

**LO:** CR-20 p: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.3, Figure 20.18

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.3 • shape A20·S5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 p.3)

a.reason: Reversed: the structural approach needs no re-simulation; simulating exposures on default paths is the intensity approach.

b.reason: Weak dependence is the intensity approach’s weakness; the structural effect is much stronger.

c.reason: Calibration against historical portfolio values and spreads describes the parametric approach.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.3 • shape A20·S5
questions.question: Following Hull and White (2011), a bank links each counterparty’s default probability to the value of its portfolio through a simple functional relationship. For one hedge fund, the team calibrates the dependency parameter by computing the value of its portfolio with the fund on dates over the past five years and comparing those values with the fund’s credit spread on the same dates. Which of the following is the most important condition for this calibration to be reliable?

options.text: The fund’s credit spread must be quoted in a liquid quanto CDS market, so that a jump in the FX rate at default can be implied.
The current portfolio must be similar in nature to the one used in the historical calibration, and the history must show a meaningful relationship between portfolio value and spread.
The correlation between the fund’s spread and interest rates must be close to +100%, otherwise the approach generates only weak dependence.
The default time and the exposure distribution must first be mapped onto a bivariate Gaussian distribution before the parameter can be estimated.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the method**

A simple functional link between default probability and portfolio value, calibrated from past portfolio values against the counterparty’s spread, is Hull and White’s parametric approach.

**Step 2 – When is the calibration reliable?**

GARP: “This approach obviously requires that the current portfolio of trades with the counterparty is similar in nature to that used in the historical calibration, in addition to the historical data showing a meaningful relationship.”

⇒ B is the condition.

**Interpretation**

If the hedge fund has changed strategy, the historical link between its portfolio value and its spread says little about today’s WWR; a what-if calibration is the alternative GARP mentions.

**LO:** CR-20 p: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.3 Wrong-Way Risk Models

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.3 • shape A20·S5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 p.4)

a.reason: Quanto CDS prices are evidence for jump approaches, not a requirement of the parametric approach.

c.reason: Weak dependence near extreme correlations is a property of the intensity approach.

d.reason: Bivariate mapping is the structural approach.

questions.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.22, 22.1 Waterfall and 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows
questions.question: A trustee’s analyst is documenting how the collateral interest collected at an interim year end is applied in a three-tranche CLO with an overcollateralization account of the type described in the reading. The deal pays trustee and management fees. Which sequence correctly describes the order of application?

options.text: Senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; fees; equity residual; overcollateralization account
Fees; senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; overcollateralization account up to its annual cap; equity residual
Fees; senior and mezzanine coupons pro rata to their par amounts; equity residual; overcollateralization account
Fees; overcollateralization account up to its annual cap; senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; equity residual

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Fees come first**

GARP: in addition to the coupons promised to the bonds, there are fees and other costs, “which typically take priority over coupons”.

⇒ Any sequence that pays coupons before fees (A) is out.

**Step 2 – Then the bonds, top down**

The senior coupon is paid in full before the mezzanine receives anything; the two are not paid pro rata.

⇒ C is out.

**Step 3 – Excess spread: account first, equity last**

Only what is left after the coupons is excess spread. Up to the cap $K$ goes to the overcollateralisation account; the equity receives the remainder.

⇒ D is out: the account is funded from excess spread, after the coupons, never ahead of them.

**Interpretation**

The order fees, senior, mezzanine, account, equity is the interim waterfall of Figure 1. It is also why the equity flow is the first casualty when defaults erode loan interest.

**LO:** CR-22 c: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.1 Waterfall; 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22, 22.1 Waterfall and 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-22 c.2)

a.reason: Puts fees after the coupons and the equity ahead of the account.

c.reason: Pays the bonds pro rata and puts the equity ahead of the account: two reversals of priority.

d.reason: Diverts to the account before the coupons are paid, which would starve the bonds the account is meant to protect.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.22, 22.1 Waterfall and 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows
questions.question: A risk committee is reviewing the overcollateralization mechanism of the CLO in the reading, in which part of the excess spread and all recoveries on defaulted loans are paid into an overcollateralization account that earns the money market rate. Which of the following statements about this mechanism is correct?

options.text: Recoveries are paid through the waterfall together with loan interest, so in a year with defaults the equity can receive more cash than in a year without defaults.
The diverted excess spread is hard credit enhancement: like the equity note, it is fully in place when the deal is issued.

The account is built up early in the deal’s life, when collateral cash flows are strongest; it pays bond interest if loan interest falls short, and any balance is released to the equity only at maturity.
The account protects the senior bond only: it may not be used to pay the mezzanine coupon, which must be met from loan interest alone.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – When the account fills**

Soft overcollateralisation builds credit enhancement “at the beginning of the life of the product, when collateral cash flows are strongest”. In Malz’s example it accumulates funds “while cumulative defaults are low”.

**Step 2 – What the account is for, and when it pays out**

GARP: the funds “will be used to pay interest on the bonds if there is not enough interest flowing from the loans”; any remaining funds “will be released to the equity tranche only at maturity”.

⇒ C states both points correctly.

**Interpretation**

Malz admits the mechanism “is not a robust mechanism for protecting the senior bonds”, but unless defaults come very early it has money in it when loan interest starts to fall short.

**LO:** CR-22 c: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), 22.1 Waterfall; 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22, 22.1 Waterfall and 22.2 Tracking the Interim Cash Flows (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-22 c.5)

a.reason: Recoveries are paid into the account, precisely so that the equity does not “perversely benefit from defaults”.

b.reason: Diverted excess spread is soft enhancement: it accrues over time and is not present at initiation. Hard overcollateralisation is collateral par above bond par at issue.

d.reason: The account pays interest on “the bonds”, both tranches; it is not reserved for the senior coupon.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
questions.question:
A risk consultant is presenting the final-year waterfall of a four-year CLO to a group of newly hired analysts at a Frankfurt bank. The deal has:

- Collateral: 120 identical floating-rate loans of EUR 1 million each, bought at par, paying the reference rate + 380 bps; surviving loans pay their final interest and redeem at par at the end of year 4
- Liabilities: senior notes EUR 96 million at reference + 70 bps; mezzanine notes EUR 15 million at reference + 600 bps; equity EUR 9 million
- The reference rate is flat at 4%; no fees
- Defaults: 13 loans in years 1 to 3 and 5 loans in year 4; 40% of defaulted par is recovered at year end
- The overcollateralisation account held EUR 7.2 million at the end of year 3 and earns 4%

Which of the following correctly states the amounts paid at the end of year 4 to the senior notes and to the equity tranche?

options.text: Senior EUR 100.512 million; equity EUR 0.432 million
Senior EUR 100.512 million; equity EUR 2.432 million
Senior EUR 96.000 million; equity EUR 6.944 million
Senior EUR 95.555 million; equity EUR 8.958 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Overcollateralisation account at maturity**

$7.2 \times1.04 = \text{EUR} 7.488$ million

⇒ The account earns one more year of interest and is now released into the terminal waterfall.

**Step 2 – Terminal available funds**

Survivors = 120−18 = 102: interest 102×7.8% = 7.956, redemption 102.0, recovery 0.4×5 = 2.0.

$F = 7.488 + 7.956 + 102.0 + 2.0 = \text{EUR} 119.444$ million

**Step 3 – Senior shortfall test**

Senior due $= 96 \times(1 + 0.047) = 100.512 \le F$

⇒ Paid in full; 119.444 − 100.512 = 18.932 is left.

**Step 4 – Mezzanine test, then the equity residual**

Mezzanine due $= 15 \times1.10 = 16.5 \le18.932, \text{Equity} = 18.932 - 16.5 = 2.432$

⇒ Both bonds are money good; the equity’s terminal claim is only what is left.

**Interpretation**

With 18 cumulative defaults (15% of the pool) the equity collects only EUR 2.432 million at maturity on a EUR 9 million tranche: it absorbed the first loss, exactly as the capital structure intends. A few more defaults would push the shortfall into the mezzanine before the senior is touched.

**LO:** CR-22 c: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization. CR-22 e: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure. CR-23 b: Explain the terms over-collateralization, first-loss piece, equity piece, and cash waterfall within the securitization process. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), Tracking the Final-Year Cash Flows, Table 22.2; Choudhry, Ch.12 (GARP CR Ch.23), Figure 23.4

CR-22 • Structured Credit Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook A9.5 • S4 • Map #9 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-22 c.6)

a.reason: Dropped term: left out the final-year recoveries of EUR 2.0 million, so $F =$ 117.444 and the equity gets 0.432.

c.reason: Paid the senior only its principal of 96.000 and forgot its final coupon, which inflates the equity residual to 119.444 − 96 − 16.5 = 6.944.

d.reason: Sibling swap with a pass-through: split $F$ pro rata to par, 119.444 × 96/120 = 95.555 and 119.444 × 9/120 = 8.958, ignoring the sequential priority of the waterfall.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.
questions.question:
A structured credit analyst at a Shanghai insurer, which holds the equity tranche of a five-year CLO, is checking the trustee’s report for the end of year 2. The deal terms are:

- Collateral: 80 identical floating-rate loans of CNY 25 million each, bought at par, paying the reference rate + 400 bps
- Liabilities: senior notes CNY 1,600 million at reference + 60 bps; mezzanine notes CNY 280 million at reference + 450 bps; equity CNY 120 million
- The reference rate is flat at 3%; all payments are annual, at year end
- Trustee and management fees of CNY 4 million a year are paid ahead of all note coupons
- Up to CNY 20 million of excess spread a year is diverted to the overcollateralisation account, which earns 3%; any remainder goes to the equity
- A loan that defaults pays no interest for that year; 40% of the defaulted par is recovered at year end and paid into the overcollateralisation account
- Defaults: 3 loans in year 1 and 5 loans in year 2; the account held CNY 50 million at the end of year 1

Which of the following correctly states the overcollateralisation account balance and the cash flow to the equity tranche at the end of year 2?

options.text: Account CNY 121.5 million; equity CNY 23.40 million
Account CNY 120.0 million; equity CNY 23.40 million
Account CNY 121.5 million; equity CNY 28.65 million
Account CNY 71.5 million; equity CNY 73.40 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Surviving loans and loan interest**

$N - \sum d = 80 - (3 + 5) = 72, L_{2} = 72 \times25 \times(0.03 + 0.04) = \text{CNY} 126.0$ million

⇒ Only loans that have not defaulted by the end of year 2 pay interest; the eight defaulted loans pay nothing.

**Step 2 – Excess spread and the custodian’s test**

$$B = 1{,}600 \times3.6\% + 280 \times7.5\% = 57.6 + 21.0 = 78.6$$

$L_{2} - \text{fees} - B = 126.0 - 4.0 - 78.6 = 43.4 > 0, 43.4 \ge K = 20 \Rightarrow OC_{2} = 20.0$

⇒ Excess spread is positive and exceeds the cap, so exactly CNY 20 million is diverted.

**Step 3 – Cash flow to the equity**

Equity$_{2} = 43.4 - 20.0 = \text{CNY} 23.40$ million

**Step 4 – Overcollateralisation account at the end of year 2**

$R_{2} = 0.40 \times5 \times25 = 50.0, 50.0 \times1.03 + 20.0 + 50.0 = \text{CNY} 121.5$ million

⇒ Last year’s balance earns 3%, then this year’s diversion and recoveries are added.

**Interpretation**

The equity flow falls from CNY 32.15 million in year 1 to 23.40 million as cumulative defaults erode loan interest. The account, now CNY 121.5 million, is soft enhancement: it pays bond interest if loan interest ever falls short and reaches the equity only at maturity. (Dropping the fee would give equity 27.40; ignoring the cap would divert all 43.4 and leave the equity nothing.)

**LO:** CR-22 e: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure. CR-22 f: Describe the treatment of excess spread in a securitization structure and estimate the value of the overcollateralization account at the end of each year. CR-22 g: Explain the tests on the excess spread that a custodian must go through at the end of each year to determine the cash flow to the overcollateralization account and to the equity noteholders. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), Tracking the Interim Cash Flows; Table 22.1

**Source:** Workbook A9.4 • S2, S3 • Map #9 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-22 e.3)

b.reason: Dropped term: did not grow the year-1 balance at 3%, 50.0+20.0+50.0 = 120.0. The equity flow is unaffected.

c.reason: Wrong input: counted only year-2 defaults, so 75 loans pay interest, $L_{2} = 131.25$, excess spread 48.65, equity 48.65 − 20 = 28.65. The cap still binds, so the account is unchanged.

d.reason: Recoveries routed through the waterfall to the equity: equity 23.4+50.0 = 73.40, account 51.5 + 20.0 = 71.5. This is exactly the perverse benefit from defaults that escrowing recoveries prevents.

questions.loText: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.22, Tracking the Final-Year Cash Flows, Table 22.2 • shape A9·S4
questions.question: A CLO analyst at a Toronto pension fund is projecting the final-year waterfall of a five-year CLO with the structure of the reading: 100 loans of USD 1 million paying Libor + 350 bps; senior notes USD 85 million at Libor + 50 bps; mezzanine notes USD 10 million at Libor + 500 bps; equity USD 5 million; Libor flat at 5%. Recoveries are 40% and are paid into the overcollateralization account, which earns 5% and held USD 16.385 million at the end of year 4. By the end of year 4, 24 loans have defaulted, and 6 more default in year 5. Surviving loans pay their final interest and redeem at par at the end of year 5. Which of the following is closest to the mezzanine bond’s credit loss at maturity?

options.text: USD 4.12 million
USD 5.12 million
USD 5.94 million
USD 7.52 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Account at maturity**

$16.385 \times1.05 = \text{USD} 17.204$ million

⇒ The year-4 balance earns one more year of interest before it is released.

**Step 2 – Terminal available funds**

Survivors = 100 − 24 − 6 = 70: final interest 70 × 0.085 = 5.950, redemption 70.000, final-year recoveries 0.4 × 6 = 2.400.

$F = 17.204 + 5.950 + 70.000 + 2.400 = \text{USD} 95.554$ million

**Step 3 – Senior test**

Senior due $85 \times1.055 = 89.675 \le F$ : paid in full, leaving 95.554 − 89.675 = 5.879.

**Step 4 – Mezzanine test**

Mezzanine due 10 × 1.10 = 11.000; it receives 5.879.

Credit loss $= 11.000 - 5.879 = \text{USD} 5.12$ million

⇒ The equity receives nothing.

**Interpretation**

With 30 cumulative defaults the mezzanine recovers only USD 5.879 million of the USD 11.0 million it is owed (it loses about 47%), while the senior is untouched: the thin junior tranche absorbs the hit once the equity is gone.

**LO:** CR-22 e: Calculate and evaluate one or two iterations of interim cashflows in a three-tiered securitization structure.

- **Reference:** Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), Tracking the Final-Year Cash Flows, Table 22.2

CR-22 • Structured Credit Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.22, Tracking the Final-Year Cash Flows, Table 22.2 • shape A9·S4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-22 e.7)

a.reason: Measured the loss against the mezzanine’s par of 10.000 only, forgetting the final coupon it is owed: 10.000 − 5.879 = 4.12.

c.reason: Did not grow the account for year 5: $F = 94.735$, so the mezzanine receives 5.060 and loses 5.94.

d.reason: Left out the final-year recoveries: $F = 93.154$, so the mezzanine receives 3.479 and loses 7.52.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures.
questions.question:
A junior surveillance analyst at an Indian asset manager is preparing the monthly investor report on a credit card master trust. The month-end ageing of receivables is:

| Status | INR billion |
|---|---|
| Total credit card receivables (month end) | 48.0 |
| 30 to 59 days past due | 2.4 |
| 60 to 89 days past due | 1.5 |
| 90 to 119 days past due | 1.2 |
| 120 days or more past due | 0.6 |
| Receivables written off during the month | 0.36 |

Which of the following is closest to the delinquency ratio as defined for credit card ABS performance analysis?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Delinquent receivables (overdue more than 90 days)**

$1.2 + 0.6 = \text{INR} 1.8$ billion

⇒ Only the 90-plus buckets meet the book’s definition of delinquent.

**Step 2 – Delinquency ratio**

Delinquency ratio $= \frac{1.8}{48.0} = 3.75\%$

⇒ 3.75% of the pool is seriously past due.

**Interpretation**

Because delinquencies precede write-offs, a rising delinquency ratio is the early warning that the default ratio and the early amortisation triggers may be hit in coming months (Figure 1).

**LO:** CR-23 g: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures. • **Reference:** Choudhry, Structured Credit Products 2e, Ch.12 (GARP CR Ch.23), Performance Analysis for Credit Card ABS

**Source:** Workbook A9.1 • S1 • Aug-2026 • Map #9 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-23 g.2)

a.reason: Sibling swap: used write-offs, which gives the default ratio 0.36/48.0 = 0.75%.

b.reason: Scope error: counted only the 90 to 119 day bucket, 1.2/48.0 = 2.50%, omitting receivables 120 days or more past due.

d.reason: Scope error: counted every past-due bucket, (2.4 + 1.5 + 1.2 + 0.6)/48.0 = 11.88%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures.
questions.question:
A rating agency analyst in Sydney is testing a credit card ABS against its monthly payment rate trigger. The trust documents set a minimum MPR of 15.0% as an early amortisation trigger: if the month’s MPR falls below it, the revolving period ends. During the month, the trust’s data are:

- Outstanding pool balance: AUD 1,500 million
- Principal collections: AUD 210 million
- Finance charge (interest) collections: AUD 27 million
- Receivables written off: AUD 6 million
- New receivables purchased by the trust (revolving period): AUD 180 million

Which of the following correctly states the MPR and whether the early amortisation trigger is hit?

options.text: MPR 3.8%; trigger hit
MPR 14.0%; trigger hit
MPR 15.8%; trigger not hit
MPR 15.8%; trigger hit

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Collections (principal and interest)**

$210 + 27 = \text{AUD} 237$ million

⇒ MPR measures the proportion of the principal and interest on the pool repaid in the period.

**Step 2 – MPR**

MPR $= \frac{\text{collections}}{\text{outstanding pool balance}} = \frac{237}{1{,}500} = 15.8\%$

⇒ Cardholders repay 15.8% of the pool in the month.

**Step 3 – Trigger test**

15.8% ≥ 15.0% (minimum) ⇒ trigger not hit.

⇒ The revolving period continues: principal collections keep buying new receivables.

**Interpretation**

A falling MPR signals slower repayment; the rating agencies require every non-amortising ABS to set a minimum MPR as an early amortisation trigger. Write-offs and new purchases do not enter the ratio (deducting write-offs would give 15.4%, still above the floor).

**LO:** CR-23 g: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures. CR-23 f: Explain the various performance analysis tools for securitized structures and identify the asset classes they are most applicable to. • **Reference:** Choudhry, Ch.12 (GARP CR Ch.23), Performance Analysis for Credit Card ABS; Table 23.2

**Source:** Workbook A9.2 • self-generated (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-23 g.4)

a.reason: Netted off the new receivables bought in the revolving period, (237 − 180)/1,500 = 3.8%, which then falls below the floor.

b.reason: Dropped interest collections, 210/1,500 = 14.0%, which falls below the floor.

d.reason: Right MPR, polarity flip on the trigger: treated the 15.0% minimum as a ceiling, so an MPR above it was read as a breach.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures.
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Canadian pension fund is reviewing an RMBS whose collateral pool consists of three loan groups. The notes pay investors a net coupon of 4.10%.

| Loan group | Balance (CAD million) | Mortgage rate | Remaining term (months) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60 | 4.0% | 300 |
| 2 | 90 | 5.2% | 240 |
| 3 | 150 | 6.0% | 120 |

Which of the following is closest to the pool’s weighted average coupon (WAC)?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Balance times rate for each group**

60 × 4.0% = 2.40, 90 × 5.2% = 4.68, 150 × 6.0% = 9.00 (CAD million)

**Step 2 – Total balance**

$60 + 90 + 150 = \text{CAD} 300$ million

**Step 3 – WAC**

WAC $= \frac{2.40 + 4.68 + 9.00}{300} = \frac{16.08}{300} = 5.36\%$

⇒ The pool earns 5.36% on average, weighted by loan balance.

**Interpretation**

Against the 4.10% net investor coupon, the pool has 1.26 percentage points of coupon headroom, an indication of its ability to pay. WAC drifts as loans repay (here the high-rate group 3 has the shortest term). The remaining terms are irrelevant to WAC; they would give a WAM of 192 months.

**LO:** CR-23 g: Define and calculate the delinquency ratio, default ratio, monthly payment rate (MPR), debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the weighted average coupon (WAC), the weighted average maturity (WAM), and the weighted average life (WAL) for relevant securitized structures. • **Reference:** Choudhry, Ch.12 (GARP CR Ch.23), Performance Analysis for MBS

**Source:** Workbook A9.3 • self-generated (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-23 g.5)

a.reason: Intermediate result: reported WAC minus the net coupon, 5.36% − 4.10% = 1.26%.

b.reason: Wrong weights: weighted the rates by remaining term, (300 × 4.0 + 240 × 5.2 + 120 × 6.0)/660 = 4.80%.

c.reason: Wrong weights: simple average of the three rates, (4.0 + 5.2 + 6.0)/3 = 5.07%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate.
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a US life insurer is reviewing the monthly trustee report on a non-agency RMBS, 18 months after the pool’s origination. The report shows:

- Collateral pool balance at the start of the month: USD 820.0 million
- Notes outstanding at the start of the month: USD 779.0 million (the deal is overcollateralised)
- Overcollateralisation reserve account: USD 6.5 million
- Scheduled principal received in the month: USD 1.4 million
- Unscheduled prepayments received in the month: USD 5.2 million

Which of the following is closest to the pool’s CPR and its speed expressed against the PSA benchmark?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – SMM**

SMM $= \frac{\text{prepayment}}{\text{pool balance} - \text{scheduled principal}} = \frac{5.2}{820.0 - 1.4} = \frac{5.2}{818.6} = 0.6352\%$

⇒ 0.635% of the pool’s start-of-month balance, net of scheduled principal, prepaid this month.

**Step 2 – CPR**

CPR $= 1 - (1 - 0.006352)^{12} = 7.36\%$

⇒ At this pace roughly 7.36% of the pool would prepay over a year.

**Step 3 – 100% PSA benchmark at month 18**

$m = 18 \le30 \Rightarrow\text{CPR}_{100\% \text{PSA}} = 0.2\% \times18 = 3.6\%$

⇒ The pool is still on the seasoning ramp, so the 6% plateau does not apply yet.

**Step 4 – PSA speed**

PSA $= \frac{7.36\%}{3.6\%} \times100 = 204\%$ PSA

**Interpretation**

The pool is prepaying about twice as fast as the benchmark (Figure 3; 204.5% on the unrounded CPR). For a given price this reduces the yield on the MBS and shortens the WAL, so the insurer should re-run its cash flow projections at the faster speed. The reserve account balance is irrelevant to the prepayment measures.

**LO:** CR-23 h: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate. • **Reference:** Choudhry, Ch.12 (GARP CR Ch.23), Example 23.2 Forecasting Prepayment Levels; Table 23.2

**Source:** Workbook A9.6 • S5, S7 • Map #9 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-23 h.5)

a.reason: Unit error: used the monthly SMM as if it were the annual CPR, 0.6352/3.6 × 100 = 17.6% PSA.

b.reason: Threshold error: compared with the 6% plateau although month 18 is still on the ramp, 7.36/6 × 100 = 123% PSA.

d.reason: Wrong input twin (the overcollateralisation twist): divided by the note balance instead of the pool balance, SMM = 5.2/(779.0 − 1.4) = 0.6687%, CPR 7.74%, 215% PSA.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate.
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore life insurer is reviewing the investment team’s methodology note on how prepayments are forecast for the insurer’s MBS holdings. Which of the following statements in the note is correct?

options.text: The WAL of a pass-through note is quoted under a stated prepayment assumption, and a faster assumed PSA speed shortens it.
For a given price, faster prepayments increase the yield on the MBS, because principal is returned to investors earlier.
For commercial MBS, prepayment speed is tracked with the DSCR, the ratio of net operating income to debt payments.
A pool at 100% PSA prepays at a constant 6% CPR from origination, and faster speeds are multiples of that rate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why A is correct**

Amortising (pass-through) structures are priced and traded on expected maturity and WAL, and “a WAL approach incorporates various pre-payment assumptions”; Malz adds that “a WAL is associated with a particular prepayment assumption”. With WAL $= \sum(a/365)$ PF$(s)$, faster prepayment cuts the pool factor sooner, so the WAL shortens.

**Interpretation**

Prepayment forecasts (SMM, CPR, PSA) drive the projected cash flows, the yield and the WAL together; an audit should check that all three are run off the same prepayment assumption.

**LO:** CR-23 h: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate. CR-23 f: Explain the various performance analysis tools for securitized structures and identify the asset classes they are most applicable to. CR-22 k: Describe risk factors that impact structured products. • **Reference:** Choudhry, Ch.12 (GARP CR Ch.23), Amortising Structures, Example 23.2, Table 23.2; Malz, Ch.9 (GARP CR Ch.22), Capital Structure and Credit Losses in a Securitization

**Source:** Workbook A9.7 • S6, S7 • Map #9 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-23 h.8)

b.reason: Polarity flip: Choudhry states that prepayments, for a given price, reduce the yield on the MBS.

c.reason: Sibling swap: DSCR (net operating income / debt payments) is the CMBS credit measure of the borrower’s ability to repay. Prepayment is measured by SMM, CPR and PSA for mortgages (Table 23.2).

d.reason: Scope error: dropped the seasoning ramp. 100% PSA starts at 0, rises 0.2% a month and reaches 6% only at month 30, because mortgages prepay slower in their first 30 months.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
questions.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
questions.topic: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.5, 5.6.3 and Ch.10, 10.3 to 10.5 • shape D20·S5
questions.question: The head of credit portfolio management at a European bank is summarising for the risk committee how four credit risk models recognise losses and treat dependence between defaults. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: CreditMetrics is a default-mode model: it books a loss only when a counterparty defaults, and default correlation enters through uncertainty about the overall default rate.
Moody’s KMV revalues each loan at the horizon using rating-specific credit spreads, so it books losses from downgrades as well as from defaults.
CreditRisk+ uses each borrower’s capital structure and asset volatility, so the correlation between defaults comes from the correlation between asset returns.
CreditRisk+ books losses only on default, and default correlation enters through uncertainty about the default rate; the greater that uncertainty, the fatter the tail of the loss distribution.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Loss recognition**

CreditRisk+ (like Vasicek) estimates losses from defaults only; CreditMetrics counts defaults and downgrades, with upgrades as negative losses. Moody’s KMV produces an EDF for a single firm; it does not revalue loans on rating spreads.

**Step 2 – Dependence between defaults**

In CreditRisk+, defaults are independent given the default rate; uncertainty about the rate (gamma-distributed, giving a negative binomial) creates the correlation. With 4 expected defaults, Hull’s 99.9th percentile rises from 11 defaults with no uncertainty to 98 when the rate’s standard deviation is 10. CreditMetrics instead correlates rating changes with a Gaussian copula calibrated to equity correlations.

⇒ D is the only statement that pairs the right loss recognition with the right correlation mechanism.

**Interpretation**

This is the four-way grid of shape S5: default mode versus mark-to-market on one axis, the source of correlation on the other (the comparison table in Section 1).

**LO:** CR-5 f: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model. CR-10 e: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation. • **Reference:** Doumpos et al. 2019, Ch.1 (GARP CR Ch.5), 5.6.3.2 and 5.6.3.3; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19 (GARP CR Ch.10), 10.3 to 10.5, Table 10.4

CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5, 5.6.3 and Ch.10, 10.3 to 10.5 • shape D20·S5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-5 f.8)

a.reason: Sibling swap: it gives CreditMetrics the default-mode recognition and the correlation mechanism of CreditRisk+.

b.reason: Sibling swap: rating-spread revaluation is CreditMetrics; KMV maps DD to an EDF.

c.reason: Sibling swap with the structural models: CreditRisk+ explicitly does not use the capital structure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
questions.question: A credit analyst at a Canadian pension fund follows a BBB-rated industrial issuer. Over the past year two things happened. First, a two-month supply disruption raised the issuer’s default probability over the next six months, with almost no effect on its three-to-five-year default probability. Later, the issuer lost its largest customer under a long-term contract, permanently reducing its cash flows. Based on how rating agencies set ratings, which response by the agency is most likely?

options.text: A downgrade after the disruption and an upgrade once it ends, so that the rating always reflects current information.
No change after the disruption; a downgrade after the loss of the customer, because that is a long-term change in creditworthiness.
No change after either event, because agencies change ratings only at fixed annual reviews.
A downgrade after the disruption and no change after the loss of the customer, because agencies weight short-term default risk most heavily.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The supply disruption**

It raises the six-month default probability but not the three-to-five-year one. Agencies rate through the cycle, so they would not usually act.

⇒ No change after the first event.

**Step 2 – The lost customer**

A permanent cut in cash flows is a long-term change in creditworthiness, the trigger for a rating change.

⇒ A downgrade after the second event.

**Interpretation**

Stability means avoiding reversals, not ignoring information. A downgrade followed by an upgrade a few weeks later is exactly the reversal agencies try to avoid.

**LO:** CR-9 a: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.1 Credit Ratings

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 a.4)

a.reason: Describes the reversal agencies avoid; a rating is not meant to track every short-term development.

c.reason: There is no fixed-review rule; a long-term change does lead to a rating change.

d.reason: Reverses the horizon: agencies look through short-term risk and act on long-term change.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 and 9.1.1
questions.question: The CRO of a regional bank asks which sources of default risk can be used for three borrowers. Borrower X is a large listed company with publicly traded bonds. Borrower Y is a listed mid-sized company with no bonds outstanding; it borrows only from banks. Borrower Z is a privately held family manufacturer. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Agency ratings are available for all three, because agencies rate every company that borrows from banks.
An equity-based estimate is the natural tool for Z, because such models need no market prices.

An agency rating is usually available only for X. Y and Z need the bank’s internal rating; an equity-based estimate (Moody’s KMV or Kamakura) is also possible for Y, whose shares trade, but not for Z.
The bank should use its internal rating for X rather than the agency rating, because agency ratings are too stable to be informative for large companies.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Agency coverage**

Agency ratings are usually available only for companies that have issued publicly traded debt.

⇒ X is likely rated; Y (bank loans only) and Z (private) are likely not.

**Step 2 – Equity-based estimates**

Moody’s KMV and Kamakura work from the equity price and other variables. Y’s shares trade, so an estimate can be produced; Z has no share price.

**Step 3 – Internal ratings**

The bank can rate any client from its financial statements, so Y and Z both get an internal rating.

**Interpretation**

The data each method needs decides where it can be used: public debt for agency ratings, a share price for equity-based estimates, financial statements for internal ratings.

**LO:** CR-9 a: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.1 and 9.1.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 and 9.1.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 a.5)

a.reason: Coverage error: many companies, especially small and private ones, have no agency rating.

b.reason: Reversed: equity-based models need a market price, which a private firm does not have.

d.reason: Stability does not make agency ratings uninformative; for a rated issuer they are a primary source, and the bank can add its own view.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 and 9.7.1 (Table 9.6)
questions.question: A risk manager at a Singapore bank sets the default probability of each agency-rated borrower in a recession stress test equal to the long-run average one-year default rate of its rating in GARP Table 9.1 (S&P, 1981 to 2020). Annual default rates for all rated companies have ranged from 0.15% (1981) to 4.19% (2009). Which statement best assesses this approach?

options.text: It is appropriate: because ratings are stable, each rating grade has the same default rate in every year.
It overstates stress PDs: in a recession agencies quickly downgrade weak borrowers, so each grade keeps only its safer members.
It is appropriate: the 1981 to 2020 average includes 2009, the worst year, so it already reflects recession conditions.
It understates stress PDs: agencies rate through the cycle, so ratings move little in a recession while each grade’s realised default rate rises; the long-run average blends good and bad years.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the Table 9.1 figure is**

It is the average default experience of each grade over 1981 to 2020, good and bad years together.

**Step 2 – How a grade’s default rate behaves in a recession**

Agencies rate through the cycle, so borrowers keep their ratings while their near-term default risk rises. Default rates vary markedly from year to year (0.15% to 4.19% for all rated companies), so the default rate of a given grade is higher in bad years.

⇒ The long-run average understates the stress default rate for each grade.

**Interpretation**

This is the price of rating stability for a risk manager: the rating is a long-horizon, through-the-cycle signal, so stress PDs must be adjusted upwards (or taken from a point-in-time system, CR-6 b).

**LO:** CR-9 a: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.1 Credit Ratings; 9.7.1 Reason for the Difference, Table 9.6

CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 and 9.7.1 (Table 9.6) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 a.6)

a.reason: Stable ratings do not imply stable default rates; the economy moves the default rate of every grade.

b.reason: Through-the-cycle agencies do not downgrade quickly on cyclical news; that is the opposite of the stability objective.

c.reason: One bad year among forty barely moves the average; the average is a typical-year figure, not a recession figure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.1 (extended with the 9.2 time profile; rewritten as multiple
questions.question:
choice)

A trainee analyst at a German bank is asked which ratings on the S&P scale are investment grade, and how the probability of default in each individual year (the marginal PD) typically evolves for those ratings in the first few years after the rating is assigned. Which answer is correct?
