options.text: AAA to A; the marginal PD falls with time because a creditworthy issuer becomes safer as it ages.
AAA to BBB; the marginal PD tends to rise with time because the issuer starts creditworthy and the longer the period, the greater the chance that its financial health declines.
AAA to BBB; the marginal PD falls with time because the next year or two are critical and the survivors are healthier.
AAA to BB; the marginal PD is constant because rating agencies rate through the cycle.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Investment-grade ratings**

On the S&P scale AAA, AA, A and BBB are investment grade; BB and below are non-investment grade.

⇒ A (stops at A) and D (includes BB) fail on the scale.

**Step 2 – The time profile**

For investment-grade bonds the PD in a year tends to increase with time in the first few years: the issuer starts creditworthy, and time gives its financial health room to decline.

**Interpretation**

GARP’s own example is the A grade: 0.05%, 0.08%, 0.09% and 0.11% in years 1 to 4. The “critical period” story in C is the explanation for the lowest grades, the opposite profile.

**LO:** CR-9 c: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.2 Historical Default Probabilities, Table 9.1; Practice Question 9.1

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.1 (extended with the 9.2 time profile; rewritten as multiple (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 c.1)

a.reason: Leaves out BBB and gives the profile the wrong direction.

c.reason: Right scale, but the falling profile and its explanation belong to poorly rated issuers.

d.reason: BB is non-investment grade, and rating through the cycle concerns how agencies change ratings, not the PD profile after a rating is assigned.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.2 and 9.2.1
questions.question:
A credit portfolio manager at a Hong Kong bank argues that the falling year-by-year default probabilities of CCC/C issuers in GARP Table 9.1 say nothing about the issuers’ health, because a shrinking pool of survivors mechanically produces fewer defaults each year. An analyst has computed the following for CCC/C issuers:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unconditional (marginal) PD (%) | 28.30 | 10.03 | 5.09 | 2.94 | 2.22 |
| Conditional PD, given no earlier default (%) | 28.30 | 13.99 | 8.25 | 5.20 | 4.14 |

Which response is correct?

options.text: The manager is right: the conditional PDs decline only because they are computed from the same cumulative table.
The manager is right: with a constant hazard rate the conditional PD would fall in exactly this way.

The manager is wrong: the conditional PD, which already removes the effect of the shrinking pool, also falls, so a CCC/C issuer that survives the first year or two is genuinely less likely to default.
The manager is wrong: if the survivors’ health were improving, the unconditional PDs would rise over time.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the conditional PD removes**

The conditional PD divides the year’s defaults by the issuers still alive at the start of the year. A shrinking pool cannot, by itself, make it fall.

**Step 2 – What a shrinking pool alone would produce**

With a constant hazard rate the conditional PD is the same every year ($1 - \text{e}^{-\lambda}$) while the unconditional PD falls slowly (CR-9 e).

**Step 3 – Compare with the data**

The CCC/C conditional PD falls from 28.30% to 13.99%, 8.25%, 5.20% and 4.14%.

⇒ The default intensity of survivors really declines: the manager is wrong.

**Interpretation**

This is the evidence behind GARP’s “critical period” explanation: an issuer that survives the first year or two is in better health.

**LO:** CR-9 c: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default. CR-9 e: Define the hazard rate and use it to define probability functions for default time as well as to calculate conditional and unconditional default probabilities. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.2 and 9.2.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.2 and 9.2.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 c.4)

a.reason: Being computed from the same table does not force a decline; the decline in the conditional PD is a feature of the data.

b.reason: Under a constant hazard the conditional PD is constant, not falling (the memoryless property).

d.reason: Unconditional PDs can fall even when survivors are unchanged, so a rise is not required; the conditional PD is the right test.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.
questions.question:
A model validator at an Indian bank reviews a sentence in the bank’s credit policy: “In the agency data, a higher rating always means a strictly lower cumulative default rate, at every horizon.” She checks an excerpt of GARP Table 9.1 (cumulative default rates, %):

| Rating | 5 years | 7 years | 10 years | 15 years |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AAA | 0.34 | 0.51 | 0.70 | 0.90 |
| AA | 0.30 | 0.49 | 0.70 | 0.99 |
| A | 0.46 | 0.76 | 1.20 | 1.84 |

Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The sentence fails: AAA’s rate is above AA’s at 5 and 7 years and equal at 10 years. The inverse relationship holds across the scale as a whole but not strictly between the top two grades.
The sentence holds: AAA has the lowest cumulative default rate at every horizon shown.
The sentence fails because A-rated issuers default less than AA-rated issuers at long horizons.
The sentence fails because AAA cumulative default rates fall at longer horizons.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Compare AAA with AA horizon by horizon**

5 years: 0.34 against 0.30 (AAA higher). 7 years: 0.51 against 0.49 (AAA higher). 10 years: 0.70 against 0.70 (equal). 15 years: 0.90 against 0.99 (AAA lower).

⇒ “Strictly lower at every horizon” fails.

**Step 2 – Check the rest of the scale**

A is above AA at every horizon shown, and the same holds down the full table.

**Interpretation**

The inverse relationship is a description of the whole scale; between the top two grades, where defaults are very rare, small reversals appear. An “always” or “strictly” option is the absolute-qualifier trap.

**LO:** CR-9 c: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.2, Table 9.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.2 (Table 9.1) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 c.5)

b.reason: AAA is not the lowest at 5 and 7 years.

c.reason: A is above AA at every horizon shown.

d.reason: Cumulative rates cannot fall; AAA rises from 0.34% to 0.90%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.
questions.question: A relationship manager at a UK bank compares two loans: a 15-year amortisation-free loan to a BBB-rated borrower and a one-year loan to a B-rated borrower. From GARP Table 9.1, the BBB cumulative default rate at 15 years is 4.54% and the B cumulative default rate at one year is 3.34%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The B loan has the higher probability of default, because a lower rating means a higher probability of default whatever the horizon.
The two probabilities cannot be compared, because one figure is cumulative and the other is marginal.
The BBB loan’s probability of default over its life is about 15 × 0.16% = 2.40%, below the B loan’s 3.34%.

The BBB loan has the higher probability of default over its life (4.54% against 3.34%): the inverse relationship between rating and PD compares borrowers at the same horizon, and cumulative PDs rise with the horizon.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read both figures as lifetime PDs**

Both are cumulative rates: 4.54% is the BBB probability of default within 15 years; 3.34% is the B probability within one year.

**Step 2 – Compare**

4.54% > 3.34%, so the long BBB loan has the higher probability of default over its life.

**Interpretation**

The rating ranks borrowers at a fixed horizon. Over different horizons the cumulative curve does the work: a 15-year exposure gives a BBB borrower time to deteriorate, exactly the rising investment-grade profile.

**LO:** CR-9 c: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.2, Table 9.1

CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.2 (Table 9.1) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 c.6)

a.reason: Absolute qualifier: “whatever the horizon” ignores that cumulative PDs rise with time.

b.reason: Both figures come from the cumulative table, so they are directly comparable.

c.reason: Linear scaling of the one-year rate; the actual 15-year cumulative rate is 4.54%, because the BBB marginal PD rises over time.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.12 (rewritten as multiple choice)
questions.question: A junior analyst at a Dubai bank is building a loss-given-default database for defaulted corporate bonds. Following the usual convention, how should the recovery rate on a defaulted bond be measured?

options.text: As the amount finally paid to bondholders at the end of the bankruptcy process, as a percentage of the bond’s market price just before default.
As the price at which the bond trades about one month after default, as a percentage of its principal amount.
As the bond’s price immediately before default, as a percentage of its principal amount.
As one minus the loss given default, with the loss measured against the bond’s market value one month before default.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Timing**

The recovery rate is read from the market price of the defaulted bond about one month after default, not at the end of the bankruptcy process and not before default.

**Step 2 – Base**

The price is expressed as a percentage of the bond’s principal (face value).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

A market price soon after default gives a timely, observable number for every defaulted bond; that is why databases and the CDS auction work this way. Loss given default is then $1 - R$.

**LO:** CR-9 f: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.3 Recovery Rates; Practice Question 9.12

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.12 (rewritten as multiple choice) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 f.1)

a.reason: Wrong timing (end of the process) and wrong base (pre-default market price).

c.reason: A pre-default price measures the market’s view before the event, not what is recovered.

d.reason: Circular, and measured against the wrong base: LGD is defined from $R$, with both relative to principal.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
questions.question: A credit analyst at a Luxembourg fund reviews Moody’s average recovery rates on corporate bonds (issuer weighted, 1983 to 2021): first lien 54.6%; second lien 44.3%; senior unsecured 38.0%; senior subordinated 31.0%; subordinated 32.1%; junior subordinated 22.3%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Recovery falls strictly with each step down in seniority, so subordinated bonds always recover less than senior subordinated bonds.
Second lien bonds recover more on average than first lien bonds, because they also have a claim on collateral.

Bonds with a claim on collateral recover more on average than unsecured bonds, and recovery broadly falls with seniority, although subordinated bonds recovered slightly more on average than senior subordinated bonds.
Seniority makes little difference: first lien and junior subordinated bonds differ by less than 10 percentage points.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Secured against unsecured**

First lien 54.6% and second lien 44.3% are both above the best unsecured class, senior unsecured at 38.0%.

**Step 2 – Down the unsecured ranking**

Senior unsecured 38.0%, senior subordinated 31.0%, subordinated 32.1%, junior subordinated 22.3%: broadly falling, with one small reversal.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Seniority is the main driver of recovery, but the averages are historical, issuer-weighted figures, so they are not perfectly ordered.

**LO:** CR-9 f: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.3, Table 9.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.3 (Table 9.2) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 f.2)

a.reason: Absolute qualifier: subordinated (32.1%) is above senior subordinated (31.0%).

b.reason: The first lien has the first claim on collateral and the higher recovery.

d.reason: The range is 54.6 − 22.3 = 32.3 percentage points.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
questions.question: A risk manager at a US mortgage lender is explaining to the board why recovery rates on defaulted mortgages fell during the 2007 to 2008 crisis. Which sequence is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Rising default rates led to more foreclosures, more houses offered for sale and falling house prices, which reduced recovery rates.
Rising default rates led lenders to hold foreclosed houses off the market, which kept house prices and recovery rates stable.
Falling house prices reduced foreclosures, so fewer houses were sold and recovery rates fell for lack of buyers.
Rising default rates gave lenders more workout experience, which raised recovery rates, but higher interest rates more than offset this.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Start from the defaults**

Higher mortgage default rates lead to foreclosures.

**Step 2 – Supply and price**

Foreclosed houses are offered for sale; the extra supply pushes house prices down.

**Step 3 – Recovery**

The lender recovers what the collateral fetches, so recovery rates fall.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The same loop runs through corporate credit: the economy that causes defaults also lowers what defaulted assets are worth.

**LO:** CR-9 f: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.3.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.3.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 f.4)

b.reason: Contradicts the reading: foreclosed houses came to market and prices fell.

c.reason: Reverses the causal chain; defaults drove foreclosures, which drove prices down.

d.reason: Gets the direction wrong; recoveries fell because collateral values fell.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
questions.question: A bank’s credit portfolio model simulates correlated defaults but assigns every defaulted loan a fixed 45% recovery rate, whatever the number of defaults in the simulated year. Which statement best describes the effect on the simulated loss distribution?

options.text: Losses in high-default years are overstated, because recoveries rise when many firms default and collateral markets deepen.
Expected loss is overstated in every year, because a fixed recovery rate is always too low.
Losses in high-default years are understated, so the tail of the loss distribution, and any credit VaR read from it, is too thin: in practice those years also bring lower recoveries.
The tail is unaffected, because once seniority is fixed, recovery rates are unrelated to default rates.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the fixed recovery is wrong**

In high-default years actual recoveries are low (as low as about 30%), so a fixed 45% is too high exactly then.

**Step 2 – Effect on the distribution**

Simulated losses in the worst years are too small, so the right tail is too thin and a credit VaR read from it is too low.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

A fixed recovery near the long-run average can leave expected loss roughly right while getting the tail wrong. Models with random recovery tied to the default environment address this.

**LO:** CR-9 f: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.3.1

CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.3.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 f.6)

a.reason: Reverses the sign of the default and recovery link.

b.reason: A fixed rate near the average is too low in good years and too high in bad years; “overstated in every year” is false.

d.reason: Seniority does not remove the cyclical link; the average recovery in a year moves with the default rate.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.13 (rewritten as multiple choice)
questions.question: A credit analyst is checking GARP Table 9.5 against Table 9.4. For B-rated issuers, Table 9.4 gives a seven-year cumulative default probability of 20.99% and an average seven-year credit spread of 481.04 basis points; the recovery rate is assumed to be 40%. Which of the following is closest to the average seven-year hazard rate calculated from the historical default probability?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Direct formula**

$$\bar{\lambda}_{\text{hist}} = -\frac{1}{7} \text{ln}(1 - 0.2099) = \frac{- \text{ln}(0.7901)}{7} = \frac{0.23560}{7} = 3.366\%$$

⇒ This matches the B entry in the second column of GARP Table 9.5.

**Step 2 – Check: back to the cumulative rate**

$$1 - \text{e}^{-7\times0.03366} = 1 - \text{e}^{-0.2356} = 20.99\%$$

**Interpretation**

The spread is a red herring for this part: it gives the spread-implied 8.02% in the third column. For B the historical rate is about 42% of the spread-implied rate.

**LO:** CR-9 j: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.7, Tables 9.4 and 9.5; Practice Question 9.13

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.13 (rewritten as multiple choice) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 j.2)

a.reason: Linear shortcut: 20.99/7 = 3.00%, which understates the hazard rate.

c.reason: Answered the other column: 0.048104/0.60 = 8.02% is the spread-implied hazard rate.

d.reason: Forgot to divide by $T = 7$: $- \text{ln}(0.7901) = 23.56\%$.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
questions.question:
A risk consultant at an Australian fund manager is explaining the gap between market-implied and historical default estimates to the investment committee for a BBB-type issuer class:

- Seven-year cumulative historical default probability: 2.80%
- Average seven-year credit spread: 150 basis points
- Expected recovery rate: 40%

Which of the following is closest to the excess of the spread-implied (risk-neutral) average hazard rate over the historical (real-world) average hazard rate, per annum?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Real-world average hazard rate (direct formula)**

$$\bar{\lambda}_{\text{hist}} = -\frac{1}{7} \text{ln}(1 - 0.028) = 0.00406 = 0.406\%$$

⇒ Historical data imply defaults arrive at about 0.41% per year.

**Step 2 – Risk-neutral average hazard rate**

$$\bar{\lambda}_{\text{spread}} = \frac{s}{1 - R} = \frac{0.0150}{1 - 0.40} = 0.0250 = 2.50\%$$

**Step 3 – Difference**

2.50% − 0.406% = 2.09%

**Interpretation**

Bond investors are compensated for about 2.09% per year more default intensity than history justifies. Hull attributes most of this to systematic (non-diversifiable) default risk, with a small liquidity component. For valuation use the 2.50%; for scenario analysis use the 0.41%.

**LO:** CR-9 j: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads. CR-9 k: Describe the difference between real-world and risk-neutral default probabilities and determine which one to use in the analysis of credit risk. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17, 9.7, Tables 9.4 and 9.5, 9.7.1 and 9.7.2

**Source:** Workbook A15.4 • S2 • Map #17 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 j.4)

a.reason: Treated the seven-year cumulative 2.80% as an annual hazard rate: 2.50 − 2.80 = −0.30%.

b.reason: Did not divide the spread by LGD: 1.50 − 0.41 = 1.09%.

d.reason: Divided the spread by the recovery rate instead of $1 - R$: 1.50/0.40 − 0.41 = 3.34%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.7, Tables 9.4 and 9.5
questions.question:
An investment committee member at a Canadian pension fund looks at an excerpt of GARP Table 9.5 (average seven-year hazard rates, %):

| Rating | From default probabilities | Implied by credit spreads |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0.109 | 1.145 |
| BBB | 0.328 | 2.126 |
| B | 3.366 | 8.017 |
| CCC/C | 10.118 | 18.395 |

Which statement is correct?

options.text: The spread-implied hazard rate is roughly ten times the historical one for every rating, so the excess is a fixed multiple of default risk.
For CCC/C bonds the historical hazard rate exceeds the spread-implied one, so investors in the lowest grade are under-compensated.
The excess falls as credit quality declines, because low-quality bonds are more liquid.
The excess rises from about 1.0 percentage point for A to about 8.3 points for CCC/C, while the ratio of the two hazard rates falls from about 10.5 to about 1.8.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Differences**

A: 1.145 − 0.109 = 1.036. BBB: 2.126 − 0.328 = 1.798. B: 8.017 − 3.366 = 4.651. CCC/C: 18.395 − 10.118 = 8.277 percentage points.

⇒ The excess rises as quality falls.

**Step 2 – Ratios**

A: 1.145/0.109 = 10.5. BBB: 6.5. B: 2.4. CCC/C: 18.395/10.118 = 1.8.

⇒ The ratio falls as quality falls.

**Interpretation**

GARP’s statement that the difference “tends to increase as credit quality declines” is about the absolute excess. The excess return grows with the credit risk taken, even though for low grades a larger share of the spread is genuine expected default loss. (GARP prints the CCC/C difference as 8.207; see the correction box.)

**LO:** CR-9 j: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.7, Tables 9.4 and 9.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.7, Tables 9.4 and 9.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 j.5)

a.reason: The ratio ranges from about 10.5 to 1.8; it is not a fixed multiple.

b.reason: The spread-implied rate is above the historical one for every grade, CCC/C included (18.395% against 10.118%).

c.reason: The excess rises, and low-quality bonds are not more liquid; illiquidity adds to the excess.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.7 (rewritten as multiple choice)
questions.question: A board member at a Swiss insurer asks why default probabilities implied by credit spreads are so much higher than those calculated from historical default experience. Which explanation does the reading identify as by far the most important?

options.text: Corporate bonds are relatively illiquid, and the liquidity premium explains most of the gap.
Bond traders allow for depression scenarios much worse than any in the historical data.
Bonds do not default independently of each other, so bondholders bear systematic risk that cannot be diversified away and earn an excess return for it.
Rating agencies understate historical default rates because they rate through the cycle.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Rule out the minor reasons**

Illiquidity explains perhaps 25 bp of the excess in normal markets. Subjective depression scenarios are hard to see explaining a large part.

**Step 2 – The main reason**

Bonds do not default independently: default rates swing from year to year (0.15% in 1981 to 4.19% in 2009), so default risk is partly systematic and cannot be diversified away. Bondholders earn an excess return for bearing it, more so as quality falls and debt becomes more equity-like.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

Two other contributions complete the picture: idiosyncratic bond risk is highly skewed and hard to diversify, and the excess return rises when spreads are high, as in 2008.

**LO:** CR-9 j: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.7.1 Reason for the Difference; Practice Question 9.7

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.7 (rewritten as multiple choice) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 j.6)

a.reason: True that bonds are illiquid, but this is a small part of the gap.

b.reason: A possible factor that GARP considers unlikely to explain much.

d.reason: Not a reason GARP gives; historical default rates are measured outcomes of rated issuers.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Australian bank is comparing three issuers using their one-year zero-coupon bonds. The analyst assumes risk-neutral pricing with a single default date at maturity. The one-year risk-free rate is 3.0%; all rates use annual compounding.

| Issuer | One-year yield | Expected recovery rate | Bond seniority |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 6.0% | 60% | Senior secured |
| Q | 7.0% | 20% | Subordinated |
| R | 6.5% | 40% | Senior unsecured |

Which of the following correctly identifies the issuer with the highest implied one-year probability of default and that probability?

options.text: Issuer P; 7.08%
Issuer P; 7.50%
Issuer Q; 3.74%
Issuer Q; 18.69%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Expected loss rate implied by each yield**

PD $\cdot\text{LGD} = 1 - \frac{1 + r_{f}}{1 + y}$

$P : 1 - \frac{1.03}{1.060} = 0.02830, Q : 1 - \frac{1.03}{1.070} = 0.03738, R : 1 - \frac{1.03}{1.065} = 0.03286$

⇒ Q has the widest spread and the largest expected loss rate: the market expects to lose 3.74% of Q’s face value.

**Step 2 – Divide by LGD** $= 1 - R$

$$P : \frac{0.02830}{0.40} = 7.08\%, Q : \frac{0.03738}{0.80} = 4.67\%, R : \frac{0.03286}{0.60} = 5.48\%$$

⇒ P loses only 40% when it defaults, so its smaller expected loss rate needs a larger default probability to explain it.

**Step 3 – Rank**

P (7.08%) > R (5.48%) > Q (4.67%).

**Interpretation**

The ranking by spread (Q, R, P) reverses once recovery is taken into account: the spread prices expected loss, which is PD times LGD. These are risk-neutral PDs, suited to valuation and CVA; Hull’s evidence (Table 9.5) is that they sit well above real-world PDs from default history, so a stress scenario would use historical rates instead. The formula is the one-period version of the idea that the hazard rate is roughly $s/(1 - R)$ (outside-source in this exact discrete form).

**LO:** CR-12 c: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads. CR-9 h: Describe CDS spreads and explain how CDS spreads can be used to estimate hazard rates. CR-9 j: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24, 12.1; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17, 9.6.1 eq. 9.3, 9.7, Table 9.5

CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D5.2 • S2, S3 • Map #42 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 j.7)

b.reason: Dropped the $1/(1 + y)$ term and treated the raw spread as the expected loss rate: (0.060 − 0.030)/0.40 = 7.50%. That is the approximation $s/(1 - R)$, not the exact one-period PD the stem asks for.

c.reason: Dropped the division by LGD and ranked on the expected loss rate: Q’s 1 − 1.03/1.07 = 3.74% is PD times LGD, not PD.

d.reason: Wrong-input twin: divided by the recovery rate instead of LGD, 0.03738/0.20 = 18.69% for Q (with P at 7.08% becoming 4.72%).

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
questions.question: A model risk analyst at a Swiss bank reviews a vendor service that converts each firm’s Merton default probability $N (-d_{2})$ into a real-world default probability, using a monotonic transformation estimated from historical default experience. Which assumption underlies this calibration?

options.text: The levels of risk-neutral and real-world default probabilities are equal, so no adjustment for risk premiums is needed.
The rankings of risk-neutral default probabilities, real-world default probabilities and Merton default probabilities are all the same.
Merton default probabilities are already real-world probabilities, so the transformation only corrects estimation error.
Real-world default probabilities exceed risk-neutral ones, so the transformation must raise every Merton probability.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a monotonic transformation preserves**

It changes levels but keeps the order of the firms.

**Step 2 – The assumption it needs**

Mapping a risk-neutral Merton output into a real-world PD works only if both measures order firms the same way as the Merton output. GARP states this directly: the rankings of risk-neutral, real-world and Merton PDs are assumed to be the same.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The service sells a change of level on top of a ranking that is assumed common to all three measures; that is why ranking quality is the thing to test.

**LO:** CR-9 n: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.8.1 and 9.8.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.8.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 n.4)

a.reason: If the levels were equal there would be nothing to calibrate; risk-neutral PDs are higher.

c.reason: $N (-d_{2})$ is risk-neutral in theory, being calculated from an option pricing model.

d.reason: Reversed: real-world PDs are below risk-neutral ones, so the real-world map sits lower.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.5, 5.6.3.1 and Ch.9, 9.8.1
questions.question: A credit analyst at a Korean bank compares a plain Merton implementation with Moody’s KMV Expected Default Frequency (EDF) model for listed borrowers. Which feature of the KMV model is designed to make its default probabilities more realistic in level than the plain Merton $N(-d_{2})$?

options.text: KMV reads the probability off the standard normal distribution, $N (-\text{DD})$, but uses total debt as the default point.
KMV replaces the equity-based distance to default with the borrower’s agency rating and a rating transition matrix.
KMV uses the book value of equity rather than its market value, which makes its probabilities more stable.
KMV maps the distance to default to a probability through an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies, and sets the default point at short-term debt plus half of long-term debt.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The mapping**

Plain Merton reads the default probability off the normal distribution, $N (-d_{2})$. KMV uses historical data to build an empirical distribution of default frequencies and maps the distance to default into it.

**Step 2 – The default point**

KMV sets it at short-term debt plus half of long-term debt, which better approximates the firm’s actual loan obligations.

⇒ Both features aim at realistic real-world levels: D.

**Interpretation**

This is the evidence of Section 1 in practice: the Merton distance to default ranks well, and KMV calibrates its level to observed defaults.

**LO:** CR-9 n: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model. • **Reference:** Doumpos et al., Ch.1 (GARP CR Ch.5), 5.6.3.1 and 5.6.3.2; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.8.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.5, 5.6.3.1 and Ch.9, 9.8.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 n.5)

a.reason: Describes plain Merton’s normal mapping, with the wrong default point.

b.reason: A true description of the wrong model: rating transition matrices belong to CreditMetrics.

c.reason: KMV uses market values, and stability is not one of its objectives.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 and 9.8
questions.question: The head of credit at an Australian bank proposes using default probabilities from Moody’s KMV or Kamakura, rather than agency ratings, as an early-warning signal for the bank’s corporate borrowers, some listed and some privately held. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: Not sensible: like agency ratings, these estimates aim for stability and avoid reversals, so they react slowly.
Sensible for every borrower, including the private firms, because the models need only accounting data.

Sensible for the listed borrowers: the estimates are based on equity prices, do not target stability and respond more quickly to market information than ratings; they cannot be produced for borrowers without traded equity.
Not sensible: the estimates are risk-neutral, so they cannot rank borrowers by credit quality.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Responsiveness**

Credit ratings are revised infrequently and aim for stability. KMV and Kamakura estimates come from equity prices and other variables, have no stability objective and respond more quickly to market information.

⇒ As an early-warning signal they suit listed borrowers.

**Step 2 – Coverage**

They need a traded share price, so they cannot be produced for the privately held borrowers.

**Interpretation**

The two sources complement each other: ratings give a stable through-the-cycle view, market-based PDs a timely one, and private borrowers still need an internal rating (CR-9 a).

**LO:** CR-9 n: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.1 Credit Ratings; 9.8 Using Equity Prices to Estimate Default Probabilities; 9.8.1

CR-10 • Credit Value at Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.1 and 9.8 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 n.6)

a.reason: Attributes the agencies’ stability objective to the market-based models.

b.reason: The models need equity prices, not just accounting data.

d.reason: Risk-neutral probabilities still rank correctly, and KMV and Kamakura report real-world probabilities anyway.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
questions.question:
A credit portfolio manager at a Canadian bank is computing the one-year Credit VaR of a CAD 400 million book that the bank’s economic capital model treats in Malz’s portfolio credit risk framework. Data:

- 40 loans of CAD 10 million each, to 40 different obligors
- One-year probability of default of each loan: 3%; recovery rate: 40%
- Defaults are assumed independent; the cumulative probability of the number of defaults is:

| Number of defaults | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cumulative probability | 0.2957 | 0.6615 | 0.8822 | 0.9686 | 0.9933 | 0.9988 | 0.9998 |

Which of the following is closest to the 99% Credit VaR of the book?

options.text: CAD 10.8 million
CAD 11.2 million
CAD 16.8 million
CAD 24.0 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – 99th percentile of the number of defaults**

The quantile is the smallest count whose cumulative probability is at least 0.99: $P (\le3) =$ 0.9686 \< 0.99, $P (\le4) = 0.9933 \ge0.99$, so the 99th percentile is 4 defaults.

⇒ In 99% of years the book suffers 4 or fewer defaults.

**Step 2 – Worst-case loss at 99%**

Loss$_{99\%} = 4 \times10 \times(1 - 0.40) = 4 \times6.0 = 24.0$

⇒ Each default costs CAD 6.0 million (LGD 60%), so the 99% loss quantile is CAD 24.0 million.

**Step 3 – Expected loss**

EL = 400 × 0.03 × 0.60 = 7.2

⇒ On average the book loses CAD 7.2 million a year, which is priced into the loans and reserved for.

**Step 4 – Credit VaR**

Credit VaR$_{99\%} = \text{Loss}_{99\%} - \text{EL} = 24.0 - 7.2 = 16.8$

**Interpretation**

CAD 16.8 million is the unexpected loss at 99%: the economic capital buffer beyond the provisioned EL. Making the book more granular (more, smaller independent loans) would shrink this number while leaving the CAD 7.2 million EL unchanged.

**LO:** CR-11 c: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR. CR-11 h: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR. CR-10 b: Define and calculate Credit VaR. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8, 8.2 Granularity and Portfolio Credit Value-at-Risk, Table 11.1; Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19

CR-10 • Credit Value at Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook B1.1 • S1, S2 • Map #10 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 b.8)

a.reason: Took the last row below 99% as the quantile: 3 × 6.0 − 7.2 = 10.8.

b.reason: Used the 40% recovery rate as the LGD in both terms: 4 × 10 × 0.40 − 400 × 0.03 × 0.40 = 16.0 − 4.8 = 11.2.

d.reason: Forgot to subtract the expected loss and reported the 99% loss quantile, 24.0.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.10, 10.2 to 10.4 and Ch.5, 5.6.3 • Workbook D20 audit format • shapes
questions.question:
D20·S1, S3

A model validation team audits four statements in a credit-model comparison memo. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Credit Risk Plus estimates each obligor’s default probability from its capital structure and asset volatility.
Vasicek’s model captures losses from both downgrades and defaults, which is why regulators use it for IRB capital.
Because it uses a Gaussian copula, Vasicek’s model generates strong tail dependence between defaults.
In Credit Risk Plus, making the default rate uncertain while keeping the expected number of defaults unchanged raises the 99.9th percentile of the number of defaults.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Test each statement against its model**

A: Doumpos says Credit Risk Plus, “in contrast to the KMV model, …does not use the capital structure”. B: Vasicek counts defaults only. C: Vasicek “incorporates very little tail correlation”.

⇒ A, B and C are false.

**Step 2 – Test D**

Holding $\mu= 4$ fixed, raising $\sigma$ from 0 to 10 moves the 99.9th percentile of the number of defaults from 11 to 98 (GARP Table 10.4).

⇒ D is correct: default-rate uncertainty is how Credit Risk Plus creates correlation and fattens the tail.

**Interpretation**

Each false statement borrows a true feature from another model: capital structure from KMV, downgrades from CreditMetrics, tail dependence from a fat-tailed copula. That is the D20 audit pattern.

**LO:** CR-10 e: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19 (GARP CR Ch.10), 10.2 to 10.4, Table 10.4; Doumpos et al., GARP CR Ch.5, 5.6.3.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10, 10.2 to 10.4 and Ch.5, 5.6.3 • Workbook D20 audit format • shapes (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 e.7)

a.reason: Sibling swap with Moody’s KMV: Credit Risk Plus is an actuarial default-count model.

b.reason: Sibling swap with CreditMetrics: Vasicek counts defaults only (downgrades enter IRB only through the maturity adjustment).

c.reason: Polarity flip: the Gaussian copula has little tail dependence; another copula is needed to add it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.10 Practice Question 10.1 (rewritten as multiple choice) • shape D20·S5
questions.question: A bank holds a loan that is downgraded from A to BBB in year 1 and from BBB to B in year 2, and defaults in year 3. A risk analyst compares how three credit VaR models would treat this loan, on (a) when a credit loss is recognised and (b) how default correlation is modelled. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Credit Risk Plus recognises no loss until the default in year 3, and it generates default correlation through uncertainty in the default rate shared by all obligors.
CreditMetrics recognises no loss until the default in year 3, and it generates default correlation by making the expected number of defaults gamma-distributed.
Vasicek’s model recognises revaluation losses in years 1 and 2 through a transition matrix, and it correlates defaults through a gamma-distributed default rate.
CreditMetrics recognises revaluation losses in years 1, 2 and 3, but it treats the rating changes of different obligors as independent.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – (a) When is the loss recognised?**

Credit Risk Plus and Vasicek: only on default, so nothing until year 3. CreditMetrics: a revaluation loss at each downgrade, in years 1, 2 and 3.

**Step 2 – (b) How is default correlation modelled?**

Vasicek: one-factor Gaussian copula with $\rho$. Credit Risk Plus: uncertainty in the default rate common to all obligors. CreditMetrics: Gaussian copula on rating changes with equity-return correlations.

⇒ A is correct on both counts.

**Interpretation**

GARP’s answer to 10.1 in one line: the models differ in the timing of losses (CreditMetrics and Credit Risk Plus should agree on the long-run total) and in the mechanism that correlates defaults.

**LO:** CR-10 e: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19 (GARP CR Ch.10), 10.2 to 10.4; Practice Question 10.1

CR-10 • Credit Value at Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.10 Practice Question 10.1 (rewritten as multiple choice) • shape D20·S5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 e.8)

b.reason: Gives CreditMetrics both Credit Risk Plus features: it books downgrade losses as they happen and uses a copula, not a gamma-distributed default rate.

c.reason: Vasicek has no transition matrix and no gamma-distributed rate: defaults only, one-factor copula.

d.reason: Right on CreditMetrics’ loss timing, wrong on correlation: its rating changes are correlated through a Gaussian copula.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.10, introduction and 10.5
questions.question: A bank’s trading desk holds a portfolio of investment-grade corporate bonds. Its current credit VaR model, built for the banking book, counts only losses from default; over a 10-day horizon the probability that any of the issuers defaults is well below 1%. The CRO asks how measuring credit spread risk would change the desk’s 10-day 99% VaR. Which response is correct?

options.text: The VaR would be unchanged, because spread changes are a market risk and credit VaR covers default losses only by definition.
The VaR would rise, because bond values fall when spreads widen or ratings fall, so losses appear at the 99th percentile even though no issuer defaults.
The VaR would fall, because spread changes diversify the default losses already captured by the model.
The VaR would rise only if spread changes in different rating categories were independent; with highly correlated spreads the effects cancel.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the current model sees**

With default probability well below 1% over 10 days, the 99th percentile of a default-only loss is zero: the model reports essentially no VaR.

**Step 2 – What spread risk adds**

Bond values fall whenever spreads widen or ratings slip, and that happens on many days with no default. Those losses populate the 99th percentile.

⇒ Measuring spread risk raises the 10-day 99% VaR.

**Interpretation**

GARP: some credit VaR models consider only losses from defaults; “others consider losses from downgrades or credit spread changes as well as from defaults”. The values of trading-book credit products “depend critically on credit spreads”. For a trading book, a default-only model badly understates risk.

**LO:** CR-10 f: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19 (GARP CR Ch.10), introduction and 10.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10, introduction and 10.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 f.2)

a.reason: GARP’s credit VaR explicitly can include downgrade and spread losses; leaving them out does not make them disappear.

c.reason: Spread losses add to default losses; they do not offset them.

d.reason: Correlation shapes how spread losses combine; GARP introduces correlation by making spread changes highly correlated across categories, which raises VaR rather than cancelling it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.10, 10.5, Example 10.1 and Table 10.5
questions.question:
A risk manager holds a two-year zero-coupon bond with a principal of USD 1,000, rated BB and priced at USD 907.03. Her one-month outcomes follow Hull’s Example 10.1:

| Outcome | Spread (bp) | Probability | Loss (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Default |  | 0.100% | 507.03 |
| Downgrade to B | 500 / 450 / 400 | 0.267% each | 44.17 / 36.47 / 28.65 |
| Stay BB | 240 / 200 / 160 | 32.833% each | 2.92 / −3.70 / −10.38 |
| Upgrade to BBB | 120 / 100 / 80 | 0.200% each | −17.14 / −20.55 / −23.98 |

Which statement correctly assesses the role of credit spread risk in the bond’s one-month 99% VaR?

options.text: The 99% VaR is the default loss of USD 507.03, because default is the worst outcome.
Spread changes within a rating category matter only below 99% confidence; at 99% and above, only migrations and default drive the VaR.
The 99% VaR is USD 2.92, a loss caused by the spread widening to 240 bp while the bond stays BB; with a single spread per rating, the 99% VaR would be a gain.
Because 98.5% of outcomes leave the rating unchanged, credit spread risk cannot affect the VaR at any confidence level above 98.5%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Walk up the tail**

Default 0.100%; adding the three B outcomes gives 0.100 + 3 × 0.267 = 0.900%, still below 1%. The next outcome, BB at 240 bp, takes the tail to 33.733%.

⇒ The 99% VaR is the BB, 240 bp loss: USD 2.92.

**Step 2 – Remove spread risk within ratings**

With one spread per rating (B 450, BB 200, BBB 100 bp), default and B still carry 0.9%, so the 99% outcome is BB at 200 bp: a loss of −3.70.

⇒ Spread risk alone turns a gain of 3.70 into a loss of 2.92 at 99%.

**Interpretation**

GARP: above 99.9% the VaR is 507.03; between 99.633% and 99.9% it is 44.17 (B at 500 bp, itself a spread outcome); at 99% it is “a modest \$2.92”. Spread dispersion inside a rating matters at every confidence level below 99.9%.

**LO:** CR-10 f: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.19 (GARP CR Ch.10), 10.5, Example 10.1, Table 10.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.10, 10.5, Example 10.1 and Table 10.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-10 f.5)

a.reason: Default has only a 0.1% probability, inside the 1% tail, so it sets the VaR only above 99.9%.

b.reason: Reversed: at 99% and between 99.633% and 99.9% the VaR comes from a spread level (240 bp in BB, 500 bp in B).

d.reason: The 98.5% of unchanged-rating outcomes are spread across three spread levels; the widest of them sets the 99% VaR.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.
questions.source: Workbook B3.1 • S1, S3, S5 • Map #16
questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at a Brazilian bank is assessing concentration in two high-yield borrowers in the same region. The bank’s one-year default model gives:

- Probability of default: borrower 1, 6%; borrower 2, 10%
- Probability that neither borrower defaults over the year: 86.5%
- Correlation of the two borrowers’ equity returns, used by the desk as an asset-correlation proxy: 0.55

Which of the following is closest to the one-year default correlation between the two borrowers?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Joint default probability from the no-default outcome**

$$P (\text{neither}) = 1 - \pi_{1} - \pi_{2} + \pi_{12} \Rightarrow\pi_{12} = 0.865 - 1 + 0.06 + 0.10 = 0.025$$

⇒ A 2.5% chance that both borrowers default in the same year, against 0.06×0.10 = 0.6% under independence.

**Step 2 – Covariance of the default indicators**

$$\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2} = 0.025 - 0.006 = 0.019$$

**Step 3 – Standard deviations**

$\sqrt{\pi_{1}(1 - \pi_{1})} \sqrt{\pi_{2}(1 - \pi_{2})} = \sqrt{0.06(0.94)} \sqrt{0.10(0.90)} = 0.23749 \times0.30000 = 0.071246$

**Step 4 – Default correlation**

$$\rho_{12} = \frac{0.019}{0.071246} = 0.267$$

⇒ A default correlation of 0.27 is very high by Malz’s yardstick (studies find about 0.05): joint default is over four times as likely as under independence.

**Interpretation**

The 0.55 equity correlation is a red herring: it proxies the asset return correlation, a sibling concept that is much larger than the default correlation for the same pair. For limits on joint exposure the bank needs the default correlation, 0.267.

**LO:** CR-11 a: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.1 Defining Default Correlation, eq. 11.1, Example 11.1

CR-11 • Portfolio Credit Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook B3.1 • S1, S3, S5 • Map #16 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 a.6)

a.reason: Stopped at the covariance, $\pi_{12} -\pi_{1}\pi_{2} = 0.019$, without dividing by the standard deviations (intermediate result).

b.reason: Used $\sqrt{\pi_{1}\pi_{2}} = 0.07746$ as the denominator, dropping the $(1 - \pi_{i})$ factors: 0.019/0.07746 = 0.245.

d.reason: Omitted the $\pi_{1}\pi_{2}$ subtraction in the numerator: 0.025/0.071246 = 0.351 (the formula-card dropped-term trap).

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.3 • shape B1·S4
questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Dutch bank runs a very large, homogeneous loan book: thousands of equal loans to different borrowers, each with a 2% one-year default probability and 100% loss given default. The bank models the book with Malz’s single-factor model and asks how the book’s 99% Credit VaR depends on the loans’ common beta $\beta$ to the market factor. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A higher $\beta$ raises the book’s expected loss rate above 2%, which is why Credit VaR rises with $\beta$.
A higher $\beta$ makes both very few and very many defaults more likely, so the 99% Credit VaR rises; for any $\beta> 0$ it stays positive however many loans are added.
As $\beta$ approaches 1, the loss rate converges to 2% in every state of the economy, so Credit VaR falls towards zero.
Once the book is this granular the market factor no longer moves the loss rate, so Credit VaR is close to zero whatever the value of $\beta$.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the granular book’s loss rate follows**

With thousands of small loans the idiosyncratic shocks average out, and the loss rate converges to the conditional default probability $p(m) = \Phi((k - \beta m)/\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}})$, with $k = \Phi^{-1}(2\%)$.

⇒ The market factor still moves the loss rate whenever $\beta> 0$, so the loss has a distribution and Credit VaR is positive.

**Step 2 – How beta changes that distribution**

A higher $\beta$ makes $p(m)$ more sensitive to $m$: defaults “mount rapidly as business conditions deteriorate”. For this book the 99% loss rate is $\Phi((k + \beta\times2.326)/\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}})$: 2% at $\beta= 0$, 8.24% at $\beta^{2} = 0.10$, 15.19% at $\beta^{2} = 0.25$.

⇒ Credit VaR as a share of the book: 0, 6.24% and 13.19%. EL stays at 2% throughout.

**Interpretation**

This is the second granularity effect seen from the correlation side: adding names removes idiosyncratic risk only, and the beta to the common factor sets the Credit VaR that remains.

**LO:** CR-11 c: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR. CR-11 h: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.3 Credit VaR Using the Single-Factor Model, eq. 11.2

CR-11 • Portfolio Credit Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.3 • shape B1·S4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 c.6)

a.reason: Sibling swap: the expected loss rate is 2% for every $\beta$; correlation reshapes the distribution around it.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the loss rate converges to $\pi$ when $\beta\to0$. When $\beta\to1$ it is either 0 or 100%.

d.reason: Absolute claim: granularity removes the idiosyncratic part only; the loss rate still moves with $m$.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.3 and Vardeez CR-11 e example • shape B3·S6
questions.question: A credit analyst at a Malaysian bank stress-tests a manufacturing borrower with the single-factor model. The borrower’s one-year unconditional default probability is 2% and its beta to the market factor is 0.60. The bank’s mild-slowdown scenario sets the market factor at $m = -0.5$. The loan has a loss given default of 45%. Which of the following is closest to the borrower’s default probability conditional on the scenario?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Threshold and conditional standard deviation**

$k = \Phi^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$; $\sqrt{1 - 0.60^{2}} = 0.80$.

**Step 2 – New distance to default**

$k - \beta m = -2.054 - 0.60 \times(-0.5) = -2.054 + 0.30 = -1.754$.

**Step 3 – Conditional PD**

$$p(-0.5) = \Phi(\frac{-1.754}{0.80}) = \Phi(-2.192) = 1.42\%$$

⇒ Below the 2% unconditional PD, even though the scenario is a slowdown.

**Interpretation**

The break-even factor is $m^{*} = k(1 - 0.80)/0.60 = -0.68$. The scenario $m = -0.5$ is milder than that, so the narrower conditional distribution outweighs the mean shift. This is the same effect as in Vardeez’s example (0.82% against 1%). The 45% LGD is a red herring: it matters for the loss, not the probability.

**LO:** CR-11 d: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.3 Conditional Default Distributions

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.3 and Vardeez CR-11 e example • shape B3·S6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 d.7)

a.reason: Sign error, treating the slowdown as a boom: $\Phi((-2.054 - 0.30)/0.80) =$ $\Phi(-2.942) = 0.16\%$.

c.reason: Assumed the conditional PD equals the unconditional PD; that happens only at $m^{*} = -0.68$ (or with $\beta= 0$).

d.reason: Dropped the $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}}$ scaling: $\Phi(-1.754) = 3.97\%$, which wrongly confirms the intuition that a negative $m$ must raise the PD.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model.
questions.source: Workbook B3.2 • S2, S3, S5 • Map #16
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK bank is sizing a stress scenario for two corporate exposures. The bank’s limit framework is breached if at least one of the two borrowers defaults within a year, and the stress report also requires the probability that both default. Inputs:

- One-year probability of default: borrower 1, 1.5%; borrower 2, 4.0%
- Default correlation between the two borrowers: 0.08

Which of the following is closest to the joint default probability and the probability that the limit is breached?

options.text: Joint default 0.06%; limit breached 5.44%
Joint default 0.19%; limit breached 5.31%
Joint default 0.25%; limit breached 5.00%
Joint default 0.25%; limit breached 5.25%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Product of the standard deviations**

$\sqrt{\pi_{1}(1 - \pi_{1})} \sqrt{\pi_{2}(1 - \pi_{2})} = \sqrt{0.015(0.985)} \sqrt{0.04(0.96)} = 0.12155 \times0.19596 = 0.023819$

**Step 2 – Joint default probability**

$$\pi_{12} = \rho_{12}\sqrt{\pi_{1}(1 - \pi_{1})}\sqrt{\pi_{2}(1 - \pi_{2})} + \pi_{1}\pi_{2} = 0.08(0.023819) + 0.015(0.04)$$

$$\pi_{12} = 0.001906 + 0.000600 = 0.002506$$

⇒ A 0.25% chance that both borrowers default, about four times the 0.06% independence figure.

**Step 3 – Probability that at least one defaults**

$P ($at least one$) = \pi_{1} + \pi_{2} - \pi_{12} = 0.015 + 0.040 - 0.0025 = 0.0525$

⇒ The limit is breached with probability 5.25%. Positive correlation lowers this number relative to independence, because defaults cluster in the same states.

**Interpretation**

Correlation pushes probability into the “both” and “neither” cells and out of the “one only” cells: the joint figure rises from 0.06% to 0.25%, and the breach probability falls from 5.44% to 5.25%.

**LO:** CR-11 a: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios. CR-11 f: Estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.1 Defining Default Correlation

**Source:** Workbook B3.2 • S2, S3, S5 • Map #16 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 f.4)

a.reason: Ignored the default correlation: $\pi_{12} = \pi_{1}\pi_{2} = 0.06\%$, breach 0.055 − 0.0006 = 5.44%.

c.reason: Correct joint PD, but computed the probability that exactly one defaults, $\pi_{1} +$ $\pi_{2} - 2\pi_{12} = 5.00\%$, which misses the joint-default state that also breaches the limit (sibling swap).

questions.loText: Estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.3 Example 11.5
questions.question: A credit portfolio analyst at a Swiss bank models two industrial borrowers with the single-factor model. Each borrower has a one-year default probability of 3% and a beta of 0.50 to the market factor; each exposure is CHF 25 million with an expected recovery of 40%. The bank’s bivariate normal routine returns a joint default probability of 0.265%. Which of the following is closest to the asset return correlation and the default correlation between the two borrowers?

options.text: Asset return correlation 0.25; default correlation 0.060
Asset return correlation 0.25; default correlation 0.091
Asset return correlation 0.25; default correlation 0.250
Asset return correlation 0.50; default correlation 0.060

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Asset return correlation**

Same beta for both: $\beta_{1}\beta_{2} = 0.50 \times0.50 = 0.25$.

**Step 2 – Covariance of the default indicators**

$\pi_{12} - \pi^{2} = 0.00265 - 0.03^{2} = 0.00265 - 0.00090 = 0.00175$.

**Step 3 – Default correlation**

$$\rho= \frac{0.00175}{0.03 \times0.97} = \frac{0.00175}{0.0291} = 0.060$$

⇒ An asset correlation of 0.25 translates into a default correlation of about 0.06.

**Interpretation**

At $\pi= 1\%$ the same beta gave 0.034 (Example 11.5): for a given asset correlation, the default correlation rises with the PD. Exposures and recovery are red herrings; they matter for losses, not for the correlation.

**LO:** CR-11 f: Estimate the probability of a joint default of any pair of credits and the default correlation between any pair of credits using the single factor model. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.3 Asset and Default Correlation, Example 11.5

CR-11 • Portfolio Credit Risk • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.3 Example 11.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 f.6)

b.reason: Dropped the $\pi^{2}$ term: 0.00265/0.0291 = 0.091 (shape S5).

c.reason: Assumed the default correlation equals the asset correlation (sibling swap).

d.reason: Reported $\beta= 0.50$ as the asset correlation; the pair correlation is $\beta^{2}$.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
questions.question: A credit portfolio manager at an Indian NBFC holds a single INR 500 crore loan to an infrastructure developer, with a one-year default probability of 3% and zero expected recovery. To make the book “granular”, she refinances it as 50 loans of INR 10 crore each, all owed by the same developer and ranking equally. Which of the following statements about the effect on the book’s Credit VaR is correct?

options.text: The book is now granular: with 50 positions the number of defaults is binomial, so the 99% Credit VaR falls.
Nothing has changed in substance: the 50 loans default together, so the book still behaves as a single credit and its Credit VaR is unchanged.
Credit VaR falls because the expected loss of each loan is now only 2% of the book’s expected loss.
Credit VaR falls almost to zero, because no single position is more than 2% of the book.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Who can default**

All 50 loans are owed by one developer and rank equally: if the developer defaults, all 50 default; if not, none does.

⇒ Malz: debts of the same obligor “would be equivalent to one large position”. The default correlation among the loans is 1.

**Step 2 – Credit VaR before and after**

The loss is INR 500 crore with probability 3% and zero otherwise, in both cases. EL = 500×3% = 15. At 99% the 1% tail lies inside the 3% default probability, so Credit VaR = 500 − 15 = INR 485 crore, before and after.

**Interpretation**

Granularity means more obligors, not more loan contracts. To cut Credit VaR the manager has to lend to different borrowers.

**LO:** CR-11 h: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR. CR-11 c: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.2 Granularity and Portfolio Credit Value-at-Risk

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.11, 11.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 h.3)

a.reason: A binomial count needs independent defaults; here the loans default together.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the book’s EL is unchanged at INR 15 crore, and EL does not drive the change in Credit VaR anyway.

d.reason: Position size alone does not diversify; the 50 positions share one default event.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
questions.question: The CRO of a Japanese regional bank wants to cut the Credit VaR of its SME loan book. She proposes replacing 20 loans of JPY 5 billion each with 2,000 loans of JPY 50 million each to similar borrowers. The default probability, the LGD and the pairwise default correlation (0.05, estimated with a single-factor model) would all be unchanged. A risk analyst is drafting the memo to the risk committee. Which of the following statements should the analyst include?

options.text: The move lowers Credit VaR, because spreading the book across more borrowers lowers the portfolio’s expected loss, and the expected loss is subtracted from the loss quantile.
The move lowers Credit VaR, and the proportional reduction from granularity is largest when the default probability of the loans is low.
The move lowers Credit VaR, but with a positive default correlation it cannot bring Credit VaR to zero, because losses on the granular book still move with the common factor.
The move lowers Credit VaR and, with enough borrowers, drives it to zero whatever the default correlation, because the loss rate converges to the default probability.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What granularity changes**

With the total exposure fixed, more and smaller positions reduce the variance of portfolio losses, so the loss quantile moves towards the expected loss and Credit VaR falls (Malz Table 11.1: at $\pi= 2\%$ and 99%, Credit VaR is USD 980 million for $n = 1$, 60 million for $n = 50$, 11 million for $n = 1{,}000$).

**Step 2 – What it cannot change**

In the single-factor model the loss rate of a granular book converges to the conditional default probability $p(m) = \Phi((k - \beta m)/\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}})$, not to $\pi$. Idiosyncratic risk is diversified away; the market factor $m$ still moves the loss rate, so Credit VaR stays positive.

⇒ The CRO’s plan removes concentration risk but leaves the systematic part of Credit VaR in place.

**Interpretation**

C is correct. The memo should present the reduction as a cut in idiosyncratic risk only; the residual Credit VaR is set by the default probability and the correlation to the common factor.

**LO:** CR-11 h: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR. CR-11 c: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR. CR-11 d: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation. • **Reference:** Malz, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.11), 11.2 and 11.3

CR-12 • Credit Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook B1.2 • S3, S4 • Map #10 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-11 h.6)

a.reason: Sibling swap. Granularity changes the dispersion and extreme quantiles of loss, not the expected loss, which stays $\pi\times$ portfolio value for every $n$.

b.reason: Polarity flip. Malz: the convergence “is more drastic with a high default probability” and “it is harder to reduce VaR by making the portfolio more granular, if the default probability is low”.

d.reason: Absolute claim / scope error. Convergence of the loss to EL and Credit VaR to zero holds for a very large number of independent positions; with correlation 0.05 the common factor remains.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.2 (Gaussian copula, Example 12.4)
questions.question: A portfolio credit analyst at a Dutch bank simulates five-year default times for ten companies with a Gaussian copula, following GARP Example 12.4. Each company has a 15% probability of defaulting within five years, and the pairwise copula correlation is set at 0.2, using the correlation of the companies’ equity returns as a proxy. Which of the following statements about the 0.2 parameter is correct?

options.text: It is the correlation between the default indicators of any two companies over the five years, so it can be used directly in the default correlation formula.
It is the correlation between the two companies’ times to default, because the copula is applied directly to the default times.
It is the correlation between the transformed standard normal variables $x_{i} = N^{-1}[Q_{i}(t_{i})]$; the default correlation it implies over five years is much lower, below 0.1.
Raising it from 0.2 to 0.4 would raise each company’s five-year default probability above 15%, because defaults would cluster.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the correlation sits**

The copula maps each $t_{i}$ into $x_{i} = N^{-1}[Q_{i}(t_{i})]$ and assumes the $x_{i}$ are multivariate normal. “The default correlation between $t_{i}$ and $t_{j}$ is measured as the correlation between $x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$. This is referred to as the copula correlation.”

⇒ 0.2 is the correlation of the transformed normals, not of the default times or the default indicators.

**Step 2 – What it implies for default correlation**

With 15% five-year PDs the default threshold is $k = N^{-1}(0.15) = -1.036$. The joint PD is the bivariate normal probability $M_{2}(k, k; 0.2) = 3.46\%$ (against $0.15^{2} = 2.25\%$ under independence), so the default correlation is

$$\frac{0.0346 - 0.0225}{0.15 \times0.85} = 0.095$$

⇒ A copula correlation of 0.2 implies a default correlation of under 0.1.

**Interpretation**

Asset, equity and copula correlations are all much larger than the default correlation they generate (the B3 trap “asset correlation is not default correlation”). Treating 0.2 as a default correlation would grossly overstate joint defaults.

**LO:** CR-12 f: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.2, footnote 3 and Example 12.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.2 (Gaussian copula, Example 12.4) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 f.2)

a.reason: Sibling swap: 0.2 is the copula correlation; the default correlation it implies is about 0.095.

b.reason: Scope error: the copula is applied to the transformed variables $x_{i}$, precisely because the times to default are not normal.

d.reason: The copula leaves the marginals untouched: each company keeps its 15% five-year PD whatever the correlation. Higher correlation changes how defaults cluster, not how likely each one is.

questions.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.2 (eq. 12.8 and footnote 4)
questions.question:
A credit portfolio manager at a Singapore bank uses a one-factor Gaussian copula with company-specific loadings $a_{i}$, each set equal to the correlation of the company’s equity returns with a well-diversified market index. Two borrowers each have a one-year probability of default of 2%:

| Borrower | Sector | Loading $a_{i}$ | One-year PD |
|---|---|---|---|
| K | Copper miner | 0.6 | 2% |
| L | Water utility | 0.2 | 2% |

In the bank’s recession scenario the common factor takes the value $F = -1.5$. Which of the following is closest to the two borrowers’ one-year default probabilities conditional on this scenario?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Common threshold**

$N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.0537$ for both borrowers.

**Step 2 – Borrower K (**$a = 0.6$**)**

$Q_{K} (1 | F ) = N (\frac{-2.0537 - 0.6 \times(-1.5)}{\sqrt{1 - 0.36}}) = N (\frac{-1.1537}{0.8}) = N (-1.4422) = 7.46\%$

**Step 3 – Borrower L (**$a = 0.2$**)**

$Q_{L}(1 | F ) = N (\frac{-2.0537 - 0.2 \times(-1.5)}{\sqrt{1 - 0.04}}) = N (\frac{-1.7537}{0.9798}) = N (-1.7899) = 3.67\%$

⇒ The cyclical miner’s PD almost quadruples in the recession; the utility’s less than doubles.

**Interpretation**

With heterogeneous loadings (eq. 12.8) the same 2% unconditional PD hides very different exposure to the common factor. The copula correlation between the two borrowers is $a_{K} a_{L} = 0.12$.

**LO:** CR-12 f: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.2, eq. 12.8 and footnote 4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.2 (eq. 12.8 and footnote 4) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 f.6)

b.reason: Polarity flip: swapped the results, as if a higher loading protected a borrower in a downturn.

d.reason: Treated each $a_{i}$ as a copula correlation $\rho$ and used $\sqrt{a_{i}}$ as the loading: K $N (-0.8918/0.6325) = 7.92\%$, L $N (-1.3829/0.8944) = 6.10\%$.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.2.6, Figure 19.17
questions.question: A counterparty risk analyst at a Canadian bank simulates the exposure of a physically settled one-year European payer swaption on a five-year swap, bought from Dealer X, alongside an otherwise identical forward-starting payer swap traded with Dealer Y. On one simulated path the underlying swap is worth −0.8% of notional to the bank on the exercise date, and then rises to +1.5% of notional by year 3 as rates rise. Which of the following correctly describes the bank’s exposure at year 3 on this path?

options.text: Both contracts have the same exposure, because after the exercise date both reference the same underlying swap.
Only the forward swap has exposure: the swaption was not exercised when the swap was out of the money, so it no longer exists on this path.
Only the swaption has exposure: the forward-starting swap is cancelled when it is out of the money on the exercise date.
Both have exposure, but the swaption’s is smaller because its negative value at the exercise date is carried forward as a loss.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The exercise decision on this path**

At the exercise date the underlying swap is worth −0.8% to the bank, so a rational holder does not exercise. The swaption expires worthless.

⇒ From the exercise date on, the swaption does not exist on this path.

**Step 2 – The forward swap**

The forward swap was an obligation; it starts regardless and is worth +1.5% at year 3.

⇒ Exposure at year 3: forward swap 1.5%, swaption zero.

**Interpretation**

This is GARP’s scenario A in Figure 19.17: a path that gives exposure on the forward swap but not on the swaption. On paths like GARP’s scenario B (exercised), the two exposures are identical.

**LO:** CR-19 e: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.2.6, Figure 19.17

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.2.6, Figure 19.17 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 e.4)

a.reason: After exercise the two are the same swap only on paths where the swaption was exercised.

c.reason: A forward-starting swap is not cancelled when it is out of the money; that is the option’s privilege.

d.reason: An unexercised option carries no value forward; it simply ceases to exist.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.1.4 and 19.2.6
questions.question: A model validator at an Australian bank is reviewing how the bank’s exposure engine treats products with exercise decisions. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Exercise decisions can be ignored when simulating exposure, as they are in 10-day VaR models, because they occur only on discrete dates.

If the exercise decision is based on the base value of the underlying swap, the simulated valuation paths are the same for cash- and physically settled swaptions, and exposure can be computed directly from the simulated future values.
If the exercise decision is based on the actual value including xVA, exposure becomes independent of the exercise boundary, which removes any recursion from the calculation.
For a Bermudan swaption with several exercise dates, only the first exercise decision needs to be modelled, because later decisions are implied by it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Base value**

With the exercise decision based on the base value of the underlying swap, the valuation paths are the same for cash- and physically settled swaps, and exposure can be calculated directly from the future values of the swaption.

⇒ B is correct.

**Step 2 – The other statements**

Over long horizons, exercise decisions, cash flows and margin postings must be carried forward (“ageing”); only short-horizon VaR can neglect them. Using actual value links the future value, exposure and exercise decision, which creates the recursive problem. With several exercise dates, all combinations of decisions should be considered.

⇒ A, C and D are false.

**Interpretation**

Base values keep the calculation tractable; the price is that exercise ignores the xVA that a real holder would weigh.

**LO:** CR-19 e: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.1.4 and 19.2.6, footnote 17

CR-19 • Future Value and Exposure • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.1.4 and 19.2.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 e.6)

a.reason: Scope error: VaR’s 10-day horizon lets it ignore exercise; exposure, defined over many horizons, cannot.

c.reason: Polarity flip: actual value makes exposure and exercise depend on each other, creating the recursion rather than removing it.

d.reason: GARP footnote 17: where multiple exercise decisions are taken, all possible combinations should be considered.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
questions.question: A senior counterparty risk analyst at a Singapore bank is reviewing a glossary of exposure metrics drafted by a junior colleague for the bank’s xVA desk. Which of the following statements is correct to keep in the glossary?

options.text: Expected future value and expected positive exposure are both additive across transactions, so the EPE of a netting set equals the sum of the EPEs of its trades.
Average EPE is the time-weighted average of the EPE profile, often called the loan equivalent, while maximum PFE is the peak of the PFE profile over the life of the portfolio.
Expected negative exposure is the exposure seen from the counterparty’s point of view, so it drives the credit value adjustment the bank charges that counterparty.
Doubling the volatility of future value leaves the expected future value unchanged but lowers expected positive exposure, because more scenarios end below zero.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Check each statement against the metric definitions**

Gregory (19.1.5): average EPE is “the average exposure across all time horizons”, “the weighted average (the weights being the time intervals) of the EPE profile”, and “this single average EPE number is often called a ‘loan equivalent’ ”. Maximum PFE is the highest point of the PFE profile (Figure 19.4; Hull’s maximum peak exposure).
