⇒ B is correct. The trap inside it is naming: average EPE is “sometimes known simply as EPE”, which differs from the single-horizon EPE.

**Interpretation**

The six-way family splits on two axes: what is averaged (all values: EFV; positive values with negatives set to zero: EPE; negative values: ENE; a quantile: PFE) and how time is handled (one horizon, a time-weighted average, or a maximum). A glossary should state both axes for every metric and flag that Basel’s effective EE and effective EPE are non-decreasing versions defined for capital (outside-source).

**LO:** CR-19 a: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure. CR-19 b: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure. CR-19 f: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11, 19.1.4, 19.1.5, 19.3.1

**Source:** Workbook C8.2 • S1, S2 • Map #37 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 f.2)

a.reason: Sibling swap: additivity belongs to EFV only. EPE and ENE are not additive; aggregated EPE can never exceed the sum, since max$(\sum v_{i}, 0) \le\sum\text{max}(v_{i}, 0)$ (Table 19.1: 18 and 4 versus 21). This sub-additivity is the whole netting benefit.

c.reason: Role misassignment: ENE “represents the positive exposure from the counterparty’s point of view”, which is the bank’s own default risk and drives DVA. CVA is driven by EPE, the bank’s exposure to the counterparty.

d.reason: Polarity flip: higher volatility raises EPE. With mean 2.0, EPE rises from 2.17 to 2.79 when the standard deviation doubles from 2.0 to 4.0, because exposure is option-like; only EFV is unchanged.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.3.1 and 19.3.2
questions.question: A counterparty risk manager at a Swiss bank is assessing the incremental exposure of a new pay-fixed interest rate swap with a corporate client. The existing netting set with the client consists of pay-fixed swaps that are deep out of the money to the bank after a fall in rates, so the new trade’s value is highly positively correlated with the portfolio. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Because the new trade is highly positively correlated with the existing swaps, aggregation gives no benefit and the incremental EPE equals the new trade’s standalone EPE.
Although the values are highly correlated, the netting set is unlikely to have positive value unless rates rise a long way, so the incremental EPE will be well below the new trade’s standalone EPE.
Because EFV is additive and the portfolio’s EFV is negative, the netting set’s EPE equals the new trade’s standalone EPE plus the portfolio’s EFV.
An out-of-the-money portfolio raises the incremental exposure of any new trade, because the bank already owes the client money.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Two sources of offset**

Aggregation reduces exposure in scenarios where values have opposite signs. That can come from structural correlation, or from relative moneyness: a portfolio that is deep out of the money stays negative in most scenarios.

**Step 2 – Apply it to the new trade**

The new pay-fixed swap gains when rates rise, and so does the portfolio, but the portfolio starts deeply negative. Unless rates rise a long way the netting set stays negative, so most of the new trade’s positive values are absorbed.

⇒ The incremental EPE is well below the standalone EPE.

**Interpretation**

GARP: the OTM portfolio “damps the positive exposure contribution of a new transaction”; even directional portfolios can have significant aggregation effects. This is why incremental CVA can be small for a trade that looks risky on its own (CR-20 i).

**LO:** CR-19 f: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.3.1 and 19.3.2, Figures 19.20 and 19.21

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.3.1 and 19.3.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 f.3)

a.reason: Ignores moneyness: positive correlation of values does not mean the positive parts move together when the portfolio is deeply negative.

c.reason: Borrows EFV’s additivity for EPE; EPE is not additive and cannot be found by adding an EFV.

d.reason: Polarity flip: an OTM portfolio damps a new trade’s exposure; it does not raise it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.1 and 19.4.2
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Korean bank is explaining to the ALCO how funding exposure relates to counterparty credit exposure on the bank’s uncollateralised derivatives. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A positive portfolio value is at risk if the counterparty defaults and is also an asset that must be funded while the counterparty survives; margin received against it reduces both the counterparty risk and the funding cost.
A positive portfolio value creates a funding cost only if the counterparty defaults, since funding needs arise from the close-out of the transactions.
A negative portfolio value creates a funding cost, because the bank must eventually pay the amount it owes to the counterparty.
Margin posted by the bank against a negative value increases the bank’s funding benefit and reduces the counterparty’s exposure to the bank’s default.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The positive value**

A positive value is at risk when the counterparty defaults and “is also the amount that has to be funded when the counterparty does not”.

⇒ A positive exposure carries both a credit and a funding dimension.

**Step 2 – Margin held against it**

“Any margin held against a positive exposure reduces both counterparty risk and the associated funding cost”, as long as the margin is reusable.

⇒ A is correct.

**Interpretation**

The parallel is why CVA and FVA share methodologies. The differences (value, MPoR, aggregation, wrong-way risk, segregation) are what stop them being the same number.

**LO:** CR-19 g: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.4.1 and 19.4.2, eq. 19.7

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.1 and 19.4.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 g.1)

b.reason: Scope error: funding arises in non-default scenarios; default is when the exposure is lost.

c.reason: Polarity flip: a negative value is a funding benefit.

d.reason: Half right: posted margin does reduce the counterparty’s exposure to the bank, but it reduces the bank’s funding benefit rather than increasing it.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.1 and 19.4.2
questions.question: The head of funding at a UK bank compares three holdings: a portfolio of liquid gilts; an uncollateralised portfolio of interest rate swaps with corporate clients that has a large positive value; and an offsetting set of uncollateralised swaps with other corporates that has a large negative value. Which statement is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Every asset with a positive value has a funding cost, so the gilts and the positive swaps must be funded in full, and the negative swaps are irrelevant to funding.

The gilts can be repoed, so the repo cash largely offsets their funding cost; the swaps cannot be repoed, but because funding is assessed at portfolio level the negative values provide a benefit that offsets part of the cost of the positive values.
Funding is assessed counterparty by counterparty, like credit exposure, so the negative swaps provide no offset to the positive swaps.
The negative swaps create a funding cost equal to their value, which adds to the cost of funding the positive swaps.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Not every asset costs funding**

Liquid, low-risk bonds such as gilts can be repoed; the cash from the repo largely offsets the cost of buying them. Derivatives cannot be repoed, so their positive values are funding costs.

**Step 2 – Funding is a portfolio quantity**

Costs and benefits partly cancel because they only need to be considered at portfolio level; values are additive across counterparties.

⇒ The negative swaps’ funding benefit offsets part of the positive swaps’ funding cost.

**Interpretation**

For credit exposure the same two swap books could not offset unless they sat in one netting set with one counterparty.

**LO:** CR-19 g: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.4.1 and 19.4.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.1 and 19.4.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 g.2)

a.reason: Ignores repo funding of liquid bonds and the portfolio-level offset.

c.reason: Sibling swap: netting-set aggregation belongs to credit exposure; funding applies at portfolio level.

d.reason: Polarity flip: a negative value is a funding benefit.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
questions.question: A bank has two uncollateralised netting sets. With Counterparty X the portfolio is worth +USD 40 million to the bank; with Counterparty Y it is worth −USD 40 million. There is no netting agreement covering the two sets. Which statement best describes the bank’s credit and funding positions?

options.text: Credit exposure and funding requirement are both zero, because the two values offset.
Credit exposure is USD 40 million to X, while the funding position across the two sets is roughly flat, because funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.
Credit exposure is USD 40 million to X and the funding requirement is USD 40 million, because funding, like credit exposure, is assessed netting set by netting set.
Credit exposure is USD 80 million, the sum of the absolute values, and the funding requirement is zero.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Credit exposure is per netting set**

Close-out netting applies only within a netting agreement. X’s set is worth +40 and Y’s −40, with no agreement linking them.

⇒ Exposure to X is USD 40 million; Y’s negative value cannot offset it in X’s default.

**Step 2 – Funding is portfolio-wide**

Values for different transactions are additive for funding: the +40 asset needs funding and the −40 liability provides it.

⇒ The funding position is roughly flat.

**Interpretation**

The same pair of trades produces a large CVA (on X) but little funding cost: aggregation is one of the five differences, and here it dominates.

**LO:** CR-19 g: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.4.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 g.4)

a.reason: Applies portfolio-level offset to credit exposure, which needs a netting agreement.

c.reason: Applies netting-set aggregation to funding.

d.reason: Adds absolute values: Y’s set is a liability for the bank, not an exposure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.2 and Ch.17, 17.5.2
questions.question: A bank trades interest rate swaps with another dealer under a two-way CSA: zero thresholds, daily cash variation margin that can be reused, and no initial margin. The xVA desk reports a material CVA on the netting set but an FVA close to zero. Which explanation is consistent with the reading?

options.text: The FVA should equal the CVA, because funding and credit exposure use the same margin period of risk; the FVA calculation is therefore in error.

CVA is measured over a margin period of risk that assumes the dealer has defaulted and stopped posting, leaving residual exposure; funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay, and the reusable cash margin offsets the value to be funded.
FVA is close to zero because wrong-way risk between the dealer’s default and the swap values is high, which reduces the funding cost.
FVA is close to zero because the cash margin must be segregated, so it provides no funding benefit.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why CVA remains**

CVA uses the MPoR, defined assuming the counterparty has defaulted and stopped posting margin; the market move over that period (at least 10 days) is uncollateralised.

**Step 2 – Why FVA vanishes**

For funding, a normal margin posting frequency applies (likely much shorter), and reusable cash variation margin offsets the value that would otherwise need funding (funding $= \text{value} -$ margin).

⇒ “This is one reason why the FVA of a collateralised derivative may be considered to be zero, even though the equivalent CVA is not.”

**Interpretation**

The MPoR is a counterparty-risk-specific concept; GARP stresses it “is not relevant when assessing funding costs” (17.5.2).

**LO:** CR-19 g: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.4.2; Ch.7 (GARP CR Ch.17), 17.5.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.19, 19.4.2 and Ch.17, 17.5.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 g.5)

a.reason: The two do not use the same MPoR; a non-zero CVA alongside a zero FVA is expected here.

c.reason: Wrong-way risk is mainly a credit-exposure concept and does not explain a low FVA.

d.reason: Variation margin is not segregated; and if it were, it would give no funding benefit and FVA would be higher, not lower.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
questions.question: The treasurer of a European manufacturing group that hedges its currency and interest rate risk with uncollateralised OTC derivatives asks the group’s risk manager whether credit value adjustment (CVA) matters for a non-bank. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: CVA matters only to banks, because it was introduced by Basel III as a regulatory capital charge and has no role in a corporate’s accounts.

CVA matters to any institution with significant OTC derivatives, including corporates that hedge economic risks; it became a key topic because of volatile credit spreads and the related accounting and capital requirements.
CVA matters only for trades outside a netting agreement, because netting and collateral remove counterparty risk entirely and leave nothing to price.
CVA needs to be computed only after a counterparty has been downgraded; until then the risk-free value of the derivative is its fair value.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why CVA became a key topic**

GARP names three drivers: the volatility of credit spreads, the associated accounting requirements (IFRS 13) and the capital requirements (Basel III).

**Step 2 – Who it applies to**

CVA calculations are a major concern for banks, but GARP states that they are also relevant for other financial institutions and corporations with significant numbers of OTC derivatives used to hedge economic risks.

⇒ The manufacturing group’s uncollateralised hedges create exactly this kind of counterparty exposure.

**Interpretation**

The group’s banks charge it CVA in the price of each hedge, and its own fair values reflect the credit risk on both sides. The answer turns on recognising CVA as a valuation concept, not only a regulatory one.

**LO:** CR-20 a: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.1 Overview

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 a.2)

a.reason: CVA is a fair-value (accounting) adjustment as well as a capital topic, and it applies beyond banks.

c.reason: Absolute claim: netting and collateral reduce CVA and must be reflected, but they do not remove counterparty risk.

d.reason: Default can happen at any time and spreads move continuously, so CVA is part of fair value from the trade date, not something triggered by a downgrade.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
questions.question: The head of the CVA desk at a global dealer reviews the default probability inputs for about 1,500 corporate counterparties, fewer than 50 of which have liquid single-name credit default swaps. Which of the following statements about this part of the CVA calculation is correct?

options.text: For counterparties without liquid CDS, accounting standards require the desk to switch to historical default probabilities, so no proxy curves are needed.
Market-implied default probabilities are generally lower than real-world estimates, so CVA based on credit spreads understates the actuarial expected loss.

Most counterparties need proxy credit spread curves; the implied default probabilities are well above real-world ones and usually cannot be hedged, yet accounting standards generally still require credit spreads.
Because the dealer warehouses its credit risk rather than hedging it, it is exposed only to risk-neutral default risk, which is the main argument for market-implied default probabilities.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The data problem**

Obtaining market-implied default probabilities in most cases requires proxy credit spread curves, because most counterparties have no liquid single-name CDS.

**Step 2 – The economic objections**

GARP lists three: market-implied PDs are significantly higher than real-world PDs; default cannot in general be hedged; and banks warehouse credit risk, so they are exposed only to real-world default risk.

**Step 3 – What practice does**

The objections are “somewhat academic”: accounting standards generally require credit spreads when reporting CVA.

⇒ C combines the proxy problem, the objections and the accounting requirement correctly.

**Interpretation**

The desk therefore spends its effort on the proxy mapping (rating, sector, region), not on choosing between real-world and risk-neutral PDs.

**LO:** CR-20 a: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.1 Overview

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 a.5)

a.reason: The standard response to missing CDS is a proxy curve; historical PDs are used only in rare cases, not by rule.

b.reason: Polarity flip: market-implied PDs are higher than real-world PDs, so spread-based CVA is the larger figure.

d.reason: Warehousing means the bank bears real-world default risk; GARP uses it as an argument against market-implied PDs.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.2 and SchweserNotes LO 38.a
questions.question: A bank’s CVA project team is extending its exposure engine from vanilla interest rate swaps to Bermudan swaptions and to collateralised netting sets. Which of the following best describes the main challenge and a typical practical response?

options.text: Exotic and path-dependent trades change only the counterparty’s default probability, so the team should recalibrate the credit curve and leave the exposure model unchanged.
Collateralised netting sets can be dropped from the CVA calculation because margin removes the exposure, so only the Bermudan swaptions need to be simulated.
Path dependency matters only for trades with a single payment at maturity, so neither the swaptions nor the collateralised netting sets raise new exposure-modelling issues.

Valuing exotics inside an exposure simulation may itself need Monte Carlo, so approximations are common (for example, a Bermudan treated as a European), and path-dependent exposure needs the whole path to each date.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Exotic products**

An exposure simulation needs the trade’s value on every path at many dates. If the trade itself needs Monte Carlo to value (nested simulation), approximations are used: a swaption treated as a forward swap, a Bermudan payoff as a European one.

**Step 2 – Path dependency**

For collateralised netting sets the exposure at a date depends on the margin already called, so the whole path to that date matters. Probabilities of path-dependent events are approximated.

**Step 3 – Effect on method**

GARP notes that the faster direct CVA approach, which values the portfolio only at a simulated default time, is less obviously applied to path-dependent portfolios such as collateralised trades and some exotics.

⇒ D names both challenges and the usual response.

**Interpretation**

These are exposure-side problems: the credit curve and the LGD are the same whatever the product.

**LO:** CR-20 a: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 2, Reading 38 (Applying CVA to exotic products and path dependency); Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.2

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.2 and SchweserNotes LO 38.a (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 a.6)

a.reason: Exotics and collateral change the exposure profile, not the counterparty’s default probability.

b.reason: Absolute claim: margin reduces CVA but does not remove it (the margin period of risk leaves residual exposure, CR-20 j).

c.reason: Path dependency means the payoff or exposure depends on the history of the underlying; Bermudan exercise and margin both do.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.1 and 20.2
questions.question: A junior valuation analyst at a Swiss bank drafts a definition of credit value adjustment (CVA) for the bank’s pricing manual. Which of the following drafts is most accurate?

options.text: CVA is the 99th percentile loss from counterparty default over one year, held as capital against the derivatives portfolio.
CVA is the difference between the value of a derivatives portfolio with and without counterparty default; in Gregory’s convention it is negative, so the risky value is the risk-free value plus CVA.
CVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.
CVA is the sum of the standalone adjustments of each trade with the counterparty, so it is unaffected by netting and collateral agreements.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The definition**

Gregory: rather than “risk-free value”, CVA can be defined as the difference between the value with and without counterparty default.

**Step 2 – The sign**

In GARP’s convention CVA is negative, a reduction in value, so $V_{\text{risky}} = V_{\text{risk-free}} +$ CVA.

⇒ B gives both the definition and the convention.

**Interpretation**

Schweser quotes the same quantity as a positive cost and subtracts it; either way the risky value is below the risk-free value. The definition is unilateral: the bank’s own default is excluded.

**LO:** CR-20 b: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA). • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.1 Overview; 20.2.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.1 and 20.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 b.1)

a.reason: A 99th percentile loss is a capital or risk measure; CVA is an expected value (a price).

c.reason: This describes DVA, which uses the expected negative exposure and the bank’s own default probability (CR-20 e).

d.reason: Netting and collateral reduce the netting-set CVA, so CVA is not the sum of standalone adjustments (CR-20 h, j).

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.1 and 20.2.2
questions.question: A model validator at a Singapore bank reviews the CVA engine, which evaluates CVA = $-\text{LGD} \sum^{m}_{i=1}$ EPE$(t_{i})$ PD$(t_{i-1}, t_{i})$ with a single average LGD for each counterparty. Which of the following statements about the assumption that justifies this form is most accurate?

options.text: It assumes the counterparty’s hazard rate is constant, so it cannot be used when the credit curve is upward sloping or inverted.
It assumes exposure and default are positively dependent, so each EPE is measured conditional on the counterparty defaulting at that date.
It assumes the LGD is zero on collateralised trades, so only uncollateralised netting sets need to enter the sum.
It assumes default time, exposure at default and LGD are independent (no wrong-way risk), which lets the expectation split into EPE times marginal PD with one average LGD.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The general definition**

Eq. 20.1 takes one expectation of the product $\mathbb{1}(\tau\le T ) \times V (t, \tau)^{+} \times$ LGD. GARP notes that the three components may be dependent.

**Step 2 – What independence buys**

If default time, exposure at default and LGD are independent, the expectation of the product is the product of expectations: the LGD becomes a single average, the exposure becomes the unconditional EPE at each date, and default enters only through the marginal PD of each interval.

⇒ That is eq. 20.3. GARP states the assumption at the start of the chapter: credit exposure and default probability are independent, which neglects wrong-way risk.

**Interpretation**

The validator’s real question is whether the counterparty has wrong-way risk. If it does, EPE must be replaced by EPE conditional on default (CR-20 p), and the simple form understates CVA.

**LO:** CR-20 b: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA). • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.1 Overview; 20.2.2, eqs. 20.1 and 20.3

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.1 and 20.2.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 b.3)

a.reason: The marginal PDs $Q(t_{i}) - Q(t_{i-1})$ can come from any credit curve shape; a constant hazard is a convenience, not an assumption of the formula.

b.reason: Describes the wrong-way risk extension (conditional EPE), which is exactly what the simple form leaves out.

c.reason: Collateral reduces EPE (CR-20 j); it does not set the LGD to zero or remove netting sets from CVA.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
questions.question: An xVA quant at a Japanese bank notes that, for one counterparty, the bank’s only position is a swap that is deeply in the money for the bank. Which of the following statements about the CVA of this position is most accurate?

options.text: Because the swap is deeply in the money, CVA should be based on its potential future exposure at a high percentile rather than on its EPE.
Because the exposure is almost certain to stay positive, CVA no longer depends on the loss given default and equals the expected future value times the cumulative default probability.
A deeply in-the-money swap requires the path-wise CVA formula, because the direct approach cannot be applied when the exposure is always positive.
When a position is very in the money, its EPE can be approximated by its expected future value, so the CVA calculation converges to a simpler, bond-like discounting calculation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – EPE of a deep in-the-money position**

EPE averages max$(V , 0)$. If $V$ is almost never negative, max$(V , 0) \approx V$ , so EPE is close to the expected future value (EFV).

**Step 2 – What that does to CVA**

GARP: in this case one can use the CVA formula with the EFV, or a discounting approach (which has to allow for the LGD). The complex swap-like calculation converges to a simpler bond-like case.

⇒ D describes GARP’s special case.

**Interpretation**

This is the link back to CR-20 a: a swap that is deep in the money behaves like a one-way claim, so its cash flows are almost fully at risk, as for a bond.

**LO:** CR-20 b: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA). • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.4 Special Cases, Figure 20.7

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 b.6)

a.reason: CVA always uses the expected exposure; PFE is a limit measure whatever the moneyness.

b.reason: The EFV part is right, but LGD still scales the loss; dropping it treats the whole exposure as lost.

c.reason: Nothing prevents the direct method here; positive exposure makes the calculation simpler, not harder.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.3 and 20.2.6
questions.question:
A swaps desk at a Canadian bank quotes CVA as a running spread using Gregory’s average-EPE approximation, and reports CVA as a negative number. For a 5-year swap with a corporate client the desk has the following data:

|  | Last month | Today |
|---|---|---|
| Average EPE (% of notional) | 3.5 | 3.5 |
| Client 5-year CDS spread (bps) | 140 | 220 |
| Recovery rate assumed for the client (%) | 40 | 20 |

Which of the following is closest to the change in the running CVA since last month?

options.text: −7.70 bps per annum
−3.22 bps per annum
−2.80 bps per annum
−1.46 bps per annum

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The approximation**

GARP eq. 20.4: UCVA $\approx-\text{average EPE} \times$ spread, in the units of the spread.

**Step 2 – Last month and today**

−0.035 × 140 = −4.90 bps, −0.035 × 220 = −7.70 bps

**Step 3 – The change**

−7.70 − (−4.90) = −2.80 bps per annum

⇒ The running CVA becomes 2.80 bps more negative.

**Step 4 – The recovery revision**

Eq. 20.4 has no LGD input: with the same LGD implying the PD and measuring the loss, the LGD cancels to first order, and the spread already embeds it.

⇒ The revision from 40% to 20% does not change the approximate answer.

**Interpretation**

Under the approximation CVA is linear in the spread, which is fine for moderate moves. The recovery revision is a red herring at first order; the exact eq. 20.5 would show only a small second-order effect.

**LO:** CR-20 d: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.3 eq. 20.4; 20.2.6

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.3 and 20.2.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 d.3)

a.reason: Reported today’s level, −7.70 bps, instead of the change.

b.reason: Multiplied each spread charge by its LGD, double counting it: 0.80 × 220 × 0.035 − 0.60 × 140 × 0.035 = 6.16 − 2.94 = 3.22.

d.reason: Used hazard rates $s/(1-R)$ in place of the spreads: 0.035×(275.00−233.33) = 1.46.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.
questions.question:
An xVA analyst at a US bank compares the CVA on identical 4-year cross-currency swaps, notional USD 500 million, with two counterparties, U and V. The swap’s discounted EPE rises over its life because of the final exchange of notionals. Both counterparties have an LGD of 60% and the same 4-year cumulative default probability of 10%, but U’s credit curve is upward sloping and V’s is inverted. CVA is reported as a negative number and there is no wrong-way risk.

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discounted EPE (% of notional) | 2.0 | 4.0 | 6.0 | 8.0 |
| Marginal PD, counterparty U (%) | 1.0 | 2.0 | 3.0 | 4.0 |
| Marginal PD, counterparty V (%) | 4.0 | 3.0 | 2.0 | 1.0 |

Which of the following is closest to the CVA with each counterparty?

options.text: U: −USD 3.00 million; V: −USD 2.00 million
U: −USD 1.80 million; V: −USD 1.20 million
U: −USD 1.50 million; V: −USD 1.50 million
U: −USD 1.20 million; V: −USD 1.80 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – EPE** × **marginal PD, counterparty U (%** × **%)**

$$2.0(1.0) + 4.0(2.0) + 6.0(3.0) + 8.0(4.0) = 2 + 8 + 18 + 32 = 60 (\times10^{-4})$$

**Step 2 – The same for counterparty V**

$$2.0(4.0) + 4.0(3.0) + 6.0(2.0) + 8.0(1.0) = 8 + 12 + 12 + 8 = 40 (\times10^{-4})$$

**Step 3 – CVA**

U: − 0.60 × 0.0060 × 500 = −1.80, V: − 0.60 × 0.0040 × 500 = −1.20 (USD million)

⇒ The same 10% cumulative PD, but U’s defaults are back-loaded into the years when the exposure is highest, so U’s CVA is 50% larger.

**Interpretation**

This matches the direction of GARP’s finding that the upward-sloping curve gives the largest CVA (there for a 10-year swap, mostly through the extrapolated long spread). For a hump-shaped or amortising profile the gap would shrink or could reverse, so compute it rather than assume it. A flat curve (2.5% a year) gives −USD 1.50 million.

**LO:** CR-20 d: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.2 eq. 20.3; 20.2.5 Credit Spread Effects

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 d.5)

c.reason: Used average EPE $\times\text{cumulative PD} \times\text{LGD} = 0.05 \times0.10 \times0.60 \times500 = 1.50$ for both, ignoring the timing of defaults; this is right only for evenly spread PDs.

d.reason: Swapped the two counterparties: the front-loaded curve meets the small early exposures.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.
questions.question:
A valuation oﬀicer at a German bank recomputes the unilateral CVA on a 5-year uncollateralised swap, notional EUR 400 million, after the credit team revises the counterparty’s expected recovery rate from 40% to 25%. The derivative claim ranks with the senior unsecured debt referenced by the counterparty’s CDS, so the bank uses the same LGD to imply default probabilities and to measure the loss. The CDS curve is flat at 300 bps and does not move. Default probabilities are implied with a constant hazard rate $\lambda= s/$LGD, and CVA is reported as a negative number.

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discounted EPE (% of notional) | 1.5 | 2.4 | 2.8 | 2.4 | 1.4 |

Which of the following is closest to the CVA after the revision?

options.text: −EUR 1.39 million
−EUR 1.14 million
−EUR 0.91 million
−EUR 0.38 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Hazard rates**

Before: $\lambda= 0.03/0.60 = 5.00\%$. After: $\lambda= 0.03/0.75 = 4.00\%$.

⇒ The higher LGD lowers the implied hazard rate.

**Step 2 – Marginal PDs after the revision**

e$^{-0.04(i-1)} - \text{e}^{-0.04i}$ for years 1 to 5: 3.921, 3.767, 3.620, 3.478, 3.341 (%).

**Step 3 – EPE** × **PD**

$1.5(3.921) + 2.4(3.767) + 2.8(3.620) + 2.4(3.478) + 1.4(3.341) = 38.08 (\times10^{-4})$

**Step 4 – CVA after the revision**

CVA $= -0.75 \times0.003808 \times400 = -\text{EUR} 1.142$ million

**Step 5 – Compare with before**

At $\lambda= 5\%$ the PDs are 4.877, 4.639, 4.413, 4.198, 3.993 (%), the sum is 46.47, and CVA = −0.60× 0.004647 × 400 = −1.115.

⇒ A 25% rise in LGD moves CVA by only 2.4%.

**Interpretation**

The lower implied PD offsets almost all of the higher loss. The bank’s reserve barely changes, which is the cancellation GARP describes; the recovery assumption matters much more when the claim’s seniority differs from the CDS (Question CR-20 d.8).

**LO:** CR-20 d: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.6 Loss Given Default, eq. 20.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 d.7)

a.reason: Loss channel only: scaled the old CVA by 0.75/0.60 with the old PDs, −1.115 × 1.25 = −1.39.

c.reason: PD channel only: new PDs but the old 60% LGD on the loss, −0.60 × 0.003808 × 400 = −0.91.

d.reason: Used the new recovery rate in place of LGD: −0.25 × 0.003808 × 400 = −0.38.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA.
questions.question:
An xVA analyst at a UK bank is pricing a 4-year interest rate swap with a project-finance vehicle. The vehicle has no CDS, so the bank uses a proxy curve flat at 240 bps for senior unsecured risk, calibrated with the market-standard 40% recovery. The swap ranks with the project’s senior secured debt, and the credit team expects a 75% recovery on it, in line with project-finance recovery data. The proxy curve was mapped from a default-probability-based rating, so the higher recovery is not already in the spread. Default probabilities are implied with a constant hazard rate, and CVA is reported as a negative number.

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discounted EPE (GBP million) | 10 | 14 | 12 | 6 |

Which of the following is closest to the CVA?

options.text: −GBP 1.17 million
−GBP 0.94 million
−GBP 0.85 million
−GBP 0.39 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – PD from the proxy curve with the market LGD**

$\lambda= 0.024/0.60 = 4.00\%$; marginal PDs for years 1 to 4: 3.921, 3.767, 3.620, 3.478 (%).

⇒ The default probability comes from the senior unsecured curve and its own 60% LGD.

**Step 2 – EPE** × **PD**

10(0.03921) + 14(0.03767) + 12(0.03620) + 6(0.03478)

= 0.3921 + 0.5274 + 0.4344 + 0.2087 = 1.5625 (GBP million)

**Step 3 – Loss with the actual LGD**

CVA $= -(1 - 0.75) \times1.5625 = -\text{GBP} 0.391$ million

⇒ About GBP 0.39 million, roughly 40% of the charge with a 60% LGD.

**Interpretation**

Seniority in the exposure waterfall is the easiest case GARP gives for an LGD$_{\text{actual}}$ that differs from LGD$_{\text{mkt}}$; the PD must still come from the market LGD. Because the proxy was mapped from a PD-based rating, the better recovery is not double counted.

**LO:** CR-20 d: Evaluate the impact of changes in the credit spread and recovery rate assumptions on CVA. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.2.6 Loss Given Default, eq. 20.5 and Figure 20.10

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.2.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 d.8)

a.reason: Multiplied by the recovery rate instead of LGD: 0.75 × 1.5625 = 1.17.

b.reason: Ignored the seniority and used the 60% market LGD for the loss: 0.60 × 1.5625 = 0.94.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.4.1 and Ch.19, 19.3.1
questions.question: A bank has two corporate counterparties with the same credit spread, each with ten uncollateralised interest rate swaps under an enforceable netting agreement. Counterparty X hedges its fixed-rate debt and pays fixed on all ten swaps. Counterparty Y is a hedge fund whose book mixes pay-fixed and receive-fixed swaps of similar size and maturity. Which of the following statements about the netting benefit in each counterparty’s CVA is most accurate?

options.text: The netting benefit is the same for both, because it depends only on the number of trades in the netting set.
The netting benefit is larger for X, because trades in the same direction reinforce each other’s exposure and netting removes this concentration.

The netting benefit is large for Y and small for X: X’s netting-set CVA is close to the sum of its standalone CVAs, while Y’s offsetting trades make its netting-set EPE far lower than the sum of standalone EPEs.
The netting benefit is larger for Y, because netting lowers Y’s default probability, which depends on its offsetting positions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – When netting helps**

Aggregation reduces exposure only in scenarios where trade values have opposite signs (GARP Table 19.1).

**Step 2 – Counterparty X**

All ten swaps are pay-fixed for X, so their values to the bank move together: they are rarely of opposite sign, and the netting-set EPE is close to the sum of standalone EPEs.

**Step 3 – Counterparty Y**

Pay-fixed and receive-fixed swaps of similar size offset, so the netting-set EPE is far below the sum.

⇒ With the same spread, the whole difference is in the exposure: a large benefit for Y, a small one for X.

**Interpretation**

GARP: netting benefits are a portfolio effect, strong for balanced and offsetting portfolios and weaker for directional ones. Corporate hedgers like X trade directionally, so netting does little for their CVA.

**LO:** CR-20 h: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.4.1; Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.3.1, Table 19.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.4.1 and Ch.19, 19.3.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 h.2)

a.reason: The number of trades does not set the benefit; the correlation (sign pattern) of their values does.

b.reason: Polarity flip: same-direction trades offset least; netting has nothing to cancel.

d.reason: Netting leaves the default probability unchanged.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.4.1 and Ch.19, 19.3
questions.question: A bank faces one corporate counterparty through three groups of trades: (1) interest rate swaps under an ISDA Master Agreement; (2) FX forwards under a separate master agreement, with no cross-agreement netting; and (3) a few trades booked through a branch in a jurisdiction where the bank’s lawyers consider close-out netting unenforceable. How should the bank incorporate netting into the CVA for this counterparty?

options.text: Net all the trades with the counterparty into a single exposure, because CVA depends on the counterparty’s one default probability.
Compute standalone CVAs for every trade and scale the total by an average netting factor, because netting acts mainly through the counterparty’s default probability.
Net groups (1) and (2) together because they face the same legal entity, and exclude group (3) from the CVA because its exposure cannot be netted.

Compute EPE separately for each enforceable netting set, netting trade values before taking the positive part; treat each trade in group (3) as its own netting set; then add the CVAs, using the same PD and LGD throughout.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a netting set is**

The trades under one legally enforceable netting agreement. GARP notes there may be more than one netting agreement with a given counterparty.

**Step 2 – Within each netting set**

Add the trade values on each simulated path, then take the positive part, giving one EPE profile per set.

**Step 3 – Where netting is not enforceable**

Each trade in group (3) is its own netting set, so its gross positive exposure counts.

**Step 4 – Counterparty CVA**

Add the netting-set CVAs, using the counterparty’s PD and the LGD (same seniority) throughout.

⇒ D follows the legal boundaries of netting.

**Interpretation**

GARP notes that a bank may sometimes judge netting enforceable for pricing while accepting the legal risk, but where its lawyers consider it unenforceable the trades are treated gross. Clients in such jurisdictions may trade only with banks that do recognise netting.

**LO:** CR-20 h: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.4.1; Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.3 and footnote 20; Ch.6 (GARP CR Ch.16), netting enforceability

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.4.1 and Ch.19, 19.3 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 h.3)

a.reason: Netting is a legal right within an agreement, not a consequence of having one default probability.

b.reason: Netting acts on the exposure, path by path; a scalar netting factor on standalone CVAs is not how GARP incorporates it.

c.reason: Groups (1) and (2) sit under separate agreements with no cross-netting, and group (3) still carries CVA on its gross exposure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.4.1 and Ch.19, 19.3.1
questions.question: An xVA desk prices BCVA without survival adjustments, applying each party’s own default probability to its leg. The counterparty and the bank have the same flat credit spread and the same LGD, and therefore the same marginal default probabilities. A trader proposes a new swap that strongly offsets the existing netting set and argues that it should earn a large BCVA benefit from netting. Which of the following is the best response?

options.text: The trader is right: the offsetting swap lowers the netting set’s EPE, so the CVA leg shrinks while the DVA leg is unaffected, giving a large BCVA benefit.
The trader is wrong: netting raises both EPE and ENE in size, so the new swap makes BCVA more negative.

The trader is wrong: with equal spreads and LGDs, BCVA depends on EPE plus ENE, which is the expected future value; that is additive across trades, so the CVA and DVA effects of netting offset and there is no incremental netting benefit.
The trader is right: netting lowers the DVA leg but leaves the CVA leg unchanged, so BCVA becomes less negative.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – BCVA without survival terms**

BCVA $= -\text{LGD} \sum$ EPE$(t_{i}) \text{PD}_{C} (t_{i-1}, t_{i}) - \text{LGD} \sum$ ENE$(t_{i}) \text{PD}_{B}(t_{i-1}, t_{i})$.

**Step 2 – Equal spreads and LGDs**

With PD$_{C} = \text{PD}_{B}$, BCVA $= -\text{LGD} \sum[\text{EPE} + \text{ENE}](t_{i})$ PD$(t_{i-1}, t_{i})$, and EPE $+ \text{ENE} =$ E$[\text{max}(V , 0)] + \text{E}[\text{min}(V , 0)] =$ EFV.

**Step 3 – Additivity**

The EFV is additive across trades (GARP Table 19.1: 10 + (−5) = 5), so the netting-set BCVA equals the sum of standalone BCVAs.

⇒ Netting cuts CVA and DVA by the same amount: no incremental netting benefit.

**Interpretation**

GARP: “for equal credit spread, BCVA is always the same and has no incremental effect.” Even with 150 against 100 bps (Table 20.4), the offsetting book halved the CVA but moved BCVA only from −20.3 to −16.3 bps.

**LO:** CR-20 h: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.4.1, Table 20.4; Ch.11 (GARP CR Ch.19), 19.3.1, Table 19.1

CR-20 • CVA • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.4.1 and Ch.19, 19.3.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 h.6)

a.reason: Ignores the DVA leg: the offset shrinks ENE in size too, so DVA falls.

b.reason: Polarity flip: netting reduces both EPE and ENE in size.

d.reason: Netting reduces both legs, not only DVA.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 and 20.6.7
questions.question: At the risk committee of a CCP, a member argues that because every cleared position carries daily variation margin and initial margin, wrong-way risk is not a material concern for the CCP. Which response is most consistent with GARP?

options.text: Disagree: margin mitigates WWR only if exposure builds gradually before a default; jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk can exhaust initial margin, and the members that post margin are mostly systemic banks whose defaults bring the most extreme WWR.
Agree: margin removes WWR at a CCP, because variation margin is received continuously as the exposure to a member rises.
Agree: WWR matters only for uncollateralised counterparties such as corporates, and corporates are not clearing members.
Disagree: margin increases WWR, because collateral posted by a member always loses its value when that member defaults.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Margin and timing**

GARP 20.6.6: if exposure increases gradually before default, margin can be received; a jump in exposure makes margin useless.

**Step 2 – Stressed close-out**

Pykhtin and Sokol: the benefit of margin under WWR must allow for jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk, so initial margin set at normal coverage can be exhausted.

**Step 3 – Who posts margin**

The parties that actively use margin, mainly banks, are highly systemic and face the most extreme WWR; non-systemic corporates often post no margin anyway.

⇒ A: at a CCP, margin is weakest exactly where WWR is worst.

**Interpretation**

CCP membership is dominated by large banks, so the WWR that matters most to a CCP is the default of a systemic member, which is when markets gap.

**LO:** CR-20 q: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.6 Collateralisation and WWR; 20.6.7

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.20, 20.6.6 and 20.6.7 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 q.2)

b.reason: Absolute claim: margin arrives with a lag and cannot keep up with a jump at default.

c.reason: The systemic, margin-posting members are the ones subject to extreme WWR.

d.reason: Absolute claim: only specific collateral, such as a member’s own bonds, is linked to its default; margin in general still reduces exposure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.2 and Ch.20, 20.6.7
questions.question: A regulator notes that credit default swaps (CDSs) were a main catalyst of the clearing mandate after the 2007 to 2009 crisis. A CCP risk oﬀicer replies that single-name CDSs are among the hardest products to clear. Which reasoning best supports the risk oﬀicer?

options.text: CDSs are illiquid by construction, so a CCP cannot compute variation margin on them at all.
Once cleared, CDSs carry no WWR, because multilateral netting offsets protection bought and sold across members, so the diﬀiculty is purely operational.
CDS exposures fall when credit spreads widen, so the CCP faces right-way risk that makes initial margins too high.

Ideally cleared products carry no WWR, but a member’s default can be adversely linked to the value of the CDSs it has traded (for example, protection sold on correlated financials), so values can move sharply just as it defaults, complicating default management and the WWR part of margin and default funds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The clearability criterion**

GARP Ch.18 lists WWR among the features of a clearable product: ideally it would have none, because if a member’s default is adversely linked to a contract’s value, that value may fall rapidly at the default, which harms default management.

**Step 2 – Why CDSs fail it**

A member that has sold protection on names correlated with itself (other financials, its sovereign) owes much more exactly when it defaults.

**Step 3 – The CCP’s task**

GARP 20.6.7: CCPs clearing products such as CDSs are particularly prone to WWR, and quantifying the WWR component of initial margin and default funds is far from easy.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

Hence GARP’s “subtle point”: the product that catalysed the clearing mandate is arguably the most diﬀicult to clear centrally.

**LO:** CR-20 q: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.18), 18.2 Mechanics of Central Clearing; Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.5 and 20.6.7

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.2 and Ch.20, 20.6.7 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 q.3)

a.reason: Liquidity is a clearability criterion, but CDSs are cleared with variation margin; illiquidity is not the reason given.

b.reason: Netting offsets market risk across members, but the CCP still faces each member’s default; WWR remains.

c.reason: Polarity flip: bought protection gains when spreads widen, so the exposure to protection sellers rises in a credit shock.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.2 and Ch.20, 20.6.7
questions.question: The treasurer of a regional bank that is a clearing member argues that, because the CCP stands between all buyers and sellers and runs a matched book, moving the bank’s credit derivatives into clearing has eliminated the wrong-way risk it used to face bilaterally. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Agree: after novation the CCP has no net market risk in any circumstances, so a member’s default cannot produce wrong-way losses for anyone.
Agree: the wrong-way risk now sits entirely in the defaulting member’s own initial margin, which by design covers every possible close-out loss.
Disagree: the book is matched only while all members perform; a default leaves it unmatched just when WWR bites, and losses beyond the defaulter’s resources and CCP equity fall on surviving members.
Disagree: clearing increases wrong-way risk mainly because the CCP must post initial margin to its members, which it loses when a member defaults.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The matched book**

Through novation the CCP faces every buyer and every seller, so with all members performing its positions offset and it has no net market risk.

**Step 2 – Conditional market risk**

GARP Ch.18: the CCP has conditional market risk, because a member default leaves it with an unmatched book that it must hedge and auction. With WWR the defaulter’s positions move sharply against the CCP at exactly that moment.

**Step 3 – Who bears the loss**

Defaulter pays first (its initial margin and default fund contribution), then CCP equity, then the surviving members’ default fund contributions: a senior, mutualised second loss concentrated in systemic scenarios.

⇒ C: the bank has swapped bilateral WWR for a share of the CCP’s tail.

**Interpretation**

Clearing changes the form of the risk, not its existence. The surviving members’ exposure is rare but systemic, which is why GARP likens it to a senior CDO tranche (CR-20 o).

**LO:** CR-20 q: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.8 (GARP CR Ch.18), 18.2 Mechanics of Central Clearing; Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.20), 20.6.7, Figure 20.24 CR-21 • The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.18, 18.2 and Ch.20, 20.6.7 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-20 q.6)

a.reason: Absolute claim: the book is matched only while every member performs; default is the case that matters.

b.reason: Defaulter-pays resources may prove insuﬀicient under WWR; initial margin is set to a confidence level, not to cover every loss.

d.reason: Members post initial margin to the CCP, not the reverse; the risk comes from the defaulter’s positions and the mutualised default fund.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate among current exposure, peak exposure, expected exposure, and expected positive exposure.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.1 (BCBS 2005 definitions)
questions.question: A junior analyst at a Korean bank is preparing the expected positive exposure (EPE) of a 7-year netting set for the minimum capital calculation. The simulation engine reports expected exposures at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months, and then annually out to year 7. Which method is consistent with the definitions used in the chapter?

options.text: The time-weighted average of the expected exposures over the first year, each weighted by the share of the year that its interval represents.
The simple average of all the expected exposures out to year 7, with each reporting date counted once.
The highest 95th-percentile exposure reported over the first year.
The expected exposure at the one-year date, since capital is held for one year.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – EPE is a time-weighted average**

EPE is “the weighted average over time of expected exposures where the weights are the proportion that an individual expected exposure represents of the entire time interval”.

⇒ With dates at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months the intervals are unequal (1, 2, 3 and 6 months), so weights of 1/12, 2/12, 3/12 and 6/12 apply, not equal weights.

**Step 2 – Which interval for capital**

For the minimum capital requirement the average is taken over the first year (or over the life of the longest contract if all mature within a year). The 7-year netting set therefore uses the first year only.

**Interpretation**

Two separate errors are on offer: the wrong weights (B) and the wrong statistic (C, D). EPE is neither a percentile nor a single date.

**LO:** CR-21 a: Differentiate among current exposure, peak exposure, expected exposure, and expected positive exposure. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.1, BCBS (2005) definitions

CR-21 • The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.1 (BCBS 2005 definitions) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 a.6)

b.reason: Wrong horizon and wrong weights: the capital EPE uses the first year, and unequal intervals need time weights.

c.reason: That is the maximum peak exposure over the year, a tail statistic.

d.reason: That is a single point of the EE profile, not its average.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question: A CCR manager is building the summary page of a stress-testing pack. Which of the following correctly assigns measures to the two ways of viewing counterparty credit risk described in the chapter?

options.text: Credit-risk view: current exposure, peak exposure and expected exposure; market-risk view: CVA and the variability of CVA, for example the VaR of CVA.
Credit-risk view: CVA and peak exposure; market-risk view: current exposure and expected exposure.
Credit-risk view: the VaR of CVA only; market-risk view: current, peak and expected exposure, since all three are marked to market.
Credit-risk view: CVA, because it is an expected loss; market-risk view: EPE, because it is a time average of market values.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The credit side**

“On the credit risk side, there are the important measures of exposure: current exposure; peak exposure; and expected exposure.”

**Step 2 – The market side**

“On the market risk side, there is the valuation aspect coming from CVA, and there is the risk generated by changes in the CVA as measured by the value-at-risk (VaR) of CVA.”

⇒ Exposures belong to the credit view; CVA and its risk belong to the market view.

**Interpretation**

This split is why the number of CCR stress results doubles: every scenario must be read through both sets of measures.

**LO:** CR-21 b: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.2

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 b.2)

b.reason: Swaps the two lists: CVA is the market view’s measure, and current and expected exposure belong to the credit view.

c.reason: Puts all the exposure measures in the market view; exposures are the credit view’s statistics, whatever their inputs.

d.reason: CVA is a market price of CCR, not the credit view’s expected loss; EPE is a credit-view exposure measure.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question: The risk committee of a regional bank treats CCR purely as a credit risk. It sets potential future exposure limits for each counterparty, requires collateral and netting agreements at inception, and does not include CVA in the valuation of its derivatives portfolio. According to the chapter, to which risk does this leave the bank most exposed?

options.text: Losses from counterparty defaults beyond its exposure limits, since the credit view provides no protection against default.
Wrong-way risk only, since collateral and netting remove every other source of counterparty risk.
Changes in the market value of counterparty risk (CVA) as credit spreads and exposures move, which can produce balance-sheet surprises.
None of significance, since limits, collateral and netting together capture all counterparty risk in a derivatives portfolio.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the committee has covered**

PFE limits, collateral and netting manage the default side of CCR: they are the credit view’s tools.

**Step 2 – What the credit view leaves open**

“If CCR is treated as a credit risk, a bank can still be exposed to changes in CVA. … it must still include CVA in the valuation of its derivatives portfolio. Inattention to this could lead to balance-sheet surprises.”

⇒ The exposure is to swings in the fair value of counterparty risk.

**Interpretation**

The 2007-08 crisis made this concrete: spreads and exposures moved together and CVA swung by large amounts, in both directions, for banks that had treated CVA as a small pricing item.

**LO:** CR-21 b: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 b.3)

a.reason: The credit view is built to manage default risk (limits, collateral, netting); its gap is the fair-value side.

b.reason: Absolute claim: collateral and netting do not remove CVA risk, and wrong-way risk is not the only residual.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the chapter says adopting one view alone leaves the bank blind to the other.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question: Two dealers share a counterparty whose credit quality deteriorates over several months before it defaults. Dealer K treats CCR as a credit risk. Dealer M treats CCR as a market risk and manages its CVA dynamically. Which statement best describes the two dealers’ experience?

options.text: K replaces the counterparty’s trades gradually, in proportion to its probability of default, so the default is a non-event for K; M must replace all the trades at once at default.

K must replace all of the defaulting counterparty’s trades in the market at once at default; M has already moved trades to other counterparties in proportion to the rising probability of default, so the default is close to a non-event for M.
Both dealers are fully protected: K by the collateral and netting set up at inception, and M by its CVA hedges.
Neither dealer can act before default, because under both views counterparty risk can be managed only at inception.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Credit view at default**

“At default, the financial institution must replace the trades of the defaulting counterparty in the market all at once in order to rebalance its book.”

**Step 2 – Market view before default**

The bank replaces trades “before it defaults by buying the positions in proportion to the counterparty’s probability of default”. As credit quality deteriorates, a larger share moves to other counterparties. “At default, the financial institution will have already replaced the trades and the default itself would be a non-event.”

⇒ K faces a one-off replacement at default; M has replaced gradually.

**Interpretation**

This is the “implication for trading activities” in the LO wording: the market view turns default management into a continuous hedging activity.

**LO:** CR-21 b: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 b.4)

a.reason: Swaps the two dealers’ behaviour.

c.reason: Absolute claim: the credit-view dealer still faces CVA swings and replacement cost, and the market-view dealer is exposed to sudden default.

d.reason: True only of the credit view; the market view acts before default.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the evolution of CCR measurement, as described in the chapter, is correct?

options.text: Stress testing of CCR evolved faster than the statistical measures of CCR, which is why the chapter builds the statistical measures on top of stress tests.

Treating CCR as a credit risk was the predominant framework from 2000 to 2006 and the basis of Basel II capital, while the market-risk treatment was largely confined to pricing CVA until the 2007-08 crisis.
Before the crisis CVA was a large and volatile part of bank derivative valuations, which prompted the FAS 157 accounting requirement.
During the crisis the combined swings in credit spreads and exposures produced large CVA losses but no gains, since credit spreads only widened.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The credit view**

Potential exposure and EPE models “are the hallmark of treating CCR as a credit risk”. This was “the predominant framework for measuring and managing CCR from 2000 to 2006, and was established as the basis for regulatory capital as part of Basel II”.

**Step 2 – The market view**

The market treatment was “largely relegated to pricing in a credit valuation adjustment (CVA) prior to the financial crisis of 2007-08”.

⇒ B is a direct statement of the chapter.

**Interpretation**

The chapter’s premise runs the other way from A: the statistical measures moved fast and stress testing lagged, so stress tests are built on the statistical measures.

**LO:** CR-21 b: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 b.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: statistical measures progressed faster than stress testing.

c.reason: Before the crisis spreads were stable and CVA was a small part of valuations; FAS 157 is a fair-value rule, not a response to volatile CVA.

d.reason: The crisis produced “both large losses and large, unusual gains”.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.3 and Table 21.1
questions.question:
A CCR manager presents the following extract from the bank’s current exposure stress report to the credit committee (scenario: equity market down 25%; US\$ million).

| Counterparty | Rating | MtM | Collateral | Current exposure | Stressed current exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | A | 0.5 | 0 | 0.5 | 303 |
| C | AA | 35 | 0 | 35 | 119 |
| D | BBB | 20 | 20 | 0 | 76 |
| H | BB | −50 | 0 | 0 | 24 |
| I | A | 35 | 20 | 15 | 17 |

Which conclusion can the committee draw from this table alone?

options.text: The equity crash would cost the bank about US\$539 million, the sum of the stressed current exposures.
Counterparty C is a greater concern than counterparty D in this scenario, because its stressed current exposure is larger.
The table shows which counterparties would owe the bank most if equities fell 25%, but it cannot say whether C or D is the greater concern, because stressed current exposure ignores credit quality.
Counterparty D needs no further attention in this scenario, because its trades are fully collateralised today.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the table measures**

Stressed current exposure is the value of the trades after the shock and before new collateral: what each counterparty would owe the bank in the scenario.

⇒ It ranks exposure, not loss.

**Step 2 – What it leaves out**

It omits each counterparty’s willingness or ability to pay. C has the larger stressed exposure (119) but is rated AA; D has 76 but is rated BBB. GARP: “it is unclear whether the CCR manager should be more concerned about counterparty C or counterparty D”.

**Interpretation**

To compare C and D, exposure must be combined with credit quality, which is what the expected-loss stress of Sections 2 and 3 does.

**LO:** CR-21 c: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.3, Table 21.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.3 and Table 21.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 c.3)

a.reason: Absolute claim: 303 + 119 + 76 + 24 + 17 = 539 is the loss only if every counterparty defaulted in the scenario.

b.reason: Ignores credit quality: a larger exposure to an AA name need not be the greater concern.

d.reason: D’s collateral covers today’s MtM of 20; the stressed exposure of 76 is measured before any further collateral is collected.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question: The CRO of a mid-sized bank asks for a stress test of the corporate loan book in the expected-loss framework that the chapter starts from before adapting it to derivatives. Which design matches that framework?

options.text: Hold the PDs fixed and stress each EAD through instantaneous shocks to equity prices and swap rates, since the loans’ exposures move with market variables.
Replace each EAD with alpha times EPE, and stress EPE by re-running the exposure simulation after a market shock.
Reprice each loan under the scenario and report the borrowers with the largest stressed current exposure, one table per scenario.

Hold EAD and LGD fixed, model each PD as a function of variables such as the unemployment rate or an important exchange rate, set those variables to stressed values, and recompute expected loss with the stressed PDs.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The loan framework**

Expected loss EL $= \sum p_{i} \text{ead}_{i} \text{lgd}_{i}$ across the pool.

**Step 2 – What is stressed**

“A stress test could take EAD and LGD as deterministic, and focus on stresses where the probability of default is subject to a stress.” The PD is a function of other variables, such as “an important exchange rate or an unemployment rate”, set to stressed values.

⇒ Stressed PDs give EL$^{S}$; the stress loss is EL$^{S} -$ EL.

**Interpretation**

Each wrong option describes a real test, but for the derivative book: B is the credit-view derivative adaptation, C is the current-exposure stress, and A wrongly gives loans market-sensitive exposure.

**LO:** CR-21 c: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.4

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 c.7)

a.reason: Loan exposures are insensitive to market variables; the loan stress works through the PD.

b.reason: $\alpha\times$EPE replaces EAD only for derivatives, whose exposure is stochastic.

c.reason: That is the current-exposure stress used for derivative counterparties.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question:
A risk manager at a Canadian bank combines the stress losses on the loan book and the derivatives book under a recession scenario that raises PDs and shocks equity markets. Derivative exposures enter the credit framework as alpha times EPE, with alpha at the expected-loss level of 1.2. LGDs are unchanged by the stress. Amounts are in CAD million.

| Loan segment | EAD | LGD | PD | Stressed PD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SME | 400 | 40% | 1.5% | 3.0% |
| Corporate | 250 | 50% | 0.8% | 1.6% |

| Counterparty | Current exposure | EPE | Stressed EPE | LGD | PD | Stressed PD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| X | 25 | 90 | 120 | 60% | 0.5% | 1.0% |
| Y | 0 | 40 | 35 | 60% | 2.0% | 2.5% |

Which of the following is closest to the combined stress loss on the two books?

options.text: CAD 3.40 million
CAD 3.90 million
CAD 3.99 million
CAD 8.29 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Loan book (PD stressed, EAD and LGD fixed)**

EL $= 400(0.40)(0.015) + 250(0.50)(0.008) = 2.4 + 1.0 = 3.4, \text{EL}^{S} = 4.8 + 2.0 = 6.8$

⇒ Loan stress loss 3.40.

**Step 2 – Derivatives book (**$\alpha\times$**EPE, PD and EPE stressed)**

EL = 1.2 \[0.005(90)(0.60) + 0.020(40)(0.60)\] = 1.2(0.27 + 0.48) = 0.900

EL$^{S} = 1.2 [0.010(120)(0.60) + 0.025(35)(0.60)] = 1.2(0.72 + 0.525) = 1.494$

⇒ Derivative stress loss 1.494 − 0.900 = 0.594.

**Step 3 – Combine the books**

$3.400 + 0.594 = 3.994 \approx\text{CAD} 3.99$ million

**Interpretation**

Both books are on the same expected-loss footing, so their stress losses add. Y’s EPE falls under the equity shock, but its PD rise still increases its EL. The current exposures are a red herring: CCR enters the portfolio credit model through $\alpha\times$EPE.

**LO:** CR-21 d: Differentiate between stressed expected loss and stress loss of a credit portfolio, and calculate the stress loss on a loan portfolio and the stress loss on a derivative portfolio. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.4, eqs. for EL and EL$^{S}$ and footnote 4

CR-21 • The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 d.6)

a.reason: Dropped the derivatives book, perhaps misreading “EPE stresses need not be aggregated with the loan book”: 3.40. That remark says loans have no EPE stress, not that derivative stress losses are left out.

b.reason: Omitted $\alpha$: derivative stress loss 1.245 − 0.750 = 0.495, total 3.90.

d.reason: Reported the total stressed EL, 6.8 + 1.494 = 8.29, instead of the change.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.question: A CVA desk applies an instantaneous 25% fall in equity prices to its equity derivatives with a hedge fund counterparty, together with the widening of the counterparty’s CDS spread that accompanies the scenario. How does the scenario enter the stressed CVA?

options.text: Only the expected exposure in the first time bucket changes, because the shock is instantaneous; later buckets keep their base values.
The shock changes today’s market values, so the expected exposures in all later periods must be recalculated, and the marginal default probabilities are restated from the shocked credit spread.
The expected exposures are left unchanged and only the LGD is stressed, since CVA is linear in LGD.
The desk replaces each period’s expected exposure with the stressed current exposure, which gives the same answer at lower cost.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Exposures**

“An instantaneous shock will have some impact on the expected exposure calculated in later time periods, so all of the expected exposures will have to be recalculated.”

⇒ The whole EE profile moves, not only the first bucket.

**Step 2 – Default probabilities**

“Stresses to the marginal probability of default are usually derived from credit spread shocks.” The wider CDS spread gives new $q^{*}$ values.

**Interpretation**

An equity crash against a hedge fund that is long equity is a natural wrong-way scenario: exposure and default probability rise together, so both inputs must be restated.

**LO:** CR-21 e: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA. • **Reference:** Lynch (GARP CR Ch.21), 21.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.21, 21.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-21 e.3)

a.reason: The shock is applied today but affects every later expected exposure.

c.reason: LGD can be stressed, but the scenario’s main effects are on exposure and default probability.

d.reason: Current exposure is not a substitute for expected exposure; that is one of the CR-21 h pitfalls.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
questions.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
questions.topic: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
