questions.question: A portfolio manager holds USD 10 million of 5-year Colombian government bonds and buys 5-year CDS protection on Colombia at 250 basis points to hedge default risk. Which of the following statements about the protection is correct?

options.text: If the bonds’ price falls sharply in a liquidity squeeze while Colombia keeps paying, the protection seller must compensate the manager for the fall.
Because the reference entity is a sovereign, the manager carries no exposure to the protection seller.

After a failure to pay, a restructuring or a bankruptcy, the seller either buys the bonds at par or pays par minus their market price, and the protection is only as good as the seller’s own credit standing.
Under cash settlement the seller pays the full par value of USD 10 million and also takes delivery of the bonds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What triggers payment**

The seller makes the buyer whole “if the issuer of the bond (reference entity) fails to pay, restructures or goes bankrupt (credit event)”, by physical settlement (buy the bond at par) or cash settlement (pay par minus the market price).

**Step 2 – The two gaps**

“If there is no credit event, and the market price of the bond collapses, you as the buyer will not be compensated”; and “the guarantee is only as good as the credit standing of the seller of the CDS”.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The premium here is 2.5% of USD 10 million, USD 250,000 a year for five years. The two gaps are why a CDS spread is not a clean default measure: it prices the seller’s risk and the market’s liquidity too.

**LO:** CR-8 g: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default. • **Reference:** Damodaran, Country Risk 2022 (GARP CR Ch.8), Credit Default Swaps: How Does a CDS Work?

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, Credit Default Swaps (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-8 g.3)

a.reason: No credit event, no payout: a price fall without default is not covered.

b.reason: The buyer is exposed to the seller’s ability to pay whatever the reference entity.

d.reason: Mixes the two settlements: cash settlement pays par minus market price, with no delivery; physical settlement pays par against delivery.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.

questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8, Market Interest Rates and Credit Default Swaps
questions.question: At an investment committee meeting of a Japanese pension fund, one member argues: “Market measures lead the agencies, so sovereign ratings are useless and we should stop using them.” Which of the following responses is best supported by the evidence in Damodaran?

options.text: A rating change is still an informational event with a price impact when it occurs, and bond markets draw on ratings just as agencies draw on market data, so ratings remain useful alongside spreads.
Ratings are better predictors of default than either market measure, because each rating is set only after a committee review.
Default spreads are uncorrelated with ratings, so the two measures carry unrelated information and both should be kept.
Ratings can be replaced by a portfolio of emerging-market sovereign CDS, because those spreads move independently of each other and so diversify country risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the default-spread studies conclude**

“Notwithstanding the lead-lag relationship, a change in sovereign ratings is still an informational event that creates a price impact at the time that it occurs. In summary, it would be a mistake to conclude that sovereign ratings are useless, since sovereign bond markets seem to draw on ratings (and changes in these ratings) when pricing bonds, just as ratings agencies draw on market data”.

⇒ A.

**Step 2 – Check the CDS claim in D**

GARP’s fourth CDS finding is clustering: CDS prices across groups of countries move together (cluster 1: average internal correlation 0.516 against 0.210 external).

**Interpretation**

The three measures are complements: ratings for stability and their information events, default spreads for granular pricing, CDS spreads as the earliest but noisiest warning.

**LO:** CR-8 g: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default. • **Reference:** Damodaran, Country Risk 2022 (GARP CR Ch.8), The Spread as a Predictor of Default; CDS and Default Risk, Table 8.11

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.8, Market Interest Rates and Credit Default Swaps (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-8 g.5)

b.reason: Polarity flip: market measures adjust faster, and CDS changes are emerging as better predictors than ratings.

c.reason: Default spreads are correlated with ratings and with actual default.

d.reason: CDS spreads cluster, so a basket of correlated sovereign CDS does not diversify country risk, and nothing in the evidence says CDS should replace ratings.

questions.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
questions.topic: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
questions.source: Workbook D23.1 • S1 • Map #56 • also CR-8 b
questions.question: A sovereign risk analyst at a Singapore asset manager is presenting to the investment committee on how to monitor default risk in a portfolio of emerging market government bonds. The analyst compares agency ratings, default spreads on US dollar sovereign bonds, and sovereign CDS spreads. Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to make?

options.text: Changes in sovereign CDS spreads tend to lead changes in bond yields and ratings, but a spike may reflect counterparty and liquidity risk rather than higher default risk.
Sovereign CDS spreads update continuously, and the evidence shows them to be clearly superior to default spreads on government bonds as a measure of default risk.
Default spreads on sovereign bonds tend to widen only after a rating downgrade, so the bond market confirms agency assessments rather than anticipating them.
Default spreads can be measured from local currency government bonds by comparing their yields across countries, without needing a default-free bond in each currency.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the evidence says about sovereign CDS**

Damodaran: “changes in CDS spreads lead changes in the sovereign bond yields and in sovereign ratings”. But “the exposure to counterparty and liquidity risk, endemic to the CDS market, can cause changes in CDS prices that have little to do with default risk”: much of the late-2008 surge followed Lehman’s failure, and the narrowness of the market adds liquidity squeezes.

⇒ A is correct: CDS spreads are the most timely signal, and their known noise has a named source.

**Interpretation**

The committee should use all three measures: ratings for stability and their information events, bond default spreads for granular and dynamic pricing in a currency with a default-free benchmark, and CDS spreads as the earliest (but noisy) warning, discounting moves that coincide with dealer stress or thin trading.

**LO:** CR-8 g: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default. CR-8 b: Evaluate the methods for measuring country risk and discuss the limitations of using those methods.

- **Reference:** Damodaran, Country Risk 2022 (GARP CR Ch.8), Sovereign Default Risk: Market Interest Rates (The Sovereign Default Spread; The Spread as a Predictor of Default) and Credit Default Swaps (CDS and Default Risk) CR-9 • Estimating Default Probabilities • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D23.1 • S1 • Map #56 • also CR-8 b (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-8 g.6)

b.reason: Absolute claim: CDS changes “provide information, albeit noisy”, but “there is little to indicate that it is superior to market default spreads (obtained from government bonds)”. The supported claim is only that CDS changes may predict default better than ratings.

c.reason: Polarity flip on the lead-lag: “the sovereign bond market leads ratings agencies, with default spreads usually climbing ahead of a rating downgrade and dropping before an upgrade”.

d.reason: Scope error: a market default spread needs “a default free security in the currency in which the bonds are issued”. Local currency yields across countries “cannot be compared to each other, since the differences in rates can be due to differences in expected inflation”.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.6 (rewritten as multiple choice)
questions.question: A junior trader at a Paris bank asks how a credit default swap can be settled after a credit event. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Physical settlement: the seller delivers the reference entity’s bonds to the buyer at their post-default price; cash settlement: the seller pays the buyer the market value of the defaulted bonds.

Physical settlement: the buyer delivers bonds with a face value equal to the notional and receives their face value; cash settlement: the seller pays the notional times one minus the auction value of the cheapest deliverable bond per unit of face value.
Physical settlement: the buyer delivers bonds and receives their market value just before the default; cash settlement: the buyer pays the seller the accrued premium only.
Physical settlement: the reference entity buys back its bonds from the buyer at face value; cash settlement: the seller pays the buyer the full notional.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Physical settlement**

The buyer has the right to sell bonds of the reference entity for their face value; the seller must buy them. Bonds with a face value equal to the notional change hands for that face value.

**Step 2 – Cash settlement**

An auction sets the value of the cheapest deliverable bond; the seller pays the notional times one minus that value (CTD at 35 gives 65% of notional).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Both routes leave the buyer with about the face value: either cash for the bonds, or cash equal to the loss on bonds it can keep or sell. Cash settlement is now usual.

**LO:** CR-9 g: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.4 Credit Default Swaps; Practice Question 9.6

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.6 (rewritten as multiple choice) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 g.1)

a.reason: Reverses who delivers, and the cash leg pays the recovery value instead of the loss (the slip in Vardeez’s notes).

c.reason: The buyer receives face value, not a pre-default market value; the accrual is owed in addition to the payoff, not instead of it.

d.reason: The reference entity is not a party to the CDS, and cash settlement pays the loss, not the full notional.

questions.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.4 and 9.4.1
questions.question: A CDS on Delta Corp allows any of three senior unsecured Delta bonds to be delivered. Several days after a credit event, the three bonds trade at 38, 35 and 41 per 100 of face value, and the contract is cash settled through the standard auction. Which statement about the payoff is correct?

options.text: The auction values the cheapest deliverable bond, the one trading at 35, so the seller pays 65% of notional; the cheapest-to-deliver option benefits the protection buyer.
The payoff is based on the average of the three prices, so neither party gains from the choice of bond.
The payoff is based on the bond trading at 41, so the seller pays 59% of notional; the choice of bond benefits the protection seller.
The payoff is based on the bond trading at 35, and the buyer pays 35% of notional to the seller.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which bond sets the payoff**

The buyer may deliver any of the eligible bonds and will choose the cheapest; the auction therefore determines the value of the cheapest deliverable bond, here 35.

**Step 2 – Who pays and how much**

The seller pays notional ×(1 − 0.35) = 65% of notional.

⇒ The choice of bond is an option held by the buyer: A.

**Interpretation**

The cheapest-to-deliver option makes protection more valuable to the buyer, one reason it pushes the CDS-bond basis in a positive direction (CR-9 i).

**LO:** CR-9 g: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.4 and 9.4.1 The Cheapest-to-Deliver Bond

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.4 and 9.4.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 g.3)

b.reason: The payoff is not an average; the cheapest bond sets it.

c.reason: The most expensive bond would favour the seller; the option belongs to the buyer.

d.reason: Reverses the direction and pays the recovery value instead of the loss.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.5 (rewritten as multiple choice) • GARP-practice numerical
questions.question: A credit default swap requires a semiannual payment at the rate of 60 basis points per year. The principal is \$300 million and the swap is settled in cash. A default occurs after four years and two months, and the calculation agent estimates that the price of the cheapest deliverable bond is 40% of its face value shortly after the default. Which of the following correctly describes the cash flows for the seller of the credit default swap?

options.text: Receives \$900,000 every six months for four years, then pays \$120 million at four years and two months.
Receives \$900,000 every six months for four years, then pays \$180 million at four years and two months.
Receives \$900,000 every six months for four years; at four years and two months receives a final accrual of \$300,000 and pays \$180 million.
Receives \$1.8 million every six months for four years; at four years and two months receives a final accrual of \$600,000 and pays \$180 million.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Regular payments to the seller**

$\frac{1}{2} \times0.0060 \times300{,}000{,}000 = \$900{,}000$ every six months, at 0.5, 1.0, … , 4.0 years (8 payments)

**Step 2 – Final accrual**

Payments are made in arrears, so the buyer owes the premium for the two months since the last payment date:

$0.0060 \times300{,}000{,}000 \times\frac{2}{12} = \$300{,}000$

**Step 3 – Cash settlement**

300,000,000 × (1 − 0.40) = \$180,000,000 paid by the seller at 4 years and 2 months

**Interpretation**

The seller collects \$7.5 million in total (8 × 0.9 + 0.3) and pays \$180 million. A GARP-practice numerical under a CONCEPT LO: the numbers only record the mechanics (who pays, how often, in arrears, and the loss rather than the recovery).

**LO:** CR-9 g: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.4; Practice Question 9.5

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.5 (rewritten as multiple choice) • GARP-practice numerical (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 g.4)

a.reason: Paid the bond’s recovery value instead of the loss (300 × 0.40 = 120), and omitted the accrual.

b.reason: Omitted the final accrual that payment in arrears requires.

d.reason: Paid the full annual rate every six months: $0.0060 \times300\text{m} = \$1.8$ million, with an accrual of \$600,000.

questions.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
questions.question: A five-year CDS on an investment-grade name trades with a standard fixed coupon of 100 basis points a year. The quoted CDS spread is 60 basis points. Which statement correctly describes the cash flows at the trade and afterwards?

options.text: The buyer pays the seller the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront, then pays 60 bp a year.
The seller pays the buyer the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront; afterwards the buyer pays the 100 bp coupon until maturity or a credit event.
No upfront payment is made because the quoted spread is below the coupon; the buyer pays 60 bp a year.
The buyer pays the seller the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront; afterwards the buyer pays the 100 bp coupon.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Who gets the better of the coupon**

Paying 100 bp a year for protection worth 60 bp overpays the seller by 40 bp a year.

**Step 2 – The upfront**

When the quoted spread is below the coupon, the seller pays the buyer the present value of the difference at the trade. After that the buyer pays the fixed coupon.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The upfront payment converts a standard coupon into a trade at the market spread: the side that gets the better of the coupon compensates the other.

**LO:** CR-9 g: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.4.3 The Use of Fixed Coupons

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.9, 9.4.3 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 g.5)

a.reason: Wrong payer, and after a fixed-coupon trade the running payment is the coupon, not the quoted spread.

c.reason: An upfront is needed whenever spread and coupon differ.

d.reason: Wrong direction: the buyer pays upfront only when the spread is above the coupon.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
questions.source: GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.20 (rewritten as multiple choice)
questions.question: A credit trainer tells a class: “The position of a buyer of a credit default swap is similar to the position of someone who is long a risk-free bond and short a corporate bond.” Which explanation of the statement is correct?

options.text: The buyer gains when the reference entity’s credit improves, as a holder of its bonds would.
The buyer pays the risk-free rate and receives the corporate yield, so the position earns the credit spread.
The statement is false: a CDS buyer has no exposure to the reference entity unless it also owns the entity’s bonds.

A corporate bond plus bought protection is approximately a risk-free bond, so bought protection is approximately a long risk-free bond plus a short corporate bond: the buyer gains as the issuer’s credit worsens and pays about the credit spread to hold the position.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The hedge**

Buying a corporate bond and buying protection on its issuer converts the bond, approximately, into a risk-free bond (GARP: a 7% bond with 200 bp protection earns about 5%).

**Step 2 – Rearrange**

Corporate bond $+ \text{protection} \approx$ risk-free bond, so protection $\approx\text{risk-free bond} -$ corporate bond.

⇒ A protection buyer is like someone long a risk-free bond and short a corporate bond: D.

**Interpretation**

Both positions gain when the issuer’s credit worsens and both cost roughly the credit spread to carry. This is also why the CDS spread should be close to the bond yield spread.

**LO:** CR-9 g: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller. • **Reference:** Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17 (GARP CR Ch.9), 9.4 and 9.5.1; Practice Question 9.20

**Source:** GARP book • Ch.9 Practice Question 9.20 (rewritten as multiple choice) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 g.6)

a.reason: Describes the seller (or a bondholder), who is long the credit.

b.reason: Earning the spread is the seller’s side; the buyer pays it.

c.reason: The buyer’s exposure comes from the contract itself; owning the bonds is not required.
