questions.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
questions.source: Workbook D14.1 • S1, S2, S3, S4 • Map #58
questions.question: A structured credit specialist at a German bank is training newly hired analysts on four instruments the bank uses to transfer or take credit risk. Which of the following statements should the specialist present as correct?

options.text: In a total return swap used to finance a bond purchase, the total return receiver retains ownership of the bond, and the spread over the floating rate compensates the receiver for the risk that the payer defaults.
In a credit default swap, the protection buyer must own bonds of the reference entity, as with an insurance contract, and receives the notional times one minus the auction price after a credit event.

In a synthetic CDO priced with the one-factor Gaussian copula, base correlation is the correlation that prices each individual tranche, while compound correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.
In a credit-linked note issued through an SPV, the investor pays the principal upfront and bears the credit risk of the assets sold to the SPV, with no credit linkage to the sponsoring entity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The CLN statement**

Choudhry (CR-23): “Unlike CLNs issued by originators direct, CLNs issued by SPVs do not have any credit-linkage to the sponsoring entity. The note is linked instead to assets that have been sold to the SPV, and its performance is dependent on the performance of these assets.” The note is funded: the investor’s principal is paid upfront and is repaid less credit losses, so the investor is the protection seller (outside-source for the funded mechanics).

⇒ D is correct: funded, investor bears the reference credit risk, and the SPV removes the sponsor’s own credit from the note.

**Interpretation**

The four instruments split cleanly by who funds and who holds the asset: a CLN investor funds and bears credit risk; a CDS seller bears credit risk unfunded; a TRS payer holds the bond and lays off its total return; a synthetic CDO tranche holder sells protection on a slice of a CDS portfolio. Each wrong option misplaces one of those attributions.

**LO:** CR-13 a: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO). CR-13 f: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach. CR-13 g: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation. CR-9 g: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25, 13.1, 13.7, 13.10; Choudhry, Ch.12 (CR-23), SPV applications

CR-12 • Credit Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D14.1 • S1, S2, S3, S4 • Map #58 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-9 g.7)

a.reason: Role misassignment: in Hull’s financing structure the payer buys and “retains ownership of the bond for the life of the swap”, and “the spread over the floating rate received by the payer is compensation for bearing the risk that the receiver will default”.

b.reason: Scope/condition error: the settlement clause is right, but ownership is not a condition. Hull: unlike an insurance contract, “in the case of a CDS, the underlying asset does not have to be owned”; CDS volume on a company can exceed its debt (Lehman).

c.reason: Sibling swap: compound (tranche) correlation is the $\rho$ that prices an individual tranche $\{a_{q-1}, a_{q}\}$; base correlation is the $\rho$ that prices the $\{0, a_{q}\}$ tranche. The definitions are reversed.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.1 (CVA and DVA)
questions.question:
A CVA analyst at a Swiss bank divides the next three years into annual intervals. The counterparty’s credit spreads, interpolated to the interval end points, and other inputs are:

| Maturity | 1 year | 2 years | 3 years |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit spread (bp) | 90 | 110 | 130 |

The expected recovery rate is 40% and the risk-free rate is 2.5% for all maturities. Following the method GARP sets out for CVA, which of the following is closest to $q_{3}$, the risk-neutral probability that the counterparty defaults during the third year?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Average hazard rates to each end point**

$$\bar{\lambda}(2) = \frac{0.0110}{0.60} = 1.8333\%, \bar{\lambda}(3) = \frac{0.0130}{0.60} = 2.1667\%$$

**Step 2 – Survival to the start and end of year 3**

$$V (2) = \text{e}^{-0.018333\times2} = 0.96400, V (3) = \text{e}^{-0.021667\times3} = 0.93707$$

**Step 3 – Interval PD**

$$q_{3} = V (2) - V (3) = 0.96400 - 0.93707 = 0.02693 = 2.69\%$$

⇒ Seen from today, a 2.69% chance that the counterparty defaults during year 3.

**Interpretation**

Each survival probability uses the average hazard rate for its own maturity, so a rising spread curve gives a forward hazard rate for year 3 of 3 × 2.1667% − 2 × 1.8333% = 2.83%, well above any of the average rates. The risk-free rate discounts the losses in the CVA sum; it does not enter $q_{3}$.

**LO:** CR-12 c: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.1 CVA and DVA

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.1 (CVA and DVA) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 c.3)

a.reason: Used the three-year average hazard for both end points: e$^{-0.021667\times2} - \text{e}^{-0.065} =$ 2.05%.

c.reason: Divided by survival to the start of year 3: 0.02693/0.96400 = 2.79%, the conditional PD (sibling swap).

d.reason: Reported the cumulative three-year PD: 1 − 0.93707 = 6.29%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.
questions.question:
A credit analyst at a Japanese life insurer is checking a colleague’s formula card, which gives the credit spread on zero-coupon debt as CS $= (1/T ) \text{ln}(D/F ) - R_{f}$ . The analyst applies the standard definition to an issuer whose only debt is a zero-coupon bond. Data (JPY billion, rates continuously compounded):

- Market value of the firm’s assets from a calibrated Merton model: 68.0
- Market value of equity: 24.5; equity volatility: 55%
- Face value of the zero-coupon bond: 50.0, maturing in 4 years
- Risk-free rate: 1.5% per annum

Which of the following is closest to the credit spread on the issuer’s debt?

options.text: −498 bps
198 bps
348 bps

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Market value of debt**

$$D_{t} = V_{0} - E_{0} = 68.0 - 24.5 = 43.5$$

⇒ Debt with a JPY 50.0 billion face value is worth JPY 43.5 billion today.

**Step 2 – Yield on the debt**

$D_{t} = F \text{e}^{-yT} \Rightarrow y = -\frac{1}{T}$ ln $\frac{D_{t}}{F} = -\frac{1}{4}$ ln $\frac{43.5}{50.0} = -\frac{1}{4}(-0.13926) = 0.03482$

⇒ The debt yields 3.48% per annum. The logarithm is negative because $D_{t} < F$ ; the leading minus sign turns it into a positive yield.

**Step 3 – Credit spread**

CS $= y - r = 0.03482 - 0.015 = 0.01982 \approx198$ bps

⇒ Investors demand 1.98% a year over the risk-free rate for this issuer’s default risk.

**Interpretation**

The promised payment is worth $50\text{e}^{-0.06} = 47.09$ risk-free, so the market charges (47.09 − 43.5)/47.09 = 7.6% of its value for expected default losses. The 198 bps spread is the rate that, added to $r$, discounts the promised JPY 50.0 billion back to its market value; it is the input a risk-neutral PD or CVA would use. Equity volatility is a red herring here: it calibrates $V_{0}$ and $\sigma_{V}$ but plays no role once the debt value is known.

**LO:** CR-12 c: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads. CR-9 l: Calculate the value of a firm’s debt and equity, the volatility of firm value, and the volatility of firm equity using the Merton model. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24, 12.1 Special Cases (eqs. 12.5, 12.6, Example 12.2); Hull, RMFI 6e, Ch.17, 9.5, 9.8, Problem 9.17

**Source:** Workbook D5.1 • S1 • Map #42 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 c.4)

a.reason: Used the card’s inverted sign: $\frac{1}{4} \text{ln}(0.87)-0.015 = -0.0348-0.015 = -0.0498$. A negative spread on risky debt is the polarity flip.

c.reason: Stopped at the intermediate result: 348 bps is the yield $y$, not the spread; the risk-free rate was not subtracted.

d.reason: Did not annualise: $- \text{ln}(0.87) - 0.015 = 0.1393 - 0.015 = 0.1243$. The 13.9% is a four-year cumulative log loss, not a per-annum yield.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.1 and Workbook D5 (one-period formula) • shape D5·S3
questions.question:
A fixed-income analyst at a Korean asset manager prices two one-year zero-coupon bonds issued by the same company. Each bond either repays its face value at maturity or defaults then, recovering a fixed fraction of face value. Valuation is risk-neutral with annual compounding, and the one-year risk-free rate is 3.0%.

| Bond | One-year yield | Expected recovery rate |
|---|---|---|
| Senior unsecured | 5.5% | 45% |
| Subordinated | ? | 15% |

Both bonds carry the same issuer default probability. Which of the following is closest to the yield at which the subordinated bond is priced consistently with the senior bond?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Expected loss rate on the senior bond**

PD $\times\text{LGD}_{sen} = 1 - \frac{1.03}{1.055} = 0.023697$

**Step 2 – Issuer PD**

PD $= \frac{0.023697}{0.55} = 0.043085$

⇒ A 4.31% risk-neutral probability that the issuer defaults within the year.

**Step 3 – Expected loss rate on the subordinated bond**

PD $\times\text{LGD}_{sub} = 0.043085 \times0.85 = 0.036622$

**Step 4 – Consistent yield**

$$\frac{1.03}{1 + y_{sub}} = 1 - 0.036622 \Longrightarrow y_{sub} = \frac{1.03}{0.963378} - 1 = 6.92\%$$

**Interpretation**

One default probability, two recoveries: the subordinated bond loses 85% instead of 55% in default, so its expected loss rate is 0.85/0.55 = 1.55 times the senior one, and its yield must rise to match. Spreads price expected loss, not PD.

**LO:** CR-12 c: Calculate the probability of default using credit spreads. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.1; Workbook D5 one-period formula (outside source)

CR-12 • Credit Risk • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.1 and Workbook D5 (one-period formula) • shape D5·S3 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 c.6)

a.reason: Ignored recovery and gave the subordinated bond the senior yield because the PD is the same.

b.reason: Used the shortcut PD $\approx(y - r_{f} )/(1 - R) = 4.545\%$ and a spread of 4.545% × 0.85 = 3.864%: 3% + 3.864% = 6.86%. The question specifies the exact one-period pricing.

d.reason: Divided by the recovery rate instead of LGD: PD = 0.023697/0.45 = 5.266%, then 1.03/(1 − 0.05266 × 0.85) − 1 = 7.83%.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.2 (Default Correlation)
questions.question: A credit strategist at a pension fund’s fixed-income team is preparing a briefing on default correlation for the investment committee. Which of the following statements should the strategist include?

options.text: Credit contagion, where one company’s default triggers another’s, reduces default correlation, because the surviving companies take over the defaulted company’s business.
In a reduced form model, perfectly correlated hazard rates for two companies make it highly likely that both default within the same short period.

Default correlation is the major reason that risk-neutral default probabilities are greater than real-world default probabilities, because correlated defaults create systematic risk that investors require compensation for.
Because default is rare, default correlation can be ignored in a well-diversified portfolio of investment-grade bonds without affecting the tail of the loss distribution.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Default correlation and risk-neutral PDs**

GARP: default correlation “means that credit risk cannot be completely diversified away and is the major reason why risk-neutral default probabilities are greater than real-world default probabilities”.

⇒ C is correct: correlated defaults are systematic risk, priced into spreads.

**Step 2 – Check the other claims**

Contagion is one of GARP’s three sources of default correlation. In reduced form models, “even when there is perfect correlation between the hazard rates of the two companies, the probability that they will both default during the same short period of time is usually very low”.

**Interpretation**

The gap between spread-implied and historical PDs (CR-9 j) is largest in relative terms for investment-grade names, exactly where correlated, systematic default risk dominates idiosyncratic risk.

**LO:** CR-12 e: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.2 Default Correlation

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.2 (Default Correlation) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 e.2)

a.reason: Polarity flip: contagion, one default causing another, is a reason default correlation exists; it increases it.

b.reason: True fact reversed: perfect hazard rate correlation still leaves joint default in a short period unlikely, which is the main weakness of reduced form models.

d.reason: Absolute claim: rarity does not make correlation negligible. Correlation drives the tail of the loss distribution, and diversification cannot remove the common component.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.3 (eq. 12.10, Example 12.5)
questions.question: A risk manager at a South African bank holds a ZAR 2,400 million portfolio of 8,000 similar small-business loans. The one-year probability of default averages 1.5%, the recovery rate averages 35%, and the copula correlation, estimated from the equity returns of listed peers, is 0.12. The CRO asks for the one-year 99.9% credit VaR, defined as the credit loss that the bank is 99.9% confident will not be exceeded, using the one-factor Gaussian copula. Which of the following is closest?

options.text: ZAR 101.3 million
ZAR 113.8 million
ZAR 164.7 million
ZAR 188.1 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Inputs to the worst case default rate**

$N^{-1}(0.015) = -2.1701$, $\sqrt{0.12} = 0.3464$, $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.0902$, $\sqrt{0.88} = 0.9381$.

**Step 2 – Worst case default rate**

$V (0.999, 1) = N (\frac{-2.1701 + 0.3464 \times3.0902}{0.9381}) = N (\frac{-1.0996}{0.9381}) = N (-1.1722) = 12.06\%$

⇒ In the 1-in-1,000 year, about 12% of the loans default, eight times the average.

**Step 3 – Credit VaR**

$2{,}400 \times(1 - 0.35) \times0.12056 = \text{ZAR} 188.1$ million

**Interpretation**

The number of loans is a red herring beyond confirming that the portfolio is large enough for the Vasicek approximation. The stem defines credit VaR as a loss quantile, so the expected loss of ZAR 23.4 million is not deducted.

**LO:** CR-12 g: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.3, eq. 12.10, Example 12.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.3 (eq. 12.10, Example 12.5) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 g.3)

a.reason: Used the recovery rate instead of LGD: 2,400 × 0.35 × 0.12056 = 101.3.

c.reason: Deducted the expected loss: 2,400 × 0.65 × (0.12056 − 0.015) = 164.7, which is unexpected loss, not the quantile the CRO defined.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.
questions.question: A credit risk analyst reproduces GARP’s Example 12.5: a USD 100 million retail portfolio, one-year PD 2%, recovery 60% and copula correlation 0.1, which gives a 99.9% worst case default rate (WCDR) of 12.8% and a credit VaR of USD 5.13 million. She then tests the sensitivity of the WCDR, changing one input at a time. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Raising the copula correlation from 0.1 to 0.2 lowers the WCDR, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.
Lowering the confidence level from 99.9% to 99% lowers the WCDR to about 8.2%.
Raising the recovery rate from 60% to 70% lowers the WCDR, because each default then costs less.
With a copula correlation of zero, the WCDR would still exceed the 2% PD, because the 99.9% confidence level always adds a tail term.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Confidence level**

At 99%, $N^{-1}(0.99) = 2.3263$: $V = N ((-2.0537+0.3162\times2.3263)/0.9487) = N (-1.3893) =$ 8.24%.

⇒ Lower confidence, smaller worst case: B is correct.

**Step 2 – Correlation and the zero-correlation limit**

With $\rho= 0.2$: $V = N ((-2.0537 + 0.4472 \times3.0902)/0.8944) = N (-0.7510) = 22.6\%$. With $\rho= 0$: $V = N (N^{-1}(0.02)) = 2\%$.

**Interpretation**

Only $Q$, $\rho$ and $X$ enter the WCDR. Recovery and portfolio size scale the credit VaR afterwards. Correlation is what turns a 2% average into a double-digit worst case: with independent defaults a large portfolio defaults at its average rate almost surely.

**LO:** CR-12 g: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24 (GARP CR Ch.12), 12.3, eq. 12.10, Example 12.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.12, 12.3 (Example 12.5) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-12 g.4)

a.reason: Polarity flip: higher correlation raises the WCDR, to 22.6%; clustering makes the bad years worse.

c.reason: Sibling swap: recovery lowers the credit VaR (to USD 3.85 million) but leaves the WCDR at 12.8%.

d.reason: With $\rho= 0$ the tail term vanishes and the WCDR equals the PD, 2%: the law of large numbers removes all uncertainty about the default rate.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO).
questions.source: New • built from Workbook D14 revision notes and GARP Ch.23, 23.1 (Choudhry, CLNs) • shape
questions.question:
D14·S1

A treasury analyst at a Malaysian insurer is offered a 5-year credit-linked note issued directly by Bank X and referencing Company Y. The insurer would pay USD 20 million at issue and receive a coupon of SOFR plus 180 basis points. Which of the following statements about the insurer’s position is correct?

options.text: The insurer is the protection buyer: if Y suffers a credit event, Bank X compensates the insurer for the loss on Y.
Like a seller of CDS protection, the insurer pays nothing at inception and pays cash only if Y suffers a credit event.

The insurer has sold protection on Y in funded form: after a credit event its principal is repaid less the loss on Y, and because Bank X issued the note directly the insurer is also exposed to Bank X’s own credit risk.
Because Bank X holds the insurer’s cash, the coupon spread compensates the insurer for Bank X’s credit risk only, and a credit event at Y would not reduce the redemption amount.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Funded protection**

The insurer pays USD 20 million at issue and is repaid less any credit loss on Y: it has sold protection on Y, and the spread in the coupon is its premium.

**Step 2 – The issuer’s credit**

Bank X holds the cash, so Bank X faces no counterparty risk on the protection. The insurer, by contrast, is repaid by Bank X: a note issued directly carries Bank X’s credit risk as well (an SPV issue would remove that link).

⇒ C is correct.

**Interpretation**

The CLN is the funded mirror of a CDS sale. The funding is what moves counterparty risk from the protection buyer to the investor.

**LO:** CR-13 a: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO). • **Reference:** Workbook D14 revision notes (CLN mechanics, outside source); Choudhry (GARP CR Ch.23), 23.1 SPV applications

CR-13 • Credit Derivatives • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from Workbook D14 revision notes and GARP Ch.23, 23.1 (Choudhry, CLNs) • shape (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-13 a.8)

a.reason: Role flip: the note investor is the protection seller and loses on a credit event at Y.

b.reason: That describes an unfunded CDS sale; a CLN is funded at issue.

d.reason: The redemption amount is reduced by credit losses on the reference entity; that is the credit link.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.2 (Recovery Rate, Binary CDS)
questions.question: A CDS desk at a Brazilian bank values protection on a corporate. It implies a constant hazard rate from the corporate’s CDS quotes using a 40% recovery rate, then uses the same 40% to value its trades. A junior analyst lists four claims about the valuation. Which claim is correct?

options.text: Leaving out the accrual payment on default lowers the breakeven spread, because the buyer is then assumed to pay less.

Re-running the valuation of a regular CDS with a 20% recovery rate, re-implying the hazard rate from the same quotes, changes its value very little; a binary CDS on the same name is far more sensitive to the assumption.
A binary CDS on the same name should trade at a lower spread than the regular CDS, because its payoff is fixed in advance.
The expected premium payments are weighted by the probability of default in each year, and the expected payoff by the probability of survival to each payment date.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recovery and a regular CDS**

If the hazard rate is implied from market spreads with recovery $R$, the implied PDs scale roughly with $1/(1-R)$ while the payoff scales with $1-R$. In GARP’s example, re-implying with $R = 20\%$ instead of 40% moves the value of a 150 bp deal from 0.0111 to 0.0112 per \$1.

**Step 2 – Recovery and a binary CDS**

A binary CDS pays the full notional, so its payoff does not shrink as $R$ falls while the implied PDs do: its spread falls from 205 bp to about 154 bp.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

GARP’s point: the value of a regular CDS is not very sensitive to the recovery rate as long as the same $R$ is used to imply the default probabilities; a binary CDS is.

**LO:** CR-13 b: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.2, Recovery Rate and Binary Credit Default Swaps

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.2 (Recovery Rate, Binary CDS) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-13 b.6)

a.reason: Polarity flip: without $B$ the denominator of $s = C/(A + B)$ shrinks, so the spread rises (2.02% against 1.99% in Vardeez’s example).

c.reason: A binary CDS pays more on default (all of the notional rather than $1 - R$ of it), so it costs more: 205 bp against 123 bp.

d.reason: Weights swapped: premiums are weighted by survival, the payoff by default probabilities.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.2 (Marking to Market a CDS)
questions.question: Two years ago a hedge fund bought 5-year protection on a retailer at 180 basis points. The retailer’s 3-year CDS spread is now 240 basis points. The fund’s risk system values the position by the standard method of GARP Section 13.2. Which of the following describes the value of the position to the fund?

options.text: Negative: the fund pays 180 bp for protection now worth 240 bp, so it would have to pay the seller to close out.
Zero: a CDS is revalued at zero after inception because its spread is reset to the market level.
Positive, equal to the present value of the expected payoff, $C$, computed with today’s hazard rate.
Positive, equal to 60 bp times $A+B$, the present value of the premium and accrual payments per unit of spread, computed with risk-neutral probabilities implied from today’s spreads.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Value to the protection buyer**

The buyer receives the protection leg and pays the deal spread: value $= C - s_{\text{deal}}(A + B)$, with $A$, $B$ and $C$ computed from today’s risk-neutral probabilities for the remaining three years.

**Step 2 – Use the market spread**

Today’s 3-year spread satisfies $C = s_{\text{mkt}}(A + B)$, so the value is $(s_{\text{mkt}} - s_{\text{deal}})(A + B) =$ $(0.0240 - 0.0180)(A + B)$.

⇒ Positive: spreads have widened, so the fund’s old protection is cheap.

**Interpretation**

The mark-to-market is the spread difference times a risky annuity (the PV of the premium and accrual payments per unit of spread). Schweser’s quiz version computes it for a given $C$; the exam usually asks only for the sign or the structure.

**LO:** CR-13 b: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.2, Marking to Market a CDS

CR-13 • Credit Derivatives • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.2 (Marking to Market a CDS) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-13 b.7)

a.reason: Polarity flip: paying 180 bp for protection now worth 240 bp is a gain for the buyer; it is the seller who would pay to close out.

b.reason: A CDS is worth zero only at inception; its spread is fixed for the life of the contract.

c.reason: Ignores the premiums still to be paid: the value is $C$ minus $s_{\text{deal}}(A + B)$, not $C$ alone.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.9 and Practice Question 13.26
questions.question: A structured credit analyst at a French bank prices the standard iTraxx Europe tranches with the one-factor Gaussian copula, keeping the index spread, recovery rate and hazard rate fixed. She raises the copula correlation from 0.10 to 0.30. Which of the following describes the effect on the tranches?

options.text: All tranche spreads rise, because higher correlation raises each company’s probability of default.
The equity tranche becomes riskier and the senior tranches safer, because defaults become more frequent in every scenario.
The equity tranche becomes less risky and the senior tranches riskier, so the equity tranche’s price for protection falls and the senior tranche spreads rise; the index spread is unchanged.
No tranche price changes, because the expected loss on the whole portfolio does not depend on correlation.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What correlation changes**

Each name keeps the same hazard rate, so the portfolio’s expected loss and the index spread are unchanged. Correlation changes how defaults cluster: few defaults and many defaults both become more likely.

**Step 2 – Effect by tranche**

More scenarios with few defaults protect the equity tranche; more scenarios with many defaults reach the senior tranches. With the January 2007 inputs (index 23 bp), the standard market model gives an equity upfront of 13.3% at $\rho= 0.10$ and 5.5% at $\rho= 0.30$, while the 12 to 22% spread rises from about 0 to 5 bp.

⇒ The equity tranche becomes less risky, the senior tranches riskier.

**Interpretation**

This is why tranche quotes carry information about correlation, and why a single implied correlation can be backed out of each tranche price (CR-13 g).

**LO:** CR-13 f: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach. • **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.9 Role of Correlation in a Basket CDS and CDO; Practice Question 13.26

CR-13 • Credit Derivatives • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.9 and Practice Question 13.26 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-13 f.6)

a.reason: Correlation does not change each name’s PD; it redistributes losses between tranches.

b.reason: Polarity flip: the equity tranche gains from clustering and the senior tranches lose.

d.reason: The expected portfolio loss is unchanged, but its distribution across the tranches changes.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.10 (Implied Correlation, Table 13.8)
questions.question:
A correlation trader at a London bank reviews GARP’s implied correlations for 5-year iTraxx Europe tranches on 31 January 2007:

| Detachment point | 3% | 6% | 9% | 12% | 22% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compound correlation | 17.7% | 7.8% | 14.0% | 18.2% | 23.3% |
| Base correlation | 17.7% | 28.4% | 36.5% | 43.2% | 60.5% |

Which statement is correct?

options.text: The base correlations form a smile: they fall from the equity tranche to the 0 to 6% tranche and then rise.
The 0 to 6% tranche has a base correlation of 7.8%, the lowest in the capital structure.
The market is pricing every tranche with the one-factor Gaussian copula and a single correlation of about 18%, the equity tranche’s correlation.

The compound correlations form a smile, lowest for the 3 to 6% tranche, while the base correlations rise steadily with the detachment point; the two coincide at 3%, where the tranche is both a single tranche and a base tranche.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the compound row**

17.7%, then 7.8% for 3 to 6%, then rising to 23.3%: down then up, a smile with its low point at the mezzanine tranche.

**Step 2 – Read the base row**

17.7%, 28.4%, 36.5%, 43.2%, 60.5%: rising with the detachment point, a skew. At 3% the tranche {0, 3%} is both the first tranche and a base tranche, so both measures are 17.7%.

⇒ D is correct.

**Interpretation**

GARP: the compound correlations exhibit a “correlation smile” and the base correlations a “correlation skew”. Both would be flat if the market priced with the model.

**LO:** CR-13 g: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.

- **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.10, Implied Correlation, Table 13.8

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.10 (Implied Correlation, Table 13.8) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-13 g.5)

a.reason: Shapes swapped: the base correlations rise throughout; the smile belongs to the compound row.

b.reason: 7.8% is the compound correlation of the 3 to 6% tranche; the base correlation for 0 to 6% is 28.4%.

c.reason: A single correlation would make both rows flat; the patterns show the market is not pricing with one correlation.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.10 (Valuing Nonstandard Tranches)
questions.question: A dealer is asked to quote the 4 to 8% tranche of iTraxx Europe, which is not one of the standard tranches. Market quotes exist for all the standard tranches. Which approach does GARP describe as the better one?

options.text: Interpolate the PV of expected loss on the 0 to $X$% tranche across the standard detachment points to estimate it for 0 to 4% and 0 to 8%; take the difference as the expected loss on the 4 to 8% tranche, then imply its compound correlation and breakeven spread.
Average the compound correlations of the 3 to 6% and 6 to 9% tranches and use the result as the 4 to 8% tranche’s correlation.
Interpolate base correlations at 4% and 8% and use them directly, because interpolated base correlations always satisfy the no-arbitrage condition on expected losses.
Quote the index spread for the 4 to 8% tranche, because a tranche straddling two standard tranches has the same risk as the index.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The traditional approach and its flaw**

Interpolating base correlations to 0 to 4% and 0 to 8% and computing expected losses from them often violates the no-arbitrage condition: the PV of expected loss on $\{0, X\}$ must increase with $X$ at a decreasing rate. The base correlation is a nonlinear function of that expected loss.

**Step 2 – The better approach**

Compute the expected loss on each standard $\{0, X\}$ tranche, interpolate the expected losses directly (which can be done so as to respect the condition), take the 0 to 8% minus the 0 to 4% value, then imply a compound correlation and breakeven spread.

⇒ A is the approach GARP prefers.

**Interpretation**

Interpolate the quantity that carries the economics (expected loss), not the model parameter that maps to it nonlinearly.

**LO:** CR-13 g: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.

- **Reference:** Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.25 (GARP CR Ch.13), 13.10, Valuing Nonstandard Tranches

CR-14 • Derivatives • Vardeez: NOT SO IMP

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.13, 13.10 (Valuing Nonstandard Tranches) (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-13 g.6)

b.reason: Averaging compound correlations of tranches with different attachment points has no pricing basis, and compound correlations are not monotonic.

c.reason: Absolute qualifier reversed: GARP says interpolated base correlations often fail the no-arbitrage condition.

d.reason: The index spread prices protection on the whole portfolio; a mezzanine tranche has a very different risk.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify and describe institutions that take on significant counterparty risk.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.1.4 and Figure 15.4
questions.question:
The head of counterparty risk at a UK bank is reviewing the following CVA breakdown, taken from GARP’s example (Royal Bank of Scotland annual report, GBP millions):

| Rating | 2016 | 2015 | Counterparty type | 2016 | 2015 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AAA | 4 | 37 | Banks | 22 | 18 |
| AA to AA+ | 22 | 66 | Other financial institutions | 70 | 126 |
| A to AA− | 52 | 49 | Corporate | 337 | 470 |
| BBB$- \text{to A}-$ | 388 | 293 | Government | 189 | 160 |
| Non-investment grade and unrated | 152 | 329 |  |  |  |
| Total | 618 | 774 | Total | 618 | 774 |

Which of the following conclusions about the 2016 figures is most consistent with the breakdown and with GARP’s explanation of it?

options.text: The largest share of CVA comes from non-investment-grade and unrated names, because their default probabilities are the highest.
Bank counterparties contribute little CVA because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.
The largest share of CVA comes from BBB$- \text{to A}-$ names and from corporates and governments, most of which trade uncollateralised.
AAA names contribute a material share of CVA because their low default probability allows large uncollateralised exposures.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Shares by rating (2016)**

BBB$- \text{to A}-$: 388/618 = 62.8%. Non-investment grade and unrated: 152/618 = 24.6%. AAA: 4/618 = 0.6%.

⇒ Medium ratings carry the majority.

**Step 2 – Shares by counterparty type (2016)**

Corporates and governments: (337 + 189)/618 = 526/618 = 85.1%. Banks: 22/618 = 3.6%.

**Step 3 – GARP’s explanation**

High-quality credits have low default probabilities; banks and other financial institutions have relatively good credit quality and are mostly collateralised; corporates and governments are mostly uncollateralised; banks are partly reluctant to trade with non-investment-grade names.

**Interpretation**

CVA needs exposure as well as default probability. The names a bank trades most with, without collateral, dominate. The 2015 column is a red herring for the 2016 question, and a warning: in 2015 the non-investment-grade bucket (329 of 774, 42.5%) was the largest rating bucket.

**LO:** CR-15 c: Identify and describe institutions that take on significant counterparty risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.1.4 Product Type, Figure 15.4

CR-15 • Counterparty Risk and Beyond • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.1.4 and Figure 15.4 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 c.6)

a.reason: In 2016 non-investment grade is 152, well below the 388 for BBB$- \text{to A}-$; GARP attributes the gap to reluctance to trade with such names.

b.reason: Banks contribute little, but because of good credit quality and collateralisation, not an exemption from collateral.

d.reason: AAA contributes GBP 4m, under 1%: a low default probability means a small CVA.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
questions.question: The credit risk department of a bank controls its exposure to a corporate counterparty with a PFE-based limit structure: a soft limit of USD 10 million and a hard limit of USD 15 million, both stepping down for later time horizons. Which of the following practices is consistent with GARP’s description of credit limits?

options.text: A rise in PFE to USD 12 million caused purely by market moves breaches the soft limit but does not by itself force trades to be unwound, whereas a breach of the hard limit requires remedial action.
A proposed trade is compared with the remaining headroom using its standalone PFE, since netting with existing trades is captured only in CVA.
The limits should step up at longer horizons, because exposures on most derivatives grow with maturity.
Because the soft limit can be breached by market moves, new trades that take PFE above USD 10 million at a future date can be booked without approval.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Two ways to breach**

A new trade that would breach a limit is refused unless escalated. A breach caused by market moves is handled through soft and hard limits.

**Step 2 – Soft against hard**

GARP: a soft limit “may be breached through market movements (but not new transactions)”, while a breach of the hard limit requires remedial action (unwind, restructure or hedge); its example is USD 10m soft and USD 15m hard.

⇒ A describes exactly this.

**Interpretation**

Figure 5 shows the logic: the proposed trade breaches the soft limit in years 2 to 3 and is refused, while the existing portfolio could drift up to the hard limit on market moves.

**LO:** CR-15 e: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.1.5 Credit Limits, Figure 15.5

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.1.5 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 e.5)

b.reason: The incremental PFE (after minus before) is what counts, and it is smaller than the standalone PFE because of portfolio effects.

c.reason: Polarity flip: limits are often reduced over time, because credit quality may deteriorate over long horizons.

d.reason: New trades that would breach the limit at any future point are refused unless specifically approved.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
questions.question: A bank’s valuation committee is reviewing why its CVA methodology moved from historical default probabilities to market-implied ones. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Under the actuarial approach, CVA is the cost of a hedging strategy built from CDS spreads, so it already uses market-implied default probabilities.
European banks reporting under IAS 39 were the early adopters of risk-neutral CVA, while US banks under FAS 157 kept actuarial reserves until IFRS 13 forced convergence.
Regulators generally accept CVA models based on expected loss from historical default rates, provided the risk premium is excluded.
The exit-price concept in FAS 157 and IFRS 13 points to risk-neutral default probabilities, and Basel III also defines CVA with respect to credit spreads, although Basel III does not permit DVA.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Accounting**

FAS 157 and IFRS 13 reference an exit price, which implies risk-neutral default probabilities (and recognition of DVA).

**Step 2 – Regulation**

Basel III defines CVA with respect to credit spreads, so it also points to risk-neutral CVA, but it does not permit DVA: a conflict with accounting.

⇒ D is accurate.

**Interpretation**

Market practice and local regulators pushed the same way; historical default probabilities are now uncommon in CVA.

**LO:** CR-15 e: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.1.7 What Does CVA Represent?

CR-15 • Counterparty Risk and Beyond • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.1.7 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 e.6)

a.reason: Reverses the definitions: the hedging-cost view is risk-neutral; the actuarial view is an expected value with a risk premium.

b.reason: Reversed: US and Canadian banks under FAS 157 adopted early; many European banks under IAS 39 used actuarial CVA.

c.reason: Regulators say models “based on expected loss or historical calculations ignoring risk premia” are not acceptable.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a bank is explaining to the derivatives desk how funding and collateral costs arise. Ignoring initial margin and capital, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A collateralised trade on which the bank makes an upfront payment needs funding just like an uncollateralised one, because margin never offsets an upfront payment.
Receiving government bonds instead of cash as collateral removes all funding and collateral costs, because bonds can always be converted to cash at no cost.
Funding costs are fully objective inputs, because the bank can read them from its bond spreads for any maturity it chooses.
An uncollateralised trade on which the bank makes an upfront payment must be funded, for example by issuing a bond, because the cash flows that repay it arrive later.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – GARP’s funding example**

An uncollateralised trade with an upfront cash payment must be funded, perhaps by issuing a bond, because the offsetting cash flows arrive later; lenders require compensation for that.

**Step 2 – The collateralised version**

With collateral, the margin offsets the upfront payment, so the funding need disappears (initial margin excepted).

**Interpretation**

Funding, collateral and capital costs are, like credit spreads, hard to assess, and they are key inputs to xVA (CR-15 h).

**LO:** CR-15 g: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.3.6 Funding, Collateral, and Capital Costs

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.3.6 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 g.5)

a.reason: Polarity flip: in a collateralised trade the margin offsets the payment.

b.reason: A repo rate defines the cost of converting bonds into cash; the collateral type changes the cost, it does not remove it.

c.reason: Some inputs are subjective, such as the maturity of funding a trade needs and the dividends shareholders will require.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
questions.question: Two banks trade a swap on which both must hold regulatory capital and post initial margin. A trainee claims that every xVA cost borne by one bank is an equal and opposite benefit to the other. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: The trainee is right for every term, because one party’s positive value is always the other’s negative value.
The trainee is wrong for every term, because CVA and DVA are costs to both parties.
The trainee is right for CVA and DVA, since one party’s CVA cost is the other’s DVA benefit, but wrong for capital and initial margin, which are costs to both parties with no offsetting benefit.
The trainee is right for capital, because one bank’s regulatory capital charge is released as capital relief at its counterparty.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the symmetry holds**

One party’s positive value is the other’s negative value, so one party’s CVA cost is the other’s DVA benefit.

**Step 2 – Where it breaks**

GARP: capital and initial margin costs “are always present and do not provide an equal and opposite benefit to the counterparties”. Both banks pay them.

**Interpretation**

That is why KVA and MVA are always costs in the xVA sign table, while CVA and DVA, and the funding terms, can mirror each other (CR-15 h).

**LO:** CR-15 g: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.2.2

CR-15 • Counterparty Risk and Beyond • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.2.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 g.6)

a.reason: Ignores the asymmetric terms, capital and initial margin.

b.reason: DVA is a benefit to the party whose own default it reflects.

d.reason: Each bank’s capital is set by its own regulator on its own exposure; there is no mirror relief.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.3.1 and Table 15.1
questions.question: An xVA analyst is documenting, for each valuation adjustment, its market component and its cost component, as in GARP Table 15.1. Which of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: CVA: credit exposure as the market component and the institution’s funding cost as the cost component.
MVA: the initial margin amount as the market component and the cost of capital as the cost component.
KVA: the valuation as the market component and the counterparty’s default probability as the cost component.
FVA: the valuation (funding position) as the market component and the funding cost as the cost component.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The structure**

Each xVA term is a market component (from the valuation) combined with a cost component (the cost of bearing it).

**Step 2 – Table 15.1**

CVA/DVA: credit exposure and default probability. FVA: valuation and funding cost. MVA: initial margin amount and funding cost. ColVA: collateral amount and collateral cost. KVA: capital amount and capital cost.

⇒ D is correct.

**Interpretation**

The valuation is the funding position: an asset if positive, a liability if negative, which is why FVA can be a cost or a benefit.

**LO:** CR-15 h: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.3.1 Overview, Table 15.1

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.3.1 and Table 15.1 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 h.5)

a.reason: CVA’s cost component is the default probability, not funding.

b.reason: MVA’s cost component is the funding cost of the margin, not the cost of capital.

c.reason: KVA pairs the capital amount with the cost of capital.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.2.3 and 15.3.2
questions.question: The head of an xVA desk is reviewing a junior quant’s summary of the framework. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Every cost belongs to exactly one xVA term, so the terms can always be added without double counting.
Since own-default risk is widely seen as a funding benefit, DVA and the funding benefit adjustment (FBA) can overlap, so adding both may double count.
xVA terms are computed from the final, fully adjusted valuation, so adding them linearly to a base value involves no approximation.
In GARP’s convention for plotting xVA profiles, benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Overlaps**

GARP: there are potential overlaps between the terms, “for example, between DVA and FBA, where own-default risk is widely seen as a funding benefit”; and since collateral must be funded, some costs could be defined as either FVA or ColVA.

**Step 2 – The other statements**

The valuation is an input to the adjustments while the correct valuation should include them: the linear approach is an approximation. GARP’s profile charts put costs on the positive axis.

**Interpretation**

Before adding up an xVA stack, check that DVA and FBA are not both claiming the same own-credit benefit.

**LO:** CR-15 h: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.3 (GARP CR Ch.15), 15.2.3 and 15.3.2

CR-18 • Central Clearing • Vardeez: MODERATE

**Source:** New • built from GARP Ch.15, 15.2.3 and 15.3.2 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-15 h.6)

a.reason: The definitions overlap, so blind addition can double count.

c.reason: The problem is non-linear and recursive; the linear approach is only an approximation.

d.reason: Reversed: costs are positive and benefits negative in GARP’s profile convention.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall.
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the default rules of a European CCP on behalf of a clearing member. In a fire drill, one clearing member defaults, and the macro-hedging and auction of its portfolio cost EUR 900 million. The resources in the CCP’s rule book are:

- Initial margin posted by the defaulter: EUR 500 million
- Default fund contribution of the defaulter: EUR 80 million
- CCP skin-in-the-game: EUR 50 million
- Default fund contributions of the surviving members: EUR 920 million
- Initial margin posted by the surviving members: EUR 6,400 million

Which of the following statements is correct for the consultant to include in the report?

options.text: The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb EUR 320 million, because the CCP’s skin-in-the-game ranks after the mutualised default fund.
The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb nothing, because the surviving members’ initial margin is applied before the mutualised default fund.
The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb EUR 270 million, shared only among the members that held trades with the defaulter.
The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb EUR 270 million, and none of the surviving members’ initial margin is used.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Defaulter pays: initial margin, then its own default fund contribution**

900 − 500 = 400, 400 − 80 = 320

⇒ After the defaulter’s own resources, EUR 320 million of loss remains.

**Step 2 – CCP skin-in-the-game**

320 − 50 = 270

⇒ The CCP’s equity takes the next EUR 50 million, which gives it an incentive to manage defaults well.

**Step 3 – Survivors pay: mutualised default fund**

270 ≤ 920 ⇒ survivors’ default fund absorbs EUR 270 million; nothing reaches assessments

⇒ About 29% of the survivors’ contributions are consumed, so the CCP may invoke a capped recapitalisation, but no further layer is needed to absorb this default.

**Interpretation**

The order is defaulter’s initial margin, defaulter’s default fund contribution, CCP skin-in-the-game, survivors’ default fund, then assessments and other loss allocation. The EUR 6,400 million of surviving members’ initial margin is a red herring: Gregory notes that none of the loss allocation methods lets a CCP use the initial margin of non-defaulting members (EMIR Article 45(4)), which is why initial margin is “in theory” risk free to the poster. The clearing member’s real exposure is its share of the EUR 270 million plus any assessment or other allocation.

**LO:** CR-18 f: Provide examples of a loss waterfall. CR-18 g: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.8, 18.3 The Loss Waterfall, Figure 18.9; 18.2 Margin and Default Funds

CR-19 • Future Value and Exposure • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Workbook D24.1 • S1 • Map #59 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-18 f.6)

a.reason: Sequence swap: moved skin-in-the-game below the mutualised fund, so the survivors absorb 900 − 500 − 80 = 320. In Figure 18.9 skin-in-the-game ranks immediately after the defaulter-pays resources.

b.reason: Role misassignment: survivors’ initial margin is not in the waterfall; only the defaulter’s initial margin is. Survivors pay through their default fund contributions.

c.reason: Scope error: correct amount, but mutualisation does not depend on trading with the defaulter. A member “can suffer default losses even if it never traded with the defaulted counterparty”, has no net position with the CCP, or has a position in the same direction.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
questions.source: Workbook C8.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #37
questions.question:
A counterparty risk analyst at a Canadian bank is estimating exposure metrics to a pension fund counterparty at the six-month horizon. The bank has two trades with the fund:

- A receive-fixed interest rate swap.
- A one-year European put on an equity index that the bank sold to the fund on 20,000 units, premium received in full at inception. Inputs: index level 4,000; strike 3,800; implied volatility 20%; risk-free rate 3%. Black-Scholes value today: CAD 3.5 million.

The two trades were booked under different master agreements, and legal counsel has confirmed that close-out netting between them is not enforceable. The bank’s simulation produces five equally likely scenarios for the value of each trade to the bank in six months (CAD million):

| Scenario | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Swap | 18.0 | 9.0 | 3.0 | −6.0 | −14.0 |
| Sold put | −0.5 | −1.0 | −2.0 | −4.5 | −9.0 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s expected positive exposure (EPE) to the fund and the expected future value (EFV) of the two trades at the six-month horizon?

options.text: EPE CAD 2.5 million; EFV CAD −1.4 million
EPE CAD 5.3 million; EFV CAD −1.4 million
EPE CAD 6.0 million; EFV CAD 2.0 million
EPE CAD 6.0 million; EFV CAD −1.4 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Decide the aggregation level**

Netting is not enforceable, so each trade is its own netting set. Exposure is computed trade by trade with max$(\text{value}, 0)$ and then summed.

⇒ The two trades cannot offset one another in a default; the bank would have to pay the put’s value in full while claiming the swap’s value as an unsecured creditor.

**Step 2 – Swap EPE**

EPE$_{\text{swap}} = \frac{1}{5}(18 + 9 + 3 + 0 + 0) = \frac{30}{5} = 6.0$

⇒ Negative scenarios count as zero but stay in the denominator: on average CAD 6.0 million is at risk from the swap.

**Step 3 – Sold put EPE**

EPE$_{\text{put}} = \frac{1}{5}(0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0) = 0$

⇒ Every value to the bank is negative or zero: having received the premium, the bank is owed nothing by the fund, so the put adds no exposure. The index level, strike, volatility and the CAD 3.5 million Black-Scholes value price the option but are irrelevant to the seller’s exposure.

**Step 4 – Total EPE**

EPE = 6.0 + 0 = 6.0

**Step 5 – EFV (additive, includes every value)**

EFV$_{\text{swap}} = \frac{18 + 9 + 3 - 6 - 14}{5} = 2.0, \text{EFV}_{\text{put}} = \frac{-0.5 - 1.0 - 2.0 - 4.5 - 9.0}{5} = -3.4$ EFV = 2.0 − 3.4 = −1.4

⇒ The two trades are expected to be worth CAD 1.4 million against the bank in six months, yet the bank still has CAD 6.0 million of expected positive exposure.

**Interpretation**

EFV and EPE answer different questions. EFV is the average of all values and is additive, so the sold put pulls it negative. EPE keeps only what the counterparty would owe the bank, so the sold put contributes nothing to it and, without enforceable netting, cannot reduce the swap’s exposure either. The CVA desk should price CAD 6.0 million of EPE, and the legal team’s view on netting is worth CAD 0.7 million of EPE here.

**LO:** CR-19 a: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure. CR-19 f: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values. CR-12 a: Assess the credit risks of derivatives. • **Reference:** Gregory, The xVA Challenge 4e, Ch.11, 19.1.1, 19.1.5, 19.3.1, Tables 19.1 and 19.2; Hull, OFOD 11e, Ch.24, 12.1

**Source:** Workbook C8.1 • S1, S2, S3 • Map #37 (Credit Risk Workbook, Question CR-19 a.5)

a.reason: Red herring used as an offset: subtracted the sold put’s Black-Scholes value from the swap EPE, 6.0 − 3.5 = 2.5. Today’s option value is neither an exposure nor a netting offset.

b.reason: Assumed netting where none is enforceable: summed values scenario by scenario, 17.5, 8.0, 1.0, −10.5, −23.0, giving EPE (17.5 + 8.0 + 1.0)/5 = 5.3. This is the netted EPE (a netting factor below 1), not the exposure the bank actually has.

c.reason: Correct EPE, but dropped the sold put from EFV because it has zero exposure, reporting only the swap’s EFV of 2.0. Zero exposure does not mean zero value; EFV averages all values.

questions.subject: Credit Risk
questions.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.23, 23.1 Example 23.1; Schweser LO 41.c
questions.question: A UK card issuer that brings a credit card ABS to market several times a year is choosing the legal form of its issuing vehicle. Its US counsel recommends a trust arrangement; its London counsel says a company incorporated in Jersey would serve. Which of the following statements about the two forms is correct?

options.text: A company SPV is the usual form in the US market, because US accounting rules are satisfied by a single entity that issues notes directly against its assets.
Choosing the trust form removes the need for a true sale, because the trustee then holds the receivables on behalf of the originator.
A company SPV cannot be bankruptcy remote, so investors in its notes keep a claim on the originator if the receivables underperform.
In the trust arrangement the receivables are sold to a master trust that deposits them in a grantor trust; the notes rest on a beneficial interest, which further distances the originator.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Both forms are SPVs**

GARP: “An SPV is a legal trust or company” that is not linked to the originator and is bankruptcy remote. A company SPV can be bankruptcy remote just as a trust can.

⇒ C fails.

**Step 2 – Where each form is used**

The trust “is more common in the US market, and its interests are represented by a Trustee”; in the Euromarkets SPVs “are often incorporated as companies”. Schweser: the company form may not distance the originator enough for US accounting purposes.

⇒ A swaps the geography.

**Step 3 – What the trust arrangement adds**

The originator sells the receivables to a master trust (SPV 1), which deposits them in a grantor trust (SPV 2) and receives a beneficial interest. The notes are backed by that beneficial claim, which further distances the originator from the assets (Figure 1).

⇒ D is correct. A true sale is still needed (B fails), and the trustee acts for the investors, not the originator.

**Interpretation**

For a card issuer that comes to market several times a year, the trust form also carries the master trust structure, which issues series after series from one pool of receivables.

a.reason: Geography swap: the single-entity company form is the Euromarkets choice; US practice favours the trust because the company may not give enough distance for accounting purposes.

b.reason: A trust is still an SPV that must buy the assets in a true sale; the trustee represents the investors’ interests.

c.reason: Absolute qualifier: GARP defines an SPV, company or trust, as bankruptcy remote from the sponsor.
